#5594. ‘Home Is Where You Spend’: How Your Neighborhood Shapes Your Buying Habits

Your home isn't just where you live; it's also where you spend the majority of your money, a new study from financial technology platform Bilt has found.

Bilt partnered with 451 Research and S&P Global on the 2026 State of the Neighborhood survey, aimed at exploring consumer spending habits as it doubles down on American business with the launch of Bilt Neighborhood OS and the expansion of its membership platform.

Bilt Neighborhood OS is an AI operating system and commerce network designed to unlock America's $6.6 trillion neighborhood commerce opportunity to help businesses grow without replacing their existing systems, the company says.

In the consumer spending survey, around two-thirds of the 6,951 survey participants conducted at least 80% of their "everyday spending" within 15 miles of their homes, and 92% of those surveyed planned on spending the same or more at local businesses in the coming months.

That's not surprising, given the results of a recent Re/Max survey, which found that 29% of prospective homeowners valued proximity to grocery stores and shopping, while 20% said they valued having restaurants and cafes nearby.

More than half of all survey respondents said future neighborhood development, including new housing or retail development, was "very important" to how they chose where to buy a home.

The results of the Bilt survey spell good news for small businesses in popular residential areas, suggesting that physical stores close to dense residential neighborhoods may continue to thrive in the age of online shopping.

"The disconnect between what people talk about versus where people actually spend is quite significant," Ankur Jain, founder and CEO of Bilt, tells Realtor.com®. "When you you look at the stats, all online shopping in the U.S. is $1.3 trillion a year. But offline, small- and medium-business local retail and food spending is $6.6 trillion."

On a quarterly basis, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, that broke down to $340.2 billion in online spending in the second quarter, making up 17.1% of total consumer spending.

Bilt's study found that 70% of food and grocery spending is still made in person.

Consumers spent an average of $375 on in-person grocery shopping each month. They spent an additional $175 on in-person dining and takeout and another $175 on in-person general shopping. Study participants reported spending an average of $50 each on entertainment and recreation; health and personal care; and transportation.

Sixty-six percent of survey respondents said they were were actively looking to support local businesses over big-box and online retailers and were willing to spend more to support them.

A recent report on consumer spending habits around the holidays from research firm Epsilon found that Gen Z in particular values in-store options for gift shopping. And while online shopping is still, overall, the preferred method for gift shopping, the study found that consumers across all generatios are doing the majority of their food and decoration shopping in person. Furthermore, they spent about an equal amount of their holiday clothing budgets online and in store.

One possible reason for the continued primacy of in-person shopping is consumers' paradoxical relationship with artificial intelligence marketing.

Research from McKinsey found that AI continues to drive sales and that AI usage in completing purchases climbed 70% year over year. However, younger, more tech-native shoppers "tend to be more skeptical of AI on average," the report found. (Sixty-seven percent of American Gen Z AI users trust AI chat and search tools versus the global average of 73%.)

The study was conducted in advance of Bilt launching its new offerings. Alongside Bilt Neighborhood OS, the Bilt Membership Platform is an expansion of the company's existing membership and loyalty technology. The company says it will enable organizations to launch their own branded membership programs via white-labeling or extend existing loyalty programs into the neighborhood.

"We are betting pretty big on the neighborhood versus online commerce," Jain says. "There is a huge gap between what the media and the Silicon Valley world talk about versus how real Americans are living. People talk about AI as 'How are we going to do online commerce AI and replace coding and jobs and all this stuff.'

"The truth is, the biggest beneficiaries of AI can be the local mom and pop businesses who don't have the ability to hire 2,000 people to go compete with, like, a Walmart or Amazon online.

"Everything is tied together. The more you can invest in the neighborhood, the more value you create in the housing. The more housing you have, the more you can invest in the neighborhood," he adds.

Bilt also announced a coalition of partners spanning payments, point-of-sale technology, reservations, and commerce platforms. Partners include Altamarea Group, AM Parking, Bungalow Hospitality Management, ByNext, FlyBox, Lettuce Entertain You, Lowe’s, Prince Street Hospitality Group, The Dinex Group, Thumbtack, among others.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5592. California Voters Reject ‘Billionaires Tax’ Amid Fears of an Exodus of Wealth From the State

California voters have rejected a proposed wealth tax, which could have meant a one-time influx of billions for the state but threatened to trigger an exodus of billionaires in the state.

The ballot measure, one of several housing issues Californians considered, is projected by the Associated Press to narrowly fail, with 53% voting against the measure with most votes counted a week after Election Day. Proposition 40 would have created a one-time 5% wealth tax on individuals with a net worth above $1 billion.

The Service Employees International Union–United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the measure, said it could have offset federal funding cuts. It estimated the one time tax could have brought in $100 billion in one-time revenue.

But the measure could have affected about 200 people, and billionaires in the state have put significant money toward fighting it. The California Budget & Policy Center estimates they hold a combined $2 trillion in wealth. Proposition 40 excludes real property holdings from determining an individual's net worth.

State leaders say tax could trigger some of those wealthy people to flee the state and take their spending with them. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimates California could collect $40 billion from the tax. But it could lose $25 billion in other taxes if wealthy people leave.

Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the measure. "This will be defeated, there's no question in my mind," Newsom told the New York Times, as it reported that several wealthy people had begun moving assets out of the state.

Palantir and PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin all have reportedly moved some assets to Florida. Voters in that state approved a measure on Tuesday that would reform its property tax system, potentially setting it up to be yet more attractive.

However, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had pledged to remain in California, where he has spent more than $112 million assembling a megacompound in Palo Alto. Earlier this year, Zuckerberg reached an agreement with the Meta board to remain in California regardless of the outcome of Prop 40. He would have faced a potential tax bill of some $12.5 billion if the measure had passed.

Taxes raised by Prop 40 would have gone to health care, education, or food assistance. But the state legislature would have had discretion to determine how those funds are used.

The California Association of Realtors President Tamara Suminski said at an elections forum last month that it opposed the measure. CAR is concerned about the potential loss of tax revenue and the state's economic competitiveness, she said.

"Prop 40 is just a bad idea," Jennifer Barrera, president & CEO, California Chamber of Commerce, said at the event. "Billionaires are the individuals who have the ability to move quickly, they have the ability to live outside the state, they don't have to be in California. And yet they pay a tremendous amount of revenue to our general fund if they're living here."

Two other items on the ballot, Proposition 41 and 42 both aimed to block or counter Proposition 40, but their language could have had much broader implications, Barrera said.

But even if Proposition 40 had passed, it would have invited years of litigation, said Joe Bishop‐​Henchman, executive vice president at National Taxpayers Union Foundation. Prop 40 applied to all of a California-domiciled billionaire's holdings across the globe, inviting Constitutional challenges.

And then there's the matter of actually calculating net worth. Wealthy individuals hold assets that can be hard to value, such as patents, artwork, and stakes in private companies. So, it would have likely taken years of expensive legal process to determine how much to tax them.

"The Franchise Tax Board currently has no infrastructure for valuing these types of assets," Bishop‐​Henchman said. "Valuing these kinds of assets will entail years of costly litigation on both ends and establishment of an extensive and costly administrative apparatus for an ostensibly 'one-time' tax."

Californians, meanwhile, also voted on a set of other measures. Voters passed Proposition 1 to authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing affordability programs. Co-chairs of its organizing campaign, Chione Flegal and Ray Pearl, called the win "a resounding show of support for affordable housing."

Voters also approved Proposition 37, which creates a $25 billion loan program for middle-income buyers to purchase new homes. Realtor.com® economist Joel Berner says this could be a boon for new-home sales. But he cautioned it might not touch the more expensive parts of the state.

"The complicating factor here is that the major California metro areas are short on newly built homes below $1.5 million, and the ballot measure does nothing to address the supply of these homes, only bolstering demand for them," Berner says.

"Proposition 37 has the potential to help prospective California homebuyers, but only if they can find new homes to buy," he notes.

The California Association of Realtors, a major supporter of Proposition 37, cheered the result.

“This measure will help create more housing, provide low-cost down payment options and give teachers, nurses, firefighters and other hardworking Californians a better opportunity to own a home in the communities they serve," Suminski said. "We look forward to working with stakeholders to bring Proposition 37 to life and deliver on its promise for California families.”

But, voters rejected the controversial Proposition 45. It would have set timelines on environmental reviews for some projects under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA.

California earned an F grade on the Realtor.com State-by-State Housing Report Card. It tracks how effectively each state balances affordability and new construction.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5591. Inflation Remains Hot in October and Strengthens Case for Another Fed Rate Hike

Inflation accelerated faster than anticipated in October, driven by surging costs for housing and food, which will bolster the case for another Federal Reserve interest rate hike next month.

On a monthly basis, overall prices rose 0.4% from September, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Tuesday. That's down from the 0.6% monthly increase recorded in September but higher than the 0.2% gain forecasted by economists.

CPI measures the average costs consumers pay for a range of goods, including food, energy, commodities, and services.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy categories, rose 0.3%, also exceeding the anticipated 0.2% gain.

The BLS did not publish an official annual inflation rate because last year's government shutdown prevented the agency from collecting survey data for October 2025.

October saw the index for shelter jump 0.3%, accounting for over 30% of the monthly all-items increase. Meanwhile, the food index increased 0.5%, and the energy index rose 0.7%, coming on the heels of a 5.2% surge in September.

Prices for a wide range of goods and services, including recreation, transportation, medical care, vehicle insurance, education, airfare, and tariff-sensitive categories like furniture and apparel all increased in October.

"These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel.

The October CPI print, coupled with the better-than-expected jobs number released last week, signals for the Federal Reserve that it must continue focusing its efforts on combating inflation.

At last month's meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), policymakers voted 10-2 to keep the overnight rate at its current 3.75%-4% range.

However, a December hike now looks all but certain, with odds of a 25-basis-point increase climbing to 99% Tuesday morning, before settling back down to 85%, according to CME FedWatch.

Krimmel says that market reaction is both due to the warmer-than-anticipated CPI print and Fed Gov. Christopher Waller’s latest comments.

Speaking before the inflation report release, Waller put a 50-basis-point move on the table for December and stressed the need to follow through on market expectations for rate increases.

"When this communication is clear and credible, what really matters is that those hikes are eventually carried out," said Waller.

Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury going up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI release.

For housing in the near term, Krimmel says the rising yields and growing speculation about future interest rate increases could put upward pressure on mortgage rates again, reversing a recent downward trend that saw the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifting to 7.18% last week.

October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back from the market.

And while rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand.

Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7%.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5588. Kora builds AI models and agents into a new Linux OS bound for Qualcomm Snapdragon PCs

Desktop software company Kora Systems Inc. today unveiled Kora, a Linux-based operating system that builds artificial intelligence models and agents into the system itself.

Qualcomm Technologies Inc. has spent close to a year working with the company to bring it to Snapdragon-powered PCs.

The launch goes after what Kora sees as a ceiling on AI in current desktop computers. Most AI software on macOS and Windows runs inside a browser tab or an app sandbox, according to the company, with little view of the computer underneath.

Because both platforms are closed, Kora argues, the integration stops at that point. Linux, by Kora’s account, is the only operating system open enough to be rebuilt around models and agents from the kernel up.

The core of that rebuild is an inference engine Kora calls Cortex. It pools the central processor, graphics processor and neural processing unit in a PC, plus any other machines on the network, and treats them as one computer. Models run locally on the user’s hardware by default, and frontier models get pulled in for heavier jobs.

On screen, the usual layout of folders and apps is gone. What Kora calls neural workspaces take its place, each one arranged around the task a user is working on. The user sets the permissions for any applications and agents sandboxed inside a workspace. Under all of it sits a neural file system, and the company says memory and context stay on the local machine.

Outside developers can build on the same pieces Kora’s own applications use through its software development kit, which opens up primitives such as memory, semantic search and email. Any model, AI service or agent will be able to integrate at the system level, the company said. An agentic service could even run as part of the operating system and take its identity, memory and compute from Kora.

Chief Executive Kirt McMaster called the desktop operating system “the ultimate harness.” About 45 million people account for 80% of spending on AI, he said, and almost all of their work happens on desktops running operating systems built 40 years ago. By 2033 the group will top 150 million people spending more than $400 billion a year, according to Kora’s own estimates. “Nobody has built an operating system for them,” McMaster said.

Kora grew out of Playtron Corp., a company McMaster founded to build a Linux alternative to Windows for gaming PCs. Playtron’s engineers wrote GameOS as a complete Linux operating system and shipped it on gaming devices, and the same team has been building Kora on that foundation since November 2025. GameOS carries on inside the new system as GameFrame, a one-click play mode that turns the desktop into a console for PC games.

With Cyanogen, Android and GameOS behind them, the founders count Kora as their fourth operating system. Chief Business Officer John Lagerling led Android business development at Google LLC, and he said he joined when the platform had 100,000 users and stayed until it had a billion. Openness got it there, in his view, and AI needs the same treatment.

The company believes “50 superpowered engineers can take on Windows,” according to Chief Technology Officer Franck De Girolami. His engineers now work side by side with AI models and agents, he said, to the point that “Kora is built inside Kora.”

The Qualcomm work is laid out in a separate joint release today. The result so far is a complete Linux desktop running on PCs with Snapdragon X2 Elite chips, the two companies said, and Cortex now spreads AI workloads across the whole chip. Qualcomm engineers worked on the project throughout, and the chipmaker is also pushing X2 Elite support into the mainline Linux kernel.

Those machines can run a 26 billion-parameter language model locally, according to the release. Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm’s senior vice president and general manager of compute and gaming, said the X2 Elite was designed to run advanced AI on the device. Kora has also built translation technology that lets selected Windows x86-64 applications run inside the Linux environment, so people switching over can keep using software they rely on.

The first machines to ship will run HUMAIN OS, an enterprise operating system KORA is co-developing with Saudi Arabian AI company HUMAIN. Those PCs are due in 2027, and the companies bill them as the first from hardware makers to pair a Linux-based desktop operating system with Snapdragon X2 Elite. Kora itself follows later in 2027, with pricing to be shared closer to availability.

Kora is a venture capital-backed startup that counts Samsung Next, Square Enix Holdings Co. Ltd., Polychain Capital LP, Van Eck Associates Corp., Circle Internet Group Inc. and Alumni Ventures among its investors. The release did not say how much the company has raised.

#5587. NAR Board Approves 2027 Budget, Installs New Leadership

At its Nov. 9 meeting during NAR NXT in New Orleans, the National Association of Realtors®’ (NAR) board of directors approved a 2027 budget and installed new leadership.

The board approved an operating budget projecting approximately $280 million in revenue and $247 million in expenses. Under the new approach, NAR departments were required to evaluate expenditures from the ground up rather than simply carry forward previous spending levels, prioritizing initiatives and identifying measures of success.

NAR Treasurer Craig Sanford described the approach as a significant step in the association’s financial modernization efforts. The board approved the budget by an overwhelming majority.

Directors also approved the following financial recommendations:

In his final board of directors meeting as NAR president, Kevin Brown highlighted progress on initiatives aimed at protecting members’ business interests, expanding housing opportunities and helping members adapt to a changing industry.

He also highlighted progress on MLS collaboration, including outreach to nearly 500 MLS executives and the formation of a work group to address emerging challenges and modernize policies. That work helped inform four policy recommendations approved by NAR’s Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee during NAR NXT, aimed at strengthening copyright protections for listing content, giving MLSs greater flexibility in setting local data feed requirements and clarifying permitted uses of MLS data.

For Realtor® members, the changes address business concerns, including protecting the time and money invested in marketing properties, preserving access to their own listing information and establishing clearer rules for how listing data can be used and shared.

Brown also pointed to NAR’s advocacy surrounding the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a housing package aimed at increasing supply, improving affordability and expanding homeownership opportunities. NAR’s attention is now turning toward implementation, including working with federal agencies and supporting state and local associations.

Other initiatives highlighted during the meeting included six “modernized” Center for REALTOR® Development courses scheduled to launch Dec. 1, more broker summits (on track for 85-plus by the end of the year) and continued advocacy, including for the bipartisan More Homes on the Market Act, which would increase the capital gains tax exclusion for homeowners selling their primary residences (something the Trump administration previously floated as well).

New NAR President Christine E. Hansen’s priorities include advancing NAR’s three-year strategic plan, improving awareness of member tools and resources, and restoring pride in the Realtor® brand.

The association’s 13 regional vice presidents were also installed.

#5586. Inside Josh Allen and Hailee Steinfeld’s Multimillion-Dollar Real Estate Portfolio

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen's football career continues to go from strength to strength, with him most recently leading the New York-based team to victory against the Minnesota Vikings.

The 30-year-old athlete, who has been with the Bills since being selected in the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft, previously added an overtime win to his resume, marking a significant personal achievement for the football star.

Now, he has once again showed off his skills in the Bills vs Vikings game, which saw the Bills leading 23-6 on Nov. 9.

The victory is another highlight in Allen's impressive career, which has seen him become one of the NFL's most recognizable quarterbacks.

However, while Allen continues to make headlines for his accomplishments on the field, his life away from football is equally impressive—particularly when it comes to the multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio he shares with his actress wife, Hailee Steinfeld.

Allen and Steinfeld, 29, tied the knot on May 31, 2025, during a romantic ceremony at San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, CA, nearly two years after their relationship first became public.

The couple welcomed their first child, a baby girl, in April 2026, adding another milestone to what has already been an eventful period in their personal lives.

Although Allen, who was born in Firebaugh, CA, spends the majority of the season in Buffalo, he has maintained a close connection to the Golden State, snapping up a $7.2 million property in Dana Point back in 2023.

The four-bedroom, three-bathroom dwelling is located inside a "prestigious" guard-gated community that features its own private beach club—and offers proximity to a host of nearby five-star resorts, including the Ritz Carlton.

It's understood that Allen spends much of the offseason at his California abode, soaking up the warm weather after a traditionally frosty Buffalo winter.

However, the sporting sensation also boasts another very sizable dwelling much closer to the Buffalo Bills' training ground and stadium: a custom-built megamansion that he had erected on a plot of land he snapped up in 2021 for the relatively low price of $500,000.

Records show that he purchased the 31-acre plot via an LLC, with Google Maps indicating that he has had quite the impressive property built on it.

Located in the tony community of Orchard Park, approximately eight minutes away from Highmark Stadium, the home features a stunning swimming pool, pool house, and a private sports court that can be used for both basketball and tennis.

Additionally, there is a private lake on the land, which has been outfitted with a small dock as well as a waterfront seating area that can be accessed via steps that lead down to the water from the pool.

Ironically, the property appears tailor-made for summertime activities, despite the fact that the football season takes place largely during the colder months.

Still, it provides the perfect place for Allen to lap up the last of the warm weather when he returns to Buffalo for preseason training camp, which kicks off on July 24.

However, thanks to his fiancée, the NFL pro also has his pick of properties over on the West Coast—where Steinfeld also owns a dazzling abode, which she picked up for $8 million back in 2021.

Located in Encino, CA, more than an hour away from Allen's Dana Point dwelling, the home was previously owned by rocker John Fogerty, who sold it to Steinfeld for $7.98 million—more than $3 million more than he had paid for it in 2018.

The actress' property spans an impressive 9,000 square feet and features six bedrooms and eight bathrooms. Much like her beau's abode in Buffalo, it has a sizable private pool, which can be accessed via a motorized window wall that opens up from the main living area into the backyard.

Upstairs, the primary suite features its own sitting room as well as two fireplaces, two walk-in closets, and two bathrooms—perfect for the couple that prefers to have their own space to get ready in the morning.

Cozy date nights can be enjoyed in the home's private movie theater, while the couple can host plenty of guests in the property's lounge, bar, or great room that has a custom "floor-to-ceiling entertainment wall."

And while the backyard has ample space for entertaining—and even includes an outdoor kitchen—that is not the only place where the pair can kick back and enjoy the open air.

In addition to the yard, there is also a roof deck on the property, which provides an additional outdoor space for relaxation or sunbathing.

However, if the pair are hoping to invest in property together, they may look elsewhere in California, specifically Malibu, which is where Allen popped the question to Steinfeld on Nov. 22, 2024.

The actress opened up about the proposal during a February interview with Who What Wear, telling the publication that Malibu serves as her "happy place" and adding that she couldn't have been happier with how the proposal happened.

"I'm so grateful that he did it the way he did so that I looked good, and we have these photos that we'll have and cherish for the rest of our lives that I'm not looking at being like, 'What was I wearing?'" she said. "We were in Malibu, which is my happy place, and it was magical."

"When you realize that so much is already out there in every other aspect of your life, you really learn to cherish the little that isn't. It just makes things extra special, and it's just for you," she explained.

#5585. Penélope Cruz Reveals Why She and Javier Bardem Chose To Raise Their Children in Madrid

Penélope Cruz has lifted the lid on why she and her husband, Javier Bardem, prefer raising their two kids in Spain.

While speaking to The Perfect Magazine, the actress, 52, revealed that she and Bardem, 57, opted to bring their son Leo, 15, and daughter Luna, 12, up in Madrid because it allows them to live a more private lifestyle.

“All our families are there, and the friends from childhood and from our teenage years; it’s easier to have a normal life, you know?” Cruz told the outlet.

She added, “You have to make an effort to keep a part of your life private, but I think when you have children, it’s really important, and they deserve that, they completely deserve that."

The Hollywood A-lister noted that when her children get older, they can decide whether they want to be in the spotlight.

"Later they can decide what they want to do in terms of their work and everything. But they need to have that freedom and not be exposed to things when they are little," she explained.

Cruz and Bardem said "I do" in 2010. The couple tends to keep tight-lipped about their private life.

However, the star has previously opened up about their parenting style, telling Elle in 2024 that they do not allow their children to have cell phones.

“It’s so easy to be manipulated, especially if you have a brain that is still forming, and who pays the price? Not us, not our generation, who, maybe at 25, learned how a BlackBerry worked. It’s a cruel experiment on children, on teenagers," Cruz said.

Cruz previously told People that her kids "finally" considered her a cool mom after she met Bad Bunny.

She revealed that the family attended the singer's residency in Puerto Rico and have since been to five of his international tour shows.

“But the first one in Puerto Rico is when Benito came to me and asked me to go with him to say the ‘Acho, PR es otra cosa,’” Cruz said, referring to the opening line of the musician’s song “VOY A LLeVARTE PA PR.”

“And finally my kids came to me and said, ‘Mom, finally you we can say you are cool.' Thank you, Benito! It took me all these years,” she teased.

#5583. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Zonda’s experts provide objective analysis on housing trends, supply and demand dynamics, and economic drivers. The team of economists, researchers, and analysts blends proprietary data with expert interpretation to help you navigate changing markets and make smarter decisions.

#5582. Century Communities Promotes Jim Francescon to President

As part of its long-term succession planning process, Century Communities has promoted Jim Francescon to president, effective January 1, 2027. Francescon currently serves as executive vice president, corporate operations.

“Today’s announcement reflects the implementation of a succession plan that our board, Rob, and I have been planning and executing over the past two years,” says Dale Francescon, executive chairman of Century Communities. “We have been very thoughtful in how we have approached succession, with the goal of best positioning Century for long-term alignment with shareholders, success, and growth.”

Dale Francescon will continue to serve as executive chairman and Rob Francescon, who currently serves as CEO and president, will solely serve as CEO. As president, Jim will oversee the company’s home building operations, land, and related corporate functions and will help drive the company’s strategy and growth.

“Jim has played an integral role in shaping our strategic direction and our growth into one of the largest home builders in the country, including leading our recent acquisitions that have deepened our footprint and strengthened our platform,” says Rob. “I look forward to continuing to work closely with Jim and our entire executive team as we position Century for continued success.”

Before serving as executive vice president, Jim was president of Century Living, the company’s multifamily platform, and prior to that served as corporate vice president. Jim also serves as a trustee of the University of Denver, Children’s Hospital Colorado Foundation, and ACE Scholarships Colorado.

“I am honored to take on this role and grateful to our board, Dale, and Rob for their confidence,” adds Jim. “We have built a strong operating platform and a talented team, and I am excited about the opportunities ahead as we continue to grow and deliver on our promise of “A Home for Every Dream.””

#5581. Andersen Partnership Helps Build Accessible Homes for Wounded Veterans

Since 2018, Andersen has worked with Jared Allen's Homes for Wounded Warriors, a nonprofit organization that builds injury-specific, accessible mortgage-free accessible homes for veterans who sustained severe injuries during their military service.

Since 2018, Andersen has partnered with Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors to help provide accessible, mortgage-free homes designed around the individual needs of severely injured military veterans.

Through the partnership, Andersen has donated windows and doors to 12 veteran families and home projects across the country. The manufacturer also supports the nonprofit through financial contributions and company matches of employee donations.

Most recently, Andersen contributed to a custom home for Marine Lance Corporal Josh Wege in Fond du Lac County, Wisconsin. Josh Wege, who sustained life-changing injuries while serving in Afghanistan, received the keys to the mortgage-free home alongside his family.

The residence was designed around Wege’s accessibility and mobility requirements, with the broader goal of providing greater independence, comfort, and quality of life.

“Building a home that meets the needs of a critically wounded veteran and their family takes a team of people who believe in our mission,” says Jared Allen, founder of Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors since 2009. “Andersen is an important part of that team, and we’re grateful for their support and commitment to the veterans we serve.”

Jared Allen, a Pro Football Hall of Famer and former Minnesota Vikings defensive end, added that the partnership helps create homes “where veterans can live more independently, and families can make memories together for years to come.”

For Andersen, the partnership also provides an opportunity to apply product selection and design considerations to the specific mobility needs of each homeowner. Depending on the project, those considerations can include wider openings, low- or zero-threshold transitions, accessible hardware placement, and patio door configurations intended to make movement easier between indoor and outdoor spaces.

Charlie Jackson, an account sales manager at Andersen, has helped project teams identify window and door solutions based on individual veterans’ accessibility requirements.

“My father was a World War II Marine, so supporting veterans has always been personally meaningful to me,” Jackson shares. “These projects bring Andersen’s work into focus because you can see how thoughtful product choices and accessible design come together to make everyday life easier for a veteran and their family.”

“As a 10-year Andersen employee, I’m proud to contribute my experience to help identify the products and solutions that best support each homeowner’s accessibility, comfort, and long-term needs,” he adds.

The homes are completed through collaboration among Jared Allen’s Homes for Wounded Warriors, manufacturers such as Andersen, local businesses, tradespeople, and other supporters.

#5580. The VA Home Loan Benefits Giving Military Buyers an Edge in a Tough Market

Thanks to the bravery and sacrifices of our veterans and active military, our country’s civilians can live the American dream in safety. So how fitting is it that one tangible way our country says "thank you for your service" to current and former members of the military is through the Department of Veterans Affairs home loan benefit?

These unique mortgage options allow veterans and those still serving to acquire their own piece of the American dream by potentially qualifying for homes they might have otherwise thought were out of reach.

In July 2025, HR 1815, the VA Home Loan Reform Act, passed with bipartisan support through the House, Senate, and President Donald Trump.

Backed by the National Association of Realtors®, the bill made permanent a policy allowing veterans to directly pay their real estate agents—ensuring equal access to the housing market. It also establishes a partial claims program to help veterans catch up on missed mortgage payments.

"The VA Home Loan Guaranty is a unique government program that allows veterans to purchase a home without a down payment," said Shannon McGahn, NAR executive vice president and chief advocacy officer at the time.

"We are grateful to the House of Representatives and the Senate for passing this measure and providing veterans and active-duty service members the same advantages as other buyers in a competitive real estate market. NAR remains committed to protecting the brave men and women who serve this country in the armed forces and ensuring they are given equal opportunities to achieve the American dream of homeownership."

Veterans, active-duty service personnel, and select reservists or National Guard members are among those who can qualify for VA loans (find eligibility requirements here). Wondering what some of the benefits of a VA loan might be? Here are five of the most popular features.

This is one of the most valuable and touted benefits—and for good reason. Saving enough for a down payment can be the biggest obstacle to buying a home. But a VA loan eliminates that roadblock.

“Most of the buyers I work with don’t have extra resources available, so the fact that they can purchase a home with zero down makes the transaction feasible,” says Benny Dinsmore, himself a veteran and a real estate agent with Coldwell Banker in Frisco, TX.

Qualified VA buyers don’t have a down payment requirement in most cases.

But beware: The “no money down” aspect of a VA loan shouldn’t be confused with “no money out of pocket,” a common misconception, notes Michael Garcia, broker and owner of Weichert, Realtors–TQS in Lake Worth, FL.

A VA purchase transaction still requires closing costs and often includes an earnest money deposit (a negotiated amount of money that the buyer puts in escrow to essentially "hold" the house).

“However, that money will often come back at the closing, when the title company will write a check back to the veteran on the spot for the total amount that was put into escrow,” Garcia says.

The required credit score for a VA loan can be lower than for a conventional loan—around 620 for a VA loan compared with a range of 650 to 700 for most conventional loans.

In addition, the required debt-to-income ratio for VA loans is often more flexible than for conventional mortgages.

“It allows someone with less-than-perfect credit and some debt to still be able to qualify for a loan,” Dinsmore says.

Most conventional buyers have to pay private mortgage insurance if they put less than 20% down. Federal Housing Administration loans come with their own forms of mortgage insurance. But a VA loan waives that insurance requirement.

"This can be a big savings in monthly payments," says real estate agent Twila Lukavich, with Russell Real Estate Services in Cleveland.

Even though there's no mortgage insurance, there is a "funding fee"—an upfront cost applied to every purchase loan or refinance. The proceeds help the VA cover losses on the few loans that go into default. But borrowers can roll it into their monthly payment, or pay it all at once. Plus, it's tax-deductible. And veterans with a service-connected disability and select others don’t have to pay the funding fee at all.

Legally, veterans might have to pay for certain closing costs, which include the following:

But there are some fees that veterans don't have to pay. And the VA allows lenders to charge no more than 1% to cover the costs of originating and underwriting the loan.

Furthermore, even those costs can be rolled into the loan. So, for example, if the purchase price is $280,000, the veteran might offer $300,000 and ask for 3% back to cover the closing costs.

“In this way, the veteran is essentially financing their closing costs into the loan, meaning less out of pocket at the start,” Dinsmore explains.

When a home that a veteran is considering purchasing is having trouble reaching the purchase price during the appraisal process, buyers and lenders can ask the VA appraiser to consider adjusting the valuation before making a final determination.

Appraisers notify lenders in the event the appraised value is likely to come in low, giving buyers and real estate agents 48 hours to supply additional information that the appraiser might not be aware of to help justify the home’s value.

"Typically, I assemble an itemized list of upgrades and improvements that the seller has performed on the home in the past three years that the appraiser didn’t know about, and therefore didn’t include in the home value," Lukavich says.

This process "gives the agents an opportunity to assist the appraiser in making sure they have the whole picture of the home and gives the local agent an opening to help an appraiser be educated on specific local values,” she adds.

It's just another benefit of VA loans aimed at helping our servicemen/women buy the home of their dreams.

#5579. For Every Condo Buyer in the U.S., There Are More Than Two Sellers. That Gives Condo Buyers Strong Negotiating Power.

Condo buyers today have more negotiating power than they’ve had in at least 13 years. There were an estimated 123% more condo sellers than buyers nationwide in September, the largest gap in records dating back to 2013. The gap widened from 95.5% a year earlier.

Redfin estimates the number of buyers using proprietary data on the typical time between a buyer’s first home tour and the closing of a purchase, along with MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers is based on active listings in the MLS. The figures in this report are national estimates. See the full methodology and explore the interactive dashboard.

Redfin defines a buyer’s market as one with more than 10% more sellers than buyers, and a seller’s market as one with more than 10% more buyers than sellers. A market is considered balanced when the difference between sellers and buyers is within 10%. Other housing-market statistics, including median sale price, are based on Redfin’s analysis of MLS data.

A buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily mean condos are affordable for buyers.

The condo market has undergone a dramatic reversal since the pandemic-era homebuying boom. In September 2021, there were 25.1% fewer sellers than buyers.

Five years later, the number of buyers fell 54%, while the number of sellers rose 36%. The shift has left sellers competing for a much smaller pool of potential buyers.

The number of condo buyers fell to an estimated 88,460 in September, down 2.5 % from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, condo sellers totaled 197,248, up 0.9 % from the prior month.

Several factors are weighing more heavily on the condo market than on the single-family home market. Rising insurance premiums, HOA fees and special assessments are making condos increasingly expensive to own, particularly in Florida and Texas, where hurricane risks and other natural disasters have contributed to higher insurance costs. That’s a problem for first-time buyers, who often turn to condos as a more affordable entry point into the housing market but lack equity from a previous home sale.

While the condo market is challenging for buyers, those who can afford housing costs will have more power in negotiations.

“For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity,” said Asad Khan, a senior economist at Redfin. “Buyers have more options and a better chance of finding a place they like. Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes.”

The single-family market saw a similar trend in September, with the number of buyers dropping to a record low since 2013. Sellers outnumbered buyers by 53.7%–a wide gap, but less than half as wide as what we’re seeing in the condo market.

The huge surplus of condo sellers over buyers is contributing to the record-breaking buyer’s market in the overall housing market, which encompasses condos, townhouses and single-family homes

The national median condo sale price fell 0.8% to about $339,000 in September, the first year-over-year decline in five months.

House hunters should keep in mind that the costs of buying and owning a condo extend beyond its purchase price, and those ongoing expenses can put additional pressure on buyers’ budgets. Rising homeowners association (HOA) fees and insurance premiums can push up the total monthly cost of ownership. Buyers should also consider the possibility of special assessments to cover major repairs or improvements to a building’s common areas.

But for buyers who can afford the upfront costs of a condo and plan to stay put for several years, today’s buyer’s  market may offer an opportunity.

“Find a motivated seller and there are a lot of them,” said Cecilia Cordova, a Redfin Premier agent in Miami, who lives in a condominium herself. Researching the buildings you’d like to live in is the key to finding a financially healthy community and avoiding surprise assessment bills later, she said.

Condo buyers have more options than they did years ago. “We have enough inventory for the next three to four years,” said Cordova.

For prospective sellers? Cordova suggests considering renting their condo out for the time being. “If you really need to sell, the strategy is to list it lower than anybody else in the same building. It’s not time for you to try to experiment with a higher price,” she said.

Today’s home prices and mortgage rates have made it harder for first-time homebuyers to enter the market, reducing demand for condos, which have traditionally served as an entry point to homeownership. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.18% as of November 5, and home prices remain near historic highs.

Sellers are increasingly dropping their asking prices to attract buyers, Redfin data shows. About 37% of condos that sold in September had a price reduction, compared with 16% during the pandemic-era housing boom five years earlier.

The typical condo that sold in September spent 63 days on the market before going under contract, up from 35 days five years earlier.

Condo buyers in Texas had more negotiating powers than anywhere else in the country in September. San Antonio had the widest seller-buyer gap among the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas, with an estimated 459% more sellers than buyers. Houston followed with 322% more sellers than buyers, then came Austin, with 258% more.

Miami also had one of the nation’s widest gaps, with an estimated 274% more condo sellers than buyers in September, ranking third.

“San Antonio condos may have an attractive purchase price, but buyers are looking at the total monthly payment. Because we have so many affordable single-family homes available, many buyers choose a house when the payments are close,” said Derrell Skillman, a Redfin Premier agent in San Antonio, TX.

Skillman added San Antonio has a large military community, and its housing market tends to follow the military’s permanent change-of-station (PCS) season.

“We usually see more military-related activity during the spring and summer when families are transferring in and out of the area. Once that period slows down, the drop in demand can be more noticeable, especially in a smaller segment like condos,” he said. “HOA costs, financing restrictions, builder incentives, softer investor demand and the slowdown after the military PCS season are all contributing to the buyer’s market for condos,” said Skillman.

Meanwhile, new construction is adding to the softness in Sun Belt markets. The Sun Belt is home to nine of the 10 metros where condo sellers outnumber buyers most.

Nassau County, NY, was the only metro area among the 50 analyzed that was a seller’s market for condos in September. There were 32% fewer sellers than buyers, with an estimated 1,545 buyers compared with 1,052 sellers.

“Condo buyers are mostly people who want maintenance-free living,” said William Ortiz, a Redfin Premier agent in Long Island, NY. “They want to have an easier lifestyle as opposed to all the maintenance and upkeep that comes with a house. Common charges are expensive, but they’re willing to pay for that convenience.”

According to Sandra Glaser, a Redfin senior agent in Long Island, condo demand is coming from three main groups: first-time buyers priced out of single-family homes, particularly those moving from the city to the suburbs; downsizers seeking less upkeep; and investors looking for rental income from properties that require minimal maintenance.

Five other metros — Chicago, Milwaukee, New Brunswick, Newark and San Francisco — had balanced condo markets, where the difference between buyers and sellers was within 10%.

San Francisco’s condo market, for example, is heating up, with the median sale price jumping 20% year over year to nearly $1.2 million in September. Khan, the Redfin senior economist, ties the area’s renewed housing demand to the AI boom, which is attracting highly paid workers and fueling homebuying.

As a senior data reporter, Dian uses data and quantitative analysis to tell stories about economy and real estate. She also builds databases and creates statistical charts that visualize data trends. Previously, Dian spent seven years as a senior data reporter at USA TODAY.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5578. Hedra’s new Model Factory cranks up the production volume for physical AI model training

Autonomous artificial intelligence agents have been a massive hit in the digital realm, and now a startup called Hedra Inc. is hoping to take the next step with physical AI systems that can automate tasks in the real world too.

The company today announced the Hedra Model Factory, a new post-training and inference platform that enables the recursive self-improvement of AI models, or RSI for short, designed specifically to power autonomous robots and other machines.

Hedra says that physical AI requires a very different and more specialized form of intelligence that can enable robots and other real-world hardware systems to perform very specific tasks, such as packing irregular-shaped parcels onto palettes. One of the main challenges of physical AI is that each robot and each task it performs requires a different model.

But training all of those models is not feasible, given the vast amounts of data required to create them. That’s why Hedra wants to use RSI to adapt existing models to new tasks.

RSI is a relatively new technique in AI that describes systems that can autonomously evaluate, train and then improve their own architectures. There has been a lot of research into these systems in frontier AI labs, but until now no one has managed to apply that continuous loop to the physical world.

The challenge is that physical AI models require massive volumes of multimodal data inputs, from sources such as high-resolution video, sensor feeds and 3D simulations. Running RSI against such enormous data environments simply is not practical given the staggering compute costs such an operation would incur.

Hedra says its Model Factory changes that. It’s an autonomous training pipeline offered as a service that’s designed for robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense workloads, pairing Hedra’s in-house research teams with AI agents that orchestrate the training runs, curate the data and iterate autonomously according to the customer’s specifications.

Hedra founder and Chief Executive Michael Lingelbach (pictured) told SiliconANGLE that RSI has already had a major impact on the way frontier models are developed. He believes that the next big frontier is physical AI, where the data primarily comes from video feeds, sensor readings and simulations. “Hedra Model Factory gives robotics, manufacturing, biology and defense teams the infrastructure to post-train, deploy and keep improving their own models,” he promised.

Lingelbach, a former reinforcement learning researcher for visual and physical systems at Stanford University and Nvidia Corp., said what his company has developed is basically an end-to-end production platform for physical AI models. The customer provides the base model, uploads their proprietary simulation and video data, which is then provisioned within a flexible graphics processing unit sandbox environment powered by its proprietary inference engine.

The RSI process then begins, with Hedra’s researchers keeping close tabs on its progress. Lingelbach said they use vision-language models to score data and provide live reinforcement learning feedback in order to continuously optimize the model to perform the task specified by the customer. Once done, customers can then deploy the model on-premises in their own systems, or with one of Hedra’s cloud data center partners.

The models can also be distilled to run on edge systems for lower-latency workloads. Once they’re up and running, they feed data back into the customer’s sandboxed environment, creating an autonomous flywheel that continuously optimizes the model, making it better over time.

Hedra has worked hard to validate the system. For instance, it retrained MiniMax Group Inc.’s open-weight H3 video model to enhance its physical consistency, creating a distilled version that bumped up its score on the Physics-IQ benchmark from 30.3 to 34.9. In another training run, the startup was able to distill the Krea 3 2K image generation model from 30 sampling steps to just 14 while reducing latency from 22 seconds to just 3.6 seconds, a sixfold speed boost that took just one week to achieve.

Lingelbach said Hedra’s ultimate goal is to help create the thousands of bespoke, cost-effective models needed to usher in the physical AI revolution by optimizing training as much as possible. With RSI, sometimes it’s possible to bypass the retraining process altogether. In one example, Hedra demonstrated that it was able to swap out a robot’s gripper with a new one and restore its task success rate to 100% without any additional training, simply by mapping the new hardware’s reach and grasp metrics to the robot’s wrist camera view.

The Hedra Model Factory service is available today, giving enterprises the option to bypass compute-intensive training and quickly develop the specialized autonomous systems needed to bring intelligence into real-world environments.

#5577. Invitation Homes Invests in HBI Training for Veterans

The Home Builders Institute (HBI) and Invitation Homes have launched a partnership aimed at helping transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families build careers in construction, property maintenance, and the skilled trades.

The partnership will expand Invitation Homes’ existing Invitation to SkillUp initiative through an investment in HBI’s Military Services program, which provides hands-on, instructor-led skilled trades training, industry-recognized certifications, and job placement assistance.

Through the partnership, HBI and Invitation Homes will connect HBI-trained veterans, military spouses, and family members with career opportunities in the build-to-rent and single-family rental sectors. The organizations also plan to expand recruitment at HBI Military Services locations, including Fort Stewart, Georgia, and Jacksonville, Florida.

Invitation Homes’ Veteran Employee Resource Group will participate in mentorship and career guidance efforts.

“Veterans and their families have dedicated themselves to serving our country, and we are proud to support them as they transition into rewarding civilian careers,” Invitation Homes president and CEO Dallas Tanner says. “Through our Invitation to SkillUp initiative, we are investing in talented individuals whose dedication and service strengthen our communities, while helping create meaningful opportunities in the skilled trades.”

HBI has spent a decade training, certifying, and placing transitioning service members, veterans, and their families in skilled trades careers. According to HBI president and CEO Ed Brady, nearly 90% of graduates from the organization’s military program find jobs, earning an average of more than three times the federal minimum wage.

“We know this model works, and with this important investment from Invitation Homes, we can help more veterans enter the skilled trades every year because the people who served this country deserve a career as strong as their service,” Brady said.

Invitation to SkillUp is Invitation Homes’ national skilled trades development initiative, which works with trade schools and organizations to expand trades education and increase awareness of career opportunities.

Invitation Homes joins other companies supporting HBI’s military programs. The Home Depot Foundation and DEWALT were early supporters, while Google recently provided a $1 million contribution to the effort.

The partnership comes as the housing industry continues to look for ways to strengthen its skilled labor pipeline. For transitioning service members and military families, the effort offers a pathway from military service into construction and housing careers while providing the industry with another source of trained workers.

#5576. Christina Haack Says She Paid Off Her College Debt by ‘Hitting It Big’ on a Las Vegas Slot Machine

Real estate investor Christina Haack doesn’t mind proving people wrong, even if that includes her own mom.

The “Flip or Flop” shared the unlikely story of her student loan payoff, after experiencing a “full circle” moment during a recent trip to Las Vegas.

In an Oct. 29 Instagram post, the HGTV personality, 43, shared a collection of photos where she’s posed in front of a slot machine while enjoying a glass of her own brand of wine, Clé Cachée.

“Really come full circle since age 21,” she explained in the caption before adding that she “paid off” her “college debt by hitting it big” on a slot machine called “top dollar.”

Haack was proud to close the loop “22 years later,” by getting to enjoy her own champagne while playing her “fav” machine. She called the experience “priceless,” and joked: “My mom always told me no one actually wins in Las Vegas. Turns out mama’s not always right.”

Her boyfriend, Chris Larocca, left a cheeky comment under the post, writing, “Maybe you have a good luck charm now…” to which she replied, “Most definitely.”

Haack has previously shared that when she was attending San Diego State, she “never thought about being on TV” and instead thought she “wanted to be a sports agent like Jerry Maguire.”

Eventually she realized she’d rather get her real estate license, and explained that she “got started in real estate at 21”—the same year she won big at a casino.

While Haack’s previous financial win may have been the luck of the draw, it’s safe to say her family is set up for success in a much more intentional way these days.

The mom-of-three recently made a splash online when she, her ex-husband Tarek El Moussa, and his new wife, Heather El Moussa, gifted daughter, Taylor El Moussa, a very expensive vehicle for her 16th birthday.

The close-knit crew of co-parents splurged on a $150,000 BMW X5, a lavish gift they said was “well deserved.”

“It’s such a beauty. I’m so happy for her,” Christina said in an Aug. 13 Instagram Reel that showcased the moment the teen was surprised with the new car, which had an enormous pink bow on it.

Heather wrote that the trio had worked together to surprise Taylor, and even joked that she was unsure if the car was more impressive, or if “the fact that three of us actually pulled this off” was a more jaw-dropping feat.

Tarek later shared more details about the purchase, explaining that the family had “good reason” to purchase the luxury vehicle during an appearance on the “Money Rehab” podcast with Nicole Lapin.

“She’s got a 4.2 GPA. She was MVP of her freshman soccer team. She’s an absolutely fantastic kid, and she didn’t just get it—she actually earned it,” he said. “If you ask me, she deserved it because she worked really, really hard.”

Noting that the car was also selected for its host of safety features, Tarek added that the vehicle was mostly his choice, as Taylor would have probably preferred a much-less-expensive Ford Bronco.

“Here’s the truth. She was flying in private jets when she was like, 1 year old,” he said. “So this kid has grown up around things. When I grew up, I didn’t have anything, right? So I’m obsessed with things because I never had things. She’s always had things.”

Staying firm in his belief that the gift was a “reward for all the work she’s done,” Tarek revealed that the family has also set her up for success financially in addition to showering her with pricey gifts.

Tarek noted that he has snapped up stocks and investment real estate for his teen daughter, and said that “if she were going to be a spoiled brat, she probably wouldn’t have got the 4.2 GPA, she probably wouldn’t have been MVP of her soccer team, and she probably wouldn’t have done the extra coaching.”

#5575. How Buyers Can Tell if a Home Price Cut Signals a True Deal

More than one in five U.S. home listings received a price cut in August, but a lower asking price does not necessarily mean the property has become a good deal. Price reductions are becoming harder for homebuyers to ignore. In August, 20.4% of U.S. listings had a price cut, matching the rate recorded a year earlier, according to the latest Realtor.com housing report.

The median asking price fell 1.3% year over year to $424,500, marking the tenth consecutive month of annual declines. Meanwhile, pending sales slipped 0.2%, ending an eight-month run of year-over-year growth.

For buyers, the growing number of reductions may look like an invitation to start bargain hunting. However, a crossed-out asking price provides little evidence of the property’s actual value.

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says Jeremy Olsher, a principal at Mizner Residential Group. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.”

Olsher recommends three checks before treating a reduced listing as a deal.

Compare the new price with completed sales. Buyers should begin with recently sold properties that are genuinely comparable in location, size, condition and features. Active listings reveal what other sellers hope to receive, while completed sales show what buyers have accepted.

A $40,000 reduction may look substantial, but it has limited meaning if the home remains $50,000 above comparable sales.

“The percentage reduction is the part buyers notice first because it is easy to understand,” Olsher says. “The more useful question is whether the new price makes sense beside the homes that have actually sold.”

Read the entire listing history. The number and timing of reductions can reveal how the seller is responding to the market. A single adjustment after several quiet weeks may indicate growing flexibility. Several small reductions can suggest the seller is chasing the market downward without fully accepting current buyer demand.

Buyers should also check whether the home was previously listed, withdrawn and returned with a new price or description. A fresh listing date does not always mean the property is new to the market.

“Days on the market need context,” Olsher says. “I want to know whether the seller made one meaningful correction or has spent months making small changes that never addressed the real pricing problem.”

Account for condition and ownership costs. A reduced property can remain expensive once repairs, insurance, taxes, association fees and immediate maintenance are considered. Buyers should compare the home’s total financial exposure with competing properties, rather than evaluating the asking price in isolation.

A lower price may represent genuine value when the cost of resolving known issues has already been reflected. It becomes less attractive when the discount is smaller than the work or ongoing expenses the buyer will inherit.

There may also be room to offer below the revised price, particularly when comparable sales support a lower figure or the property has remained available after multiple reductions. Olsher advises buyers to base that offer on evidence rather than choosing an arbitrary percentage below asking.

“The strongest offer is not necessarily the closest to the seller’s latest number,” he says. “It is the one a buyer can explain with recent sales, property condition and realistic costs. A reduction opens the conversation. The numbers still have to hold up.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5574. Lennar, Operation Finally Home Surprise Two Military Families With New Homes

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier with their families.

Two military veterans and their families received life-changing news ahead of Veterans Day when Lennar and Operation Finally Home surprised them with the gift of new homes.

U.S. Army Specialist Jordan Taylor and U.S. Marine Corps Sergeant Kevin Gallmeier were surprised with the announcement during the inaugural Operation Finally Home Golf Classic reception in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 9.

Neither family knew about the plans beforehand and attended the event as guests of Operation Finally Home.

The announcement followed a live performance by country music artist and Army Reserve soldier Craig Morgan. Operation Finally Home founder Dan Wallrath and Lennar San Antonio division president Brian Barron then revealed that each family would receive a new Lennar home.

The partnership builds on Operation Finally Home’s mission of providing mortgage-free homes and home modifications to wounded, ill, and injured veterans, first responders, and their families.

Gallmeier served in the Marine Corps from 2005 to 2015 after being motivated to enlist by the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. During his service, he deployed twice to Iraq in support of combat operations and later deployed to Okinawa, Japan, as part of the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit.

Gallmeier sustained a traumatic brain injury following a grenade blast during combat operations in Iraq. He also developed post-traumatic stress disorder and continues to manage PTSD, amongst other conditions, according to Operation Finally Home.

Following his military career, Gallmeier earned bachelor’s and master’s degrees in divinity from Biola University and became a pastor. He currently lives in California with Tatiana Zaragoza and their three children, Alyssa, Caspian, and Everett.

A formal groundbreaking for the family’s new Lennar home is scheduled for Nov. 10 in the Freedom Crossing community in Killeen, Texas.

Taylor enlisted in the U.S. Army in August 2004 shortly after graduating from high school in Washington state. He served as an infantryman and filled roles including Squad Automatic Weapon gunner, driver, and team leader.

From June 2006 to September 2007, Taylor deployed to Baghdad in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. His unit lost 21 soldiers during the deployment.

After completing his military service in December 2007, Taylor continued serving his community as a firefighter and emergency medical technician.

A serious back injury in January 2024, combined with the lasting physical and emotional effects of his military service, ultimately forced Taylor to medically retire from firefighting in March 2025.

Following the injury, Taylor and his wife, Aylynn, and their four children faced financial uncertainty and eventually sold their home and moved in with relatives. The family’s new Lennar home will provide a fresh start. A groundbreaking for the Taylor residence is slated in December.

#5573. Mortgage Rates Dip Ahead of a Big Week for Inflation Data

In A Nutshell:  Mortgage rates are coming down as investors dial back expectations for rate hikes. But that could change: Key inflation data comes out this week.

Two highlights from a busy election week:

This week’s economics highlight is the CPI inflation data coming Tuesday, coupled with Friday’s PPI data. Together, the two will form a complete picture of the core PCE inflation measure the Fed uses. The consensus forecast has core CPI coming in at 0.2% month-over-month, down slightly from last month. Forecasters are expecting a small statistical distortion in the data due to last year’s government shutdown. A very low read for inflation might convince the Fed to hold off on hiking rates at the December meeting, but they could just as easily write it off as one data point. They would evaluate how broader financial conditions have changed since the last meeting, including any further improvement in rates.

#5572. Police Raid $4.4 Million San Francisco Squatter Mansion—Arresting Woman and Rescuing 7 Dogs

The woman allegedly at the center of a squatting dispute in San Francisco’s luxury Sea Cliff community was arrested on Friday during a raid of the property and following a monthslong investigation into her claims on the home. Diana Peng, 42, was charged with fraud, driving without a license, narcotics possession, improper care of animals, and being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition. Police also removed seven dogs from the home and put them in the care of a local shelter.

Peng and her alleged accomplice, Brandon Aadee, are in the midst of a civil lawsuit brought by San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu. Chiu accused the pair of illegally obtaining the $4.4 million property through forged, fraudulently notarized deeds, intending to sell it.

According to Chiu’s complaint, Peng and Aadee took over the 3,000-square-foot Tudor-style home at 250 32nd Ave. in 2025 by claiming that the previous owner had transferred the deed to Aadee. Peng and Aadee transferred the property title back and forth between them eight times, and at least five of those were forged, including the initial deed from the legitimate owner, Wei Wang, which includes a forged notary signature.

Wang and her husband, Xiangdong Guo, purchased the property in 2013 for $2.41 million. But the pair moved abroad around 2019, and the property fell into disrepair and appeared to be abandoned.

It also racked up more than $340,000 in unpaid property taxes, which prevented a sale of the property.

This past October, however, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors approved a resolution to pay off the property taxes, paving the way for the home to be put up for auction later this year.

Neighbors in the wealthy enclave, where both Sharon Stone and Twitter founder Jack Dorsey have homes, said they spent much of the past year on edge, watching people come and go from the property at all hours.

"I'm probably in touch with one city official or another at least six times every day," neighbor Whitney Lynn told ABC 7. "We really have been asking for help, and it feels like people finally heard us.Most recently, in August, a neighbor called 311 to complain that the property was “being used as a group home.”

“The home was abandoned for over 5 years, and squatters moved in May 2025 using burglary tools. Over the past couple of days, a new group of about a dozen squatters moved in," the complaint read. Nearly a dozen complaints were also filed with the Department of Building Inspection, the most recent on Oct. 13. That complaint stated that unpermitted plumbing and irrigation work had been taking place in the backyard.

Neighbors told the San Francisco Chronicle that Friday’s raid lasted about four hours and that police removed several boxes and bags of documents. Police went in with guns drawn and came out with Peng, and seven dogs were removed from the property and taken to a local shelter. Police also towed Peng's Porsche.

Deb Campbell, the public information officer with San Francisco Animal Care and Control, tells Realtor.com® the two adult pit bulls and five puppies are “doing well in our care.” She otherwise couldn’t comment on the animals' condition because of the ongoing investigation.

“We appreciate SFPD’s work to pursue accountability and keep our neighborhoods safe,” Jen Kwart, the communications director for the city attorney’s office, tells Realtor.com. "As our civil case moves forward, we look forward to continuing to work closely with SFPD to ensure the courts understand that Defendants are effectively trying to steal a house and sell it to make millions in profit.”

Both Peng and Aadee have long criminal records. In 2008, she was convicted of perjury and sentenced to 90 days in jail and three years’ probation. Four years later, she pleaded guilty to identity theft and burglary and served seven months in prison. And then in 2015, she was sentenced to an additional two years in jail for forgery of a driver’s license and using another person's identification.

In 2009, Aadee was convicted of defrauding FEMA out of thousands of dollars and ordered to pay $48,000 in restitution. He also has convictions for credit card fraud and passing bad checks.

Following Friday’s raid, Peng was booked and is being held without bail at the San Francisco County Jail.
