#5524. Non-deterministic agents break the rules traditional software security was built on

AI agent security has become the critical gating factor for enterprises that want autonomous software doing real work.

Unlike chatbots that answer questions, agents take actions, and every tool or credential they touch widens the potential damage. To that end, Red Hat Inc. has spent the past year building guardrails for that shift, including a sandbox for OpenClaw agents. The complexity lies in the fact that agents break the assumptions traditional software security was built on, according to Joe Fernandes (pictured, right), vice president and general manager of Red Hat AI at Red Hat.

“For forever, we’ve been building software, but that software is deterministic. It does what we program it to do,” Fernandes said. “Agents are different. They’re non-deterministic; you’re giving them a goal. You don’t know what actions they’re going to take to get to that goal.”

Fernandes and Jessica Forrester (left), senior distinguished engineer and chief architect of Red Hat AI at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Red Hat is building layered security for autonomous AI agents through sandboxing, identity management, access controls and enterprise-scale agent management. (* Disclosure below.)

Red Hat learned lessons through its own engineering teams. When it first built an agentic software development life cycle, it handed agents prefetched data and let them touch nothing else, Forrester explained. OpenShell, the open-source agent runtime Nvidia Corp. launched in March with Red Hat as a founding member, let the company loosen that grip safely. The two companies have since expanded their partnership around securing autonomous agents. One approach from Red Hat involves giving agents access to the tools they need while keeping sensitive credentials out of reach.

“With OpenShell, your agent doesn’t ever get any real keys to anything. It gets masked on the way in and then swapped on the way out,” Forrester said. “If something convinces it to give away its keys, it’s not actually giving any real keys away. That really helps you have a little bit more faith in what’s happening inside that agent box.”

OpenShell can also run agents in Kata Containers with their own kernels, inside full virtual machines on OpenShift Virtualization and behind network egress controls, Forrester noted. Red Hat has also detailed kernel-level agent isolation in its platform. Identity comes next, with every agent assigned its own identity and the narrowest set of permissions, Fernandes added.

“It’ll integrate with different identity systems to basically allow you to assign agent identity,” he said. “Then you can authorize what that agent can do — and more importantly, what it can’t.”

Red Hat is now looking beyond individual agents. It is working with OpenAI Group PBC on OpenClaw Enterprise, a project for managing thousands of personal agents at scale, while OpenShell is available in preview in Red Hat AI. For enterprises still weighing AI agent security, the project’s maturity is the moment to watch, Fernandes explained.

“We’re really now approaching that stable milestone,” Fernandes said. “That’s when we feel like, ‘Okay, we’re comfortable enough. We can actually rely on this for enterprise production.'”

#5522. Remodeling Activity Holds Flat in Q2 Amid Housing Slowdown

The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) reported that remodeling activity was flat in the second quarter amid a broader nationwide housing slowdown, in its latest State Projections of Remodeling (SPR).

The SPR showed a near-even split in the second quarter: Remodeling spending declined in 26 states and increased in 24 states, according to a release. The average growth rate across all states broke even at 0.0%.

“These flat results are consistent with NAHB’s forecast for remodeling spending in 2026,” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said. “Second-quarter spending growth was concentrated in smaller states. Among the 10 states with the largest market shares, only North Carolina and Illinois recorded growth.”

“Rising construction costs and weak consumer sentiment are weighing on projects and keeping spending flat, but the remodeling sector has solid long-term growth potential,” Elliott Pike—NAHB Remodelers chairman—stated. “An aging housing stock, the mortgage rate lock-in effect, home equity gains and more home owners choosing to age in place will support future growth.”

Remodeler confidence has also held steady. The release noted that NAHB’s Remodeling Market Index (RMI)—which measures confidence in the sector—has remained above 60 for the past year.

#5521. What 1,000 U.S. real estate ads reveal about lead generation

Reviewing 1,000 active U.S. residential Meta ads found pricing mentioned in 38% of ads, while explicit qualification cues appeared in 7.7%. The findings suggest lead handling and follow up should differ by offer type and destination.  AI Summary

In Texas, a homebuilder advertised new homes starting around $240,000 and sent visitors to its community website. A property search service offered free listing alerts through a Meta Instant Form. Both wanted buyer inquiries, yet the buyers were signing up for different experiences. I would hesitate to hand those contacts to an agent as if they meant the same thing.

I reviewed 1,000 active residential real estate ads across 20 U.S. regions, collected from Meta’s public Ad Library on October 15, 2026. Buyer-focused ads accounted for 73% of the sample. The sharpest divide was between property-search and lead-generation pages, which used Instant Forms in 66% of their ads, and homebuilders, where that figure was 4%. It is a striking difference for businesses competing for many of the same people.

The sample excluded rentals, commercial properties, mortgage services and unrelated promotions. I capped the number of ads from each Facebook page so large advertisers would not overwhelm the results, then classified the intended audience, advertiser type, offer, written price information, qualification cues and click destination. The data went through additional checks before the figures were calculated.

Individual listings made up 29% of the sample, new construction 27.5%, and broader home-search offers roughly 17%. An inquiry on a specific listing gives an agent an immediate subject for a conversation. Someone requesting alerts for an entire neighborhood may have no property in mind and could be months from making a decision.

When I look at a lead-generation campaign, that difference shapes my advice more than the choice between a form and a website. I want to know whether the sales team is set up for property inquiries or for a longer search relationship. Those are different workloads, even if both begin with a name and a phone number.

Seller advertising offered another contrast. It accounted for 19% of the ads, with agents and teams responsible for 41% of that group and cash homebuyers for 27%. One Utah cash buyer cited a $420,000 sale completed in 33 days, a claim I could not independently verify. Its offer emphasized selling without repairs or a traditional listing. An agent replying with a generic home-valuation ad would be competing against a much more specific promise.

Price or monthly-payment information appeared in the written copy of 38% of ads. For individual listings it was 60%; for new-construction offers, 53%. Among broad buyer campaigns, it fell to 22%. Only 9% of seller-focused ads mentioned a price-related figure.

I was more interested in what the copy left unsaid. Just 7.7% of ads included an explicit qualifying cue, such as budget, financing readiness or purchase timing. For ads using Meta Instant Forms, the figure was about 10%. We did not inspect the questions inside those forms, so I would not claim advertisers skipped qualification altogether.

Still, an agent cannot respond intelligently to every inquiry in the same way. If a campaign advertises homes within a defined price range, I would rather see that range stated clearly than leave the salesperson to discover a basic mismatch on the first call. With monthly-payment offers, financing assumptions deserve equal attention.

Overall, 51% of ads led to websites or landing pages, 30% used Meta Instant Forms, and about 5% invited conversations through Messenger, Instagram or WhatsApp. Among builders, 88% sent traffic to their websites. A development page can explain a property before anyone speaks to sales; an instant form can capture interest sooner.

Neither choice tells us how well a campaign performs. But it does affect the work that follows. A search service can use saved listings and alerts to keep a buyer engaged. If a small brokerage has no process for staying in touch, borrowing that same offer may fill its CRM with people it will never properly serve.

My first check would happen after the click. I would submit the form myself, open the resulting CRM record and see what the agent actually receives. Does it identify the property that attracted the buyer? Could someone on the team call back without asking the prospect to repeat the entire inquiry? If the answer is no, I would fix that before buying more traffic.

For listing ads, I would test putting a realistic price range in the written copy, then listen to the conversations it produces. The point is to find out whether prospects arrive with clearer expectations. A higher cost per inquiry could be acceptable if more of those conversations lead to relevant showings.

For a broad search offer, I would make sure the team has a reason to contact people again. Asking about purchase timing may be helpful if an agent uses the answer to plan follow-up. Adding five questions to a form that nobody reads solves nothing.

I also would not copy a large search platform’s campaign simply because its ads are everywhere. It may have an entire operation built around people who are still browsing. A brokerage with a handful of agents needs a funnel suited to the people it can actually help. That is the decision I would make before choosing the ad format.

Oleh Odukalets is a performance marketer with seven years of experience in paid acquisition and more than $1 million in real estate ad spend managed across international markets.

#5518. Davidson Homes, loanDepot launch in-house mortgage JV

loanDepot and Davidson Homes have launched Davidson Mortgage, a mortgage joint venture serving buyers in Alabama, Tennessee, Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Arizona. The move reflects a broader builder trend toward affiliated mortgage operations to reduce fallout, manage incentives and improve closing predictability in a volatile rate environment.  AI Summary

Davidson Homes and loanDepot have formed a new joint venture, Davidson Mortgage, to provide integrated mortgage services for Davidson Homes buyers across six states.

The partnership expands loanDepot’s joint venture channel while giving Davidson Homes an in-house mortgage option aimed at keeping buyers inside the builder’s ecosystem from contract to closing, the companies said in a joint announcement.

Davidson Mortgage will serve homebuyers in Alabama, Tennessee, Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Arizona, where Davidson Homes currently operates communities.

The JV combines loanDepot’s mortgage platform and product menu with Davidson Homes’ regional footprint and new-home sales pipeline. For builders, this type of structure can help reduce fallout, shorten cycle times and create more predictable closings, especially in a higher-rate, high-friction lending environment.

“Davidson Homes has built tremendous momentum by continuing to grow while building homes that reflect what today’s buyers want and need, with a strong focus on quality and the customer experience,” loanDepot President of Partnership Lending Dan Peña said in the announcement. “Davidson Mortgage builds on that success, pairing loanDepot’s lending platform and service with Davidson Homes’ customer-first approach to deliver a smooth financing experience homebuyers can trust.”

Davidson Mortgage is part of loanDepot’s strategy to grow its core mortgage franchise through a multi-channel platform that includes joint ventures, distributed retail and direct lending. For Davidson Homes, a private builder ranked No. 43 on the 2026 Builder 100, the move aligns with a broader industry push to capture more of the homebuying value chain through affiliated services.

“Our success has always been grounded in the relationships we build with homebuyers and the communities we serve,” Davidson Homes CEO Brandon Jones said. “With loanDepot’s reputation for combining technology with a customer-first approach, we’re providing buyers with a frictionless and personal financing experience.”

Joint venture and affiliated business models have become increasingly important profit and risk-management tools for builders as they navigate volatile rates, tighter underwriting and shifting buyer demand. Integrated mortgage operations can help builders manage incentives more strategically, coordinate rate locks with construction timelines and identify qualification issues earlier in the sales funnel.

LoanDepot, founded in 2010 and licensed in all 50 states, reports it has funded $600 billion in volume directly to consumers. Davidson Homes, founded in 2009 and based in Huntsville, Alabama, builds communities across Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas and continues to expand into high-growth markets, according to the company.

#5516. What real estate agents should watch on Election Day, per NAHB

NAHB’s Ken Wingert on housing and the midterms, from state ballot measures and the ROAD to Housing Act to tariffs, labor and mortgage rates.

Housing may not be on many ballots by name on Nov. 3, but it’s running through nearly every race.

With the midterms set for Tuesday, candidates from both parties are pitching voters on affordability. Lawmakers are campaigning on the recently passed 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, states from California to Massachusetts are voting on measures meant to make building easier, and homebuilders are grappling with tariffs and immigration enforcement that have driven up costs and thinned out job-site crews.

Inman spoke with Ken Wingert, chief advocacy officer at the National Association of Home Builders, about the races and ballot measures NAHB is watching, whether data centers are really competing with housing for land, and what agents should keep an eye on as votes are counted.

Inman: What are two or three outcomes to the midterms you think matter most for housing — on the federal- level and state-level?

Ken Wingert: The overall theme is that this is turning out to be, once again, an affordability election, and housing is at the top of that pain point … because we don’t have enough of it. So regardless of who controls Congress or who wins the governor’s race in any given state, I think housing will be near or at the top of the agenda going into 2027. That gives us, and other groups you’re probably talking to, a lot of opportunity to advocate for more housing supply.

On specific issues, people are starting to understand that supply matters. You’re seeing ballot initiatives in a number of states aimed at making it easier for builders to build and cutting some of that red tape. Members of Congress are running on the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. Congress is still debating permitting reform that may pass in the lame-duck session or get kicked to the next Congress.

From a congressional standpoint, if Democrats win at least one chamber, there will probably be more pushback and oversight on issues like tariffs and immigration, which have made it harder for builders to build more housing, or at least more expensive.

Are there specific races that NAHB is watching closely, at the state, federal or local level?

We’re not quite NAR size, but we’re involved in a lot. At the federal level, I think we’ll see how big a wave is, if one materializes, and whether it takes out some folks who have been very helpful on housing over the years.

Financial Services Chairman French Hill will be fine, I think, but he’s in a tighter race than expected. Mike Hill, chairman of the House Financial Services Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, faces the same challenge. In Michigan, Bill Huizenga is a former Realtor and builder. Sherrod Brown, former chair of the Banking Committee, is potentially coming back to the Senate from Ohio. A lot of folks are watching that race.

But really, at the state level: California has a couple of ballot initiatives, one in particular we’ve been involved with on changes to CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act. The legislature had made some changes, and this would codify them in state law. In Massachusetts, we’re supporting a ballot initiative that would reduce minimum lot sizes, meaning how big your lot has to be to build on it. And there are a bunch of funding ballot initiatives around the country. All of those aim to increase supply, so we’re keyed in on those state-level races.

I’ve seen candidates from both parties campaigning on the recently passed ROAD to Housing Act. Does that kind of policy achievement resonate with voters, or does a general affordability pitch resonate more?

Both parties are campaigning on the fact that Congress passed major housing legislation with overwhelming bipartisan support. Beyond affordability, another theme in this election is that people want less divisiveness and more collaboration to solve problems. ROAD to Housing was a great example of both parties giving up a few things to get a bill they wanted.

I don’t know that the average voter is digging into a bill with 60 titles, but they understand that Congress recognized a housing supply problem and is at least trying to fix it. If I’m running for Congress, that’s something I’m going to go out and tell people.

Have you noticed more local candidates running explicitly on pro-housing or YIMBY platforms? Any examples?

Our state and local associations make their own endorsements and funding decisions, so, honestly, I’m too far removed to say whether a certain state rep in Texas is doing X.

One interesting part of this election is that the NIMBY focus has shifted from housing to data centers. The recognition that we need more housing has shifted more in the YIMBY direction. That’s a dynamic we’re not encouraging, because data centers are a separate issue, but it’s been interesting.

Talking to our locals, more folks at the city council and county level, where the rubber really meets the road on development, are talking about the need to build more affordable and workforce housing.

We’ve seen in our own polling a real desire, and real angst, from younger voters who feel they can’t afford a home, and from their parents, who are also worried their kids can’t afford a home, may be living with them for a long time, and want them to stay in their state and area and raise their families there. That underlying affordability challenge is driving a lot of the rhetoric and, quite frankly, a lot of the ads. They may not mention housing specifically, but it’s embedded in broader affordability concerns.

You mentioned data centers. I’ve written a couple of stories about data centers competing with housing development for the same land. Is that something NAHB has seen? Is it a real phenomenon?

I think it’s a little overblown, at least right now. A lot of the areas where they’re looking to build data centers aren’t necessarily areas where you would build housing. So there may be some competition over land, but it’s not as big an issue as people may think.

The larger issue is competition for labor. Residential construction always competes with commercial construction for talent and labor, whether it’s somebody building an office building or a house. That competition is real, but it also means more investment in workforce training and more attention to the trades.

We’ve seen many large tech companies announce they’ll fund apprenticeship and training programs because they also need those workers. So there may be some trickle-down help for homebuilding. But it’s still too soon to see real impact, beyond utilities and similar things.

Speaking of labor, I’ve seen quite a few stories about how immigration policy and enforcement have affected construction labor. Has NAHB seen that, what’s your stance, and how have you worked with lawmakers on it?

We’ve definitely heard a lot about it, especially in the last few months. It’s been primarily in Southern states, but not exclusively.

The big concern from members is that the way enforcement is being carried out, whether at the local level, by ICE or some combination, is scaring off all Hispanic workers, regardless of immigration status or citizenship. They’re coming onto job sites, rounding everyone up and detaining folks for hours, repeatedly showing up or pulling people over in a van on the way to a job site. That’s made it very hard to retain workers or get them to show up, because there’s a fear factor in the Hispanic community about even U.S. citizens and green card holders getting roped in with folks who may not be here legally.

That’s caused delays on job sites and made it hard to find labor, period, because there’s no immediate replacement. That’s why we’re so focused on workforce training.

I think it’ll be a factor in places like Texas and Florida, and in the electoral outcome. You’re already seeing Hispanic turnout larger than historic levels. Some polling shows that even folks who supported the president on immigration, who maybe voted for him based on closing the border and enforcement, feel the enforcement has gone too far. It’ll be interesting to see what the exit polls show.

Inman’s core audience is real estate agents. What should agents pay the most attention to in these midterms? Does it depend on their local market, or is there something general to watch?

Disclosure: I used to work for NAR, too, so I understand where they’re coming from. I don’t know if there’s one particular issue, or whether it’s about the House or Senate flipping. It’s the overall voter mindset. If Congress changes control, or a governorship flips one way or the other, does it have an immediate impact? Does it change the [Trump] administration’s course? Those are all open questions.

Ultimately, voters hope inflation can be tamed, and interest rates obviously drive much of this for agents. Resolving the situation in Iran, and maybe dialing back some tariff policies, could affect the inflation numbers driving interest rates. If we can get rates back down, certainly below 7 percent and into the mid-6s, that will unlock a lot of demand that’s still out there but has moved to the sidelines over the last six months.

It’s hard to see how those things will change, no matter the outcome. They all feel very up in the air.

Yeah, but there’s a certain psyche to it. We saw this after the 2024 election. Everyone’s so wrapped up in politics now that people go into a weird holding pattern for the last month or two before an election. They say, “I’m going to wait until after the election and see, and then make a major decision.”

Uncertainty is a factor, and depending on your political outlook, you may be much happier on Nov. 4, or you may not be. But at least it resolves one more question mark for the next two years before we start a presidential cycle.

I hope that, whatever the outcome, having the election behind us will ease angst for potential buyers and sellers, calm the overall market, and get it moving again.

#5515. Seller’s choice or Compass choice? Here’s what Robert Reffkin said to his investors

On Compass’s Q3 earnings call, CEO Robert Reffkin framed private first marketing as a listing win and traffic driver. He cited 63% adoption in some markets and 68% year over year website traffic growth, raising questions about seller outcomes.  AI Summary

For two years, the case for private listings has come down to two words: seller’s choice. The homeowner decides. Who could argue with that? Not me. I’ve said for years that a seller who understands the trade-offs has every right to keep a sale quiet.

But here is an interesting question: When the largest brokerage in the country explains its private listing program to the people who own its stock, does it sound like a program built for sellers?

On Nov. 5, we found out. Compass CEO Robert Reffkin spent an hour with Wall Street analysts on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. It was a strong quarter. Record third-quarter revenue of $3.9 billion, and the first profitable third quarter in company history. Credit where it’s due.

Analysts don’t ask how sellers are doing. They ask how the company wins. So Reffkin told them. After reviewing the call, eight things stood out to me. I’m paraphrasing, except where you see quotation marks. Don’t take my word for any of it. The call is public. Go listen.

Reffkin introduced three-phase marketing as a listing strategy that helps Compass agents win more business. That was the stated benefit. In an hour of talking, nobody offered a single number on whether this is helpful to sellers or not, only that it is beneficial to the agents and company.

In cities with no industry marketing restrictions, he said 63% of new Compass-brand listings now launch with the three-phase plan. In some cities it topped 70%. He told investors that once the restrictions he considers artificial are gone, a good majority of listings would start as a private exclusive or a Coming Soon.

A choice is something some people make and others don’t. When seven out of 10 go the same way, maybe every one of those sellers got there on their own. Or maybe that’s what’s being pushed at the kitchen table.

He said competitors have tried to label Compass listings as hidden, and that the See It First campaign is part of a rebranding exercise to answer that. He insisted every listing is available to all agents and all buyers. Then he explained the goal in plain English: “We just want you to see it first on our site.” He called that a natural thing for a company to want.

I agree. It is natural for a company to want that. But let’s be clear – it is still hidden from all the MLSs and portals. The name of the program should be “See It First At Compass, See It Last On MLS.”

He reported that traffic to the Compass website was up 68% year over year in September, and said he expects it to keep climbing with See It First. He said the company’s sites now show 89,000 homes you can see early (which means 89,000 homes hidden or not allowed to be shown through the traditional MLS).

Reffkin said that within a year, the website of every sister brand will have the same features and the same inventory that is unique to the company. Sit with that word, unique. A home for sale was never supposed to be unique to one company’s website.

He described the pitch an agent can now make to a seller: list with me, and your home goes in front of every agent on our platform and the 225 million contacts in our system. He framed that as a way to compete against brokerages that haven’t built a platform of their own. He also said the more agents who are on the platform, the easier it gets to recruit more agents and bring over whole brokerages.

Reffkin told a story about an agent in Houston who had a client moving to Dallas. The agent searched the company platform for off-market Dallas listings, and the client made an offer on one. One agent was with Compass. The other was with Sotheby’s International Realty, now a Compass sister brand. It was presented as a win.

I’ve never had a problem with a broker selling their own listing, as long as the seller isn’t hurt. But when a home never reaches the open market, and the listing agent, the buyer’s agent, the lender and the title company can all belong to one company, who is left to tell that seller whether the price was the best one out there?

Three things belong on the record. First, Reffkin says nothing is hidden, and that every one of these listings is open to every agent and every buyer. Second, on the same call he welcomed Open Real Estate and said he sees a path to being involved. Third, he’s the CEO of a public company. Telling shareholders how the company wins is his job, and he’s very good at it.

I don’t fault him for that call. I’m grateful for it. It’s the clearest explanation of the strategy any of us have been given.

Any one of those statements is just business. Put them in a row and you see why so much of this industry is nervous.

Listen to what the listings are for. Winning the listing appointment. Driving traffic to the company website. Feeding leads to company agents. Recruiting other brokerages’ agents. Keeping the mortgage and the title in-house. Every one of those is a benefit to Compass. In a full hour, the benefit to the seller never got a number.

That’s why I’ve started calling it Compass Choice, not Seller’s Choice. Seller’s choice starts with what the homeowner needs. Compass Choice starts with what the company needs and wants, and then gets explained to the homeowner as their idea.

In my read of that call, this was never mainly about seller’s choice. It’s about earnings and the stock price. And when a listing strategy is built for the shareholder first, somebody else picks up the tab. The seller, when fewer buyers see the home. The buyer, when they see fewer homes.

For generations, the American way of selling homes has rested on one odd, beautiful habit. We compete for the listing. Then we cooperate on the sale. That habit is why a seller in this country gets every buyer in the market, not just one company’s buyers.

Compete for the listing. Compete for the traffic. Compete for the agents. Compete for the mortgage. Cooperating shows up in one place only: between Compass and its own sister brands. That isn’t cooperating. That’s a very big company talking to itself.

And here’s a principle, not an accusation. If launching homes privately truly got sellers more money, every one of us would have a duty to shut down the MLS tomorrow. Nobody on that call made that case. They made the case for market share.

There’s also a way to give a seller an exclusive without leaving the open market, but the MLSs and NAR have to wake up and get rid of the Clear Cooperation Policy and replace it with this model: the seller lists with one broker. That broker markets the home publicly and handles the showings. The listing still goes into the MLS, so every agent knows it’s for sale, any agent with a real buyer can call and ask the listing agent to co-broke the listing to their buyer.  Appraisers get the data. The seller keeps control. The market stays transparent. This is what all MLS and NAR should support.

Seller’s choice puts the homeowner at the head of the table. Compass Choice puts the shareholder there. I choose seller’s choice. What about you?

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a nationally recognized real estate speaker, coach, and bestselling McGraw-Hill author, including How to Become a Power Agent in Real Estate. He has trained hundreds of thousands of real estate professionals worldwide and leads the POWER AGENT® Coaching Program. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

Recognizing that many patients value additional time, communication, and support from their physician, the doctors have introduced the CCP Hybrid Choice concierge program as an option for those seeking a more personalized healthcare experience. #5513. AI operations expand to Kubernetes upgrades as IT teams do more with less

AI operations are moving out of the slide deck and into the platform itself. Hiring freezes and smaller teams are colliding with growing workloads, so enterprises now expect the infrastructure layer to investigate, plan and help fix problems.

Kubernetes platforms are among the first places that shift is landing. Red Hat Inc. launched OpenShift 5 this week, the platform’s first major version in seven years, with Model Context Protocol servers, guardrails and agent skills built into the stack. Customers’ expectations of the platform have changed enough to justify a new version number, according to Mike Barrett (pictured, left), vice president and general manager of hybrid platforms at Red Hat.

“We started putting in guardrails. We started putting in agent skills, and now you can really have an agentic experience with the platform,” Barrett said. “The platform itself can actually do things for you. It can notice what’s running.”

Barrett and Ju Lim (pictured, right), senior manager of product management at Red Hat, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how OpenShift 5 builds AI into upgrades, troubleshooting and day-to-day operations. (* Disclosure below.)

On paper, upgrades look like routine, predictable work. In practice, a single cluster can run hundreds of applications, each with its own dependencies, release notes and Kubernetes version requirements. OpenShift 5 uses AI to sort through all of that and produce an upgrade plan, Barrett explained.

“We have customers that sometimes plan this out in weeks and months,” Lim said. “Now, through what Mike was just saying, we have a way where, through a single click, you can actually generate an AI plan that actually does all that risk analysis and assessment for you.”

Troubleshooting gets the same treatment. OpenShift 5 pulls in telemetry, logs and Kubernetes resource metadata to investigate problems and suggest fixes, according to Lim. Every action is opt-in, and a human operator stays in control. Fully autonomous troubleshooting and agentic updates remain in technology preview, according to Virtualization Review. Red Hat’s own site reliability engineering team offers an early test case.

“We run OpenShift as a managed service, and they’re seeing anywhere between an 8x and 10x time improvement to find the root cause of issues,” Barrett said.

Security is adding urgency. A surge of software vulnerabilities and exploits has cut the time between disclosure and attack from days to hours, according to Barrett. Customers want help moving older applications faster, and running existing virtual machines in Kubernetes clusters is part of Red Hat’s answer.

“We felt that really emphasized a number change,” Barrett said. “How people want to work with the platform is completely different now, and so we needed a major number.”

#5512. Why real estate agents wanted Barbara Corcoran for ICNY ’27

Barbara Corcoran (l) onstage at Inman Connect San Francisco 2015, Holly Meyer Lucas (r) onstage at Inman Connect San Diego 2026 |

As our team at Inman began planning Inman Connect New York this January, we asked real estate agents a fairly straightforward question: “In this market, who do you want to hear from most right now?”

The overwhelming response was Barbara Corcoran.

I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about that answer, because I think it tells us something interesting about the current state of real estate, the people who work in it and what they’re looking for from our industry’s leaders.

For context, before becoming Inman’s CMO, I spent years building a $100 million-plus producing real estate team in South Florida. I’ve personally sold more than 1,000 homes, ranging from properties under $20,000 to deals north of $20 million.

I’ve represented distressed sellers, helped families through extraordinarily difficult circumstances and negotiated transactions where getting to the closing table meant everything to the people involved. I’ve also mentored, trained and managed hundreds of agents through slow markets, busy markets and everything the last decade has thrown at us.

My point: I’ve carried the bag, and I understand my real estate agent brethren.

So, all summer when agents told me how much they are struggling (in what should be peak homebuying season), I took that seriously. For the past several months, I’ve heard from some of the most successful agents in the country who were going months without closing a transaction. These are experienced professionals who have built substantial businesses and survived multiple market cycles, suddenly finding themselves in unfamiliar territory.

Meanwhile, the industry around them is in a rather extraordinary state of upheaval. Major brokerages are consolidating, brokerages and MLSs are suing one another, the debate over private listings continues to divide the industry, and NAR is working to rebuild trust following several tumultuous years.

And somewhere in the middle of all this, agents are trying to sell houses while being told to post more on social media, stay hydrated and use more AI.

Our industry has some consequential decisions ahead of it, and the people making those decisions deserve to be questioned. Inman’s newsroom has an important responsibility to cover these issues, and our events should provide a place for the people involved to explain their positions.

But there’s another conversation agents want to have, and I think their overwhelming request for Barbara tells us exactly what it is.

They want to hear from someone who has been in their shoes, knows how to get scrappy in a down market to sell real estate, and can offer an experienced perspective without having to defend a corporate agenda.

One of my favorite anecdotes about Barbara is one that she shares often and seems to take enormous pride in — how gritty she was in her early life. Her LinkedIn bio opens with: “Barbara Corcoran’s credits include straight D’s in high school and college and 20 jobs by the time she turned 23.”

Tell me that doesn’t win the heart of a real estate agent. Our industry has a remarkable way of attracting people who struggled to find their place elsewhere.

Some weren’t great students. Others bounced around between jobs before finding real estate. I’ve met extraordinarily successful agents who can negotiate their way through an impossible transaction, recognize an opportunity before anyone else and build a relationship with practically anyone, and yet were kicked out of school when they were younger. (Looking at you, James Harris!)

Barbara herself has spoken openly about her struggles in school and dyslexia and how the challenges she experienced influenced the way she approached business. (I’ve got a completely unscientific theory about how I think many of America’s top-producing real estate agents who claim they struggled in school but are elite at selling are all actually just dyslexic, but I’ll save that for another time.)

Real estate agents find Barbara’s story particularly inspiring because real estate has always been an industry where people can build extraordinary careers around abilities that aren’t necessarily rewarded in a classroom, and Barbara took those abilities and turned a $1,000 loan into one of the most recognizable real estate brokerages in the country. She is one of us, and she made it out on the other side a literal Shark. And agents love her for it.

To boot, she built The Corcoran Group in New York City, where competition was fierce and standing out required creativity — something agents covet and understand deeply. Long before agents were being told to become content creators, Barbara understood how to make herself and her business interesting to the public. She launched market reports, generated publicity and became a recognizable authority on New York real estate.

She understood personal brand marketing before most of our industry knew what to call it.

She sold her brokerage in 2001 and went on to build another career as an entrepreneur, investor and television personality. And now, after all of that, there she is sitting in a chair on Shark Tank, evaluating other entrepreneurs and deciding which businesses deserve her money.

Barbara understands something that most successful real estate agents figure out, and the new ones need to hear: A willingness to take risks, build relationships and solve problems can take you a very long way in this business.

And she’s spent enough time carrying the bag to know how to find business when everyone else is convinced there isn’t any. Her perspective on this is particularly valuable for agents to hear, if we consider the voices dominating our industry’s conversations right now.

The real estate conversations are dominated by brokerage executives defending their business models, MLS leaders explaining their policies and industry organizations navigating enormous changes; senators are filing FTC complaints against industry leaders, too. It’s overwhelming, and yet, none of it helps Susie Realtor or Mike Agent close a home this quarter.

There are important questions being debated about how homes should be marketed, who controls listing information, and how real estate professionals will operate in the years ahead, and while I do believe all of those discussions deserve a place on highly influential stages such as Inman Connect New York, agents also desperately need to hear from voices right now who don’t have a dog in the fight, who can hunker down on a mic and say, “OK, listen up, this is exactly what I would do right now if I were in your shoes.”

Barbara Corcoran is the real estate fairy godmother who is uniquely positioned to say that, without an obvious bias, something to sell the audience or any other ulterior motive. That dynamic really appeals to agents right now, who are growing tired of the industry’s constant infighting.

A real estate agent trying to figure out how to get their listing sold after sitting for 90-plus days, so they can get their client the win and feed their own family, is less concerned with which brokerage executive launches their AI tool most effectively and who is winning the latest argument about private listings.

Agents need a change of scenery right now, and Barbara knows how to generate business, find the buyer and create buzz around listings that have been sitting for weeks.

She’s also famously candid, and I suspect she will have plenty to say about what is happening in our industry.

My takeaway from the overwhelming request for Barbara is that agents are craving an independent voice of reason. Someone who understands the realities of selling real estate and can speak from experience.

And when our community made that request, we listened.

I want to give credit to Inman CEO Tom Bohn for taking the feedback seriously and making Barbara a priority for New York. One of the things I’ve appreciated about working with Tom is his willingness to listen to the real estate professionals who make up our community with fresh perspectives, while also prioritizing the industry leadership who are critical to our ecosystem as an industry.

We have an opportunity to put some of the smartest people in the business on our stages. I think we should pay particular attention when the people in our audience tell us whose perspective they value.

So, we got Barbara, and she’s going to tell our audience exactly what she would do right now. And we can’t wait to hear it.

Join us at Inman Connect New York, Jan. 26–28, 2027, at the New York Hilton Midtown.

#5511. Compass bars employees from Realtor leadership roles

Compass International Holdings adopted a policy preventing salaried employees and brokerage managers from holding leadership roles at state and local Realtor associations. Compass said the change was informed by a similar policy previously implemented at Anywhere, and the policy scope remains unclear for non-Realtor MLSs.   AI Summary

Compass International Holdings has confirmed that it has adopted a new policy preventing salaried employees and brokerage managers from holding leadership roles at state and local Realtor associations.

In remains unclear if employees and managers currently in Realtor leadership role have been instructed to step down from their positions. Additionally, Compass did not clarify if this ban also extended to non-Realtor owned MLSs.

In an emailed statement a spokesperson for Compass International Holdings told HousingWire that the policy was “informed by a similar policy previously implemented at Anywhere.”

“We periodically review our policies and have decided to extend this approach across our business,” the spokesperson added.

This news was first reported by Inman and confirmed by HousingWire.

Compass acquired Anywhere in early January of 2026. In October of 2023, as part of its proposed commission lawsuit settlement, Anywhere said that it would no longer require brokerages, brokers or agents affiliated with its brands to be Realtor association members, leaving the decision to join up to the agents, brokers and affiliates.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for the National Association of Realtors (NAR) told HousingWire that the association has “served the industry as a member-led organization since 1908.”

“NAR welcomes all staff, agents, independent contractors, brokers and others involved in the real estate industry who align with our mission,” the spokesperson added. “Our members and leaders throughout the nation empower the work NAR does to preserve, protect and advance the American dream of homeownership and the right to real property for all, including by getting the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act passed into law with bipartisan support.”

In July, Compass announced this it was joining the American Real Estate Association (ARA) and that all agents affiliated with the firm through franchises or owned-brokerage operations would receive complimentary membership for remainder of 2026 and all of 2027.

#5510. Garage Raises $41M Series B to Scale AI-Powered Marketplace for America's Essential Equipment, Surpassing $100M in Annual Platform Sales

The platform is already saving communities tens of millions of dollars by reducing the cost of more than 90% for essential equipment including fire engines, garbage trucks, and other heavy-duty vehicles.

NEW YORK, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Garage, the leading AI-powered marketplace for America's essential equipment, today announced $41 million in Series B funding led by Invus Opportunities, along with Infinity Ventures, Initialized Capital, Y Combinator, Benchstrength, and FJ Labs. The round brings the company's total capital raised to $60 million and will accelerate hiring and expansion into new heavy-duty verticals, including public works and sanitation.

The Problem: A Trillion-Dollar Heavy Duty Equipment Market Still Running Offline

Despite representing a $1 trillion market, the process of buying and selling heavy duty assets remains fragmented, opaque, and largely offline. Local governments and essential service providers still rely on labor intensive and archaic means to manage the procurement and disposition of their most essential assets. The broken system strips communities of critical capital and time that could otherwise be reinvested directly back into local communities nationwide.

"Garage is digitizing a massive, trillion-dollar secondary market that has been entirely overlooked by modern technology," said Bryan Kim, Partner at Invus Opportunities. "Reaching $100 million in annual sales with zero logistics employees is a testament to the power of their AI-driven platform. Martin and his team have not only built a highly efficient marketplace, but they've fundamentally rewired how local governments and private operators procure essential heavy equipment across all 50 states."

Garage's Solution: AI-Powered Marketplace Connecting Every Community in America

Garage has built the first AI-powered marketplace specifically for transacting the heavy equipment that keeps America's communities moving. By streamlining every step of the transaction, the platform connects local communities directly to a national market, transforming a complex, months-long process into a modern, transparent digital experience.

"Garage has been a game changer for us. We recently sold an almost 40 year old fire truck for nearly $40,000, an apparatus that traditionally may have brought little more than scrap value," said Chief Rob Reardon, Duxbury Fire Department (MA). "Garage made the process simple and helped us recover real value that we would not have seen otherwise. Those funds were put towards the cost of future apparatus, ultimately saving our community money."

Delivering Unprecedented Value to Taxpayers

Garage is currently serving over 1000 communities in all 50 states, as well as Canada. By facilitating a more efficient secondary market, Garage has saved municipalities an estimated $100M+ by facilitating the capture of higher surplus asset recovery values and assisting with the procurement of pre-owned assets to enhance fleets with limited budgets. Today a new fire truck can cost as much as $2 million while on Garage communities can acquire a high-quality used truck for approximately $150,000, a more than 90% cost reduction.

"An extra million dollars has a real impact on a community. Those funds can be reinvested in schools, roads, and local employees without increasing the burden on taxpayers," said Martin Hunt, Co-Founder and CEO of Garage. "We started Garage to guarantee that every community, regardless of size, can maintain their essential services without bankrupting their town. First, it was fire trucks, then it was sanitation vehicles, but the underlying problem exists across any asset that is expensive, specialized, and hard-to-move."

Garage was founded by Martin Hunt (CEO), who served as a firefighter and EMT before attending Columbia University and later working at Goldman Sachs. In late 2023, after receiving a call from a fellow firefighter looking for a better way to procure equipment, he left Wall Street to digitize a notoriously manual, paper-driven industry. He teamed up with Alaz Sengul (CTO), an experienced software developer and launched Garage which rapidly became the largest source of used fire trucks in the country. The platform recently crossed $100 million in annual platform sales, experiencing over 400% year-over-year growth.

Municipalities and essential services businesses can buy or sell essential equipment today at https://www.shopgarage.com.

Garage is the leading AI-powered marketplace for America's essential equipment. Serving local governments, fire departments, and private operators in all 50 states, the platform modernizes a $1 trillion secondary market by eliminating traditional geographic barriers and manual procurement processes. The company is headquartered in New York City and is backed by Infinity Ventures, Invus Opportunities, Initialized Capital, Y Combinator, Benchstrength, and FJ Labs. Learn more at https://www.shopgarage.com.

#5509. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5508. Mortgage rates ease as buyers gain leverage with concessions, ARMs

Mortgage rates slipped to 7.35% this week but remain high enough to keep buyers extremely payment-sensitive. Economists say hotter inflation data could delay meaningful rate relief, limiting demand to needs-based movers. In many markets, leverage is shifting toward buyers as inventory builds, prompting sellers and builders to offer larger concessions to fund temporary and permanent rate buydowns and adjustable-rate mortgages.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates eased slightly this week but stayed above 7.3%, keeping affordability tight and forcing loan officers to lean on seller concessions and adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) to close deals.

At HousingWire’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, 30-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.35%, down from 7.38% one week earlier. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.56%, a 6-basis-point decline, while 30-year Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans were up 6 bps to 7.22%.

“Since early October, rates have improved about 100 basis points, which can equate to an eighth of a point to 0.375, so that’s helping affordability,” said Shannon Hoff, a California-based mortgage broker at Hoff Home Loans.

Inflation remains a key obstacle. Data released Tuesday showed the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% on a monthly basis in October, hotter than expected, keeping the door open for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its December meeting.

“Because that’s creating uncertainty, I am seeing buyers are still extremely payment-sensitive,” Hoff said. “However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, people were having to pay $100,000 over for the listing price. If your payment is going to change $100 or $200 from where you want the rate to be, in the big picture, that’s not so worrisome.”

First American senior economist Sam Williamson said hotter inflation is likely to prolong the wait for real mortgage rate relief.

“Stronger job growth may give some households the income to move, but elevated borrowing costs raise the hurdle for everyone,” Williamson said in a statement. “Until mortgage rates ease, life moves will keep the housing market moving, while discretionary buyers wait on the sidelines.”

In this context, Optimal Blue‘s October 2026 Market Advantage mortgage data report showed that rate-lock volume fell 19% month over month and 38% year over year. But ARMs represented 17% of total lock volume, the highest share in the report going back to 2019.“ARM share reached another high, FHA gained share and first-time buyers took a larger share across the major agency programs,” Brennan O’Connell, director of data solutions at Optimal Blue, said in a statement. “For lenders, that means the opportunity is increasingly in helping borrowers find the product and payment structure that works for their circumstances.”

As fewer borrowers are able or willing to buy at today’s rates, inventory is starting to build in parts of the country. That’s giving buyers more leverage, while pushing sellers and builders to participate more heavily in financing costs.

That’s the opposite of a few years ago, when rock-bottom rates, intense competition and limited supply forced buyers to bid far above list price and waive contingencies.

“I’m licensed in nine states, I get to see various markets, and a lot of them are leaning toward the buyer,” said Gay Veale, a 30-year U.S. Air Force veteran and owner of Guidon Mortgage Group. “Because of that, there’s often seller concessions involved, and I am seeing people use those seller concessions for as many different ways to do rate buydowns or get their mortgage to be cheaper in the beginning, at least, if possible.”

Veale cited one deal in which a borrower received $58,000 in seller concessions — an unusually high figure — and locked a 6% rate. With a 3-2-1 temporary buydown, a permanent buydown and an adjustable-rate mortgage, the borrower’s effective initial rate fell to 2.75%.

“Around 75% of my clients are getting seller concessions. They’re not all that much, but at least $10,000 is an average for me,” Veale said.

Veale said most buyers using ARMs today are opting for products that provide about five years of lower rates before they reset. That roughly matches borrower expectations that rates could ease somewhat over the medium term.

She added that most of her current clients are “need-to-move” borrowers rather than investors, such as people relocating for a job, dealing with a death in the family, welcoming a new child or trying to get closer to relatives. Investment purchases are far less common than during the pandemic period, she said.

Veale said her business volume this year looks very similar to last year, an outcome she called “very atypical of the market” and not something she expects to see again under normal conditions.

In Northern California, Hoff said weaker demand is allowing some buyers to negotiate steep price cuts and substantial credits.

She pointed to a client scheduled to sign on Wednesday for a new home after securing $50,000 off the purchase price and $10,000 in seller credits. That $60,000 swing would have been unattainable in a hotter market, she said.

“That $60,000 is much more than paying a half of a point or a point higher in rate,” she said. “Not only is it the uncertainty affecting the buyers, it’s also affecting the sellers.”

Down payment dynamics have shifted as well. During the pandemic, borrowers using down payment assistance or putting 3% down struggled to compete with cash offers and large down payments. Today, Hoff said, these buyers are reappearing.

She is seeing “more first-time homebuyers jump in the market with challenged credit, down payment assistance, outside-the-box loans, bank statements. My loans are definitely a lot more challenging now.”

#5507. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

NEW YORK and LONDON, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Pearl Diver Credit Company Inc.
