#5505. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5504. From chaos to close: Holly Mabery says agents need to quell confusion

eXp Realty chief brokerage officer Holly Mabery told NAR NXT attendees to separate headlines from actionable local impacts. She said clearer, story-driven communication and stronger CRM follow-up can help agents win share even if 2027 sales fall below 4 million.  AI Summary

In Holly Mabery’s view, 2026 has been a year filled with chaos. The year started off full of optimism and promise and much like many new year’s resolutions quickly turned. But, Mabery, who serves as eXp Realty’s chief brokerage officer, believes agents can turn the chaos into closed transactions.

“You see a bunch of headlines and does anybody feel like they just want to go back to bed? And then it is like how do I stay ahead? What does that look like? What do I say to people, consumers, team members?” Mabery said during a session at the National Association of Realtors 2026 NXT conference over the weekend.

For agents, brokers and team leaders feeling overwhelmed by it all, Mabery said it’s first important to remember that they are not going through this alone and that other agents and brokers are asking themselves the same questions. From there, the key to navigating the chaos, according to Mabery is figuring out what the most important things are and making them relevant to the person sitting in front of them.

“I can’t teach advanced geometry to a six-year-old. But I can show them the difference  between a square and a triangle,” Mabery, a HousingWire Woman of Influence, Insider and Vanguard award winner, said. “The more you and I make things relevant and connect the dots for people, it becomes easier. But also I find that in connecting the dots, that trust layer opens up and everybody exhales.”

In markets and environments currently experienced by real estate professionals, Mabery said it is easy to allow the chaos to turn in confusion.

“When we have confusion, then there is no action as we lose opportunities. The more people are confused, the more they are afraid to move. It is like being stuck in really deep, thick mud,” she said.

To prevent this from happening with their agents and clients, Mabery said brokers and agents need to recognize what has happened and explain it using no jargon terms and then translate it to their specific market or situation by employing a noise versus action filter. This will allow them to understand what a national headline means for them and what actions they may need to take as a result.

Mabery used an example of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in September, noting that most people feel this is a buyer problem and would have a conversation with their buy-side clients about how this impacts them and how they may need to change their offer strategy. But, Mabery said in her view it is actually a seller problem.

“This is a seller problem because now, when less buyers feel like they can take action, it falls to the seller to take action,” Mabery said. “What are you willing to do in this market to actually make a difference to get people into your home and writing an offer?”

When you provide consumers or even agents with information like this, Mabery says it enables them to feel empowered and hopeful.

“As you look at 2027, I’m not scared for 3.8 million transactions, I’m just hunting for my piece of it,” Mabery said.

With agents and brokers seriously contending with the possibility of a sub-4 million home sales environment in 2027, Mabery said it is important that agents and brokers find news and data sources they can trust, that they get back in touch with past-clients in their CRM and that they work on their story-telling skills.

For Mabery, keeping client-facing messages short, personal and story-driven will enable agents to better connect with consumers and build trust.

“The relationships you and I have are making all the difference in the world,” Mabery said. “The more confidence you build the more you inspire people to take action. When people are confused they stop taking action and we don’t sell anything and that is what we saw in 2026.”

Despite this, Mabery noted that people still move and buy homes due to life events, inviting real estate professionals into their inner circles during some of the most exciting and trying times, but in order to be invited into these moments agents need to build trust in advance.

“Take away the chaos and talk about what is next,” she said. “I want you to calm the fears as we go forward. The more you share your knowledge, your value goes up. And if I don’t take action, is anybody hurt? No. But if I do, I get to help them.”

MWC26 Doha brought together senior industry leaders, policymakers and regulators for three days of exhibition, discussion, networking and dealmaking in Doha

DOHA, Qatar, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MWC26 Doha closed today as over 10,000 attendees from 100 countries and territories convened in Qatar, proving the scale and ambition of the Middle East and North Africa's digital growth and transformation. The result was sharper conversations, stronger connections and a clearer path from policy to progress. We look forward to seeing the partnerships forged in Doha deliver impact across the region and beyond. Thank you to everyone who joined us - and especially to our hosts at MCIT."

GSMA now turns its attention to MWC27 Barcelona on 1-4 March 2027, with registration now open. We look forward to welcoming the region's connectivity ecosystem back to Doha, from 15-17 November 2027.

#5502. Anthropic launches IPO roadshow with $64B fundraising goal

Anthropic PBC today kicked off the roadshow for its upcoming initial public offering.

An IPO roadshow is a series of promotional events aimed at persuading institutional investors to buy shares. Anthropic plans to sell 825 million units of common stock for $70 to $78 per share, which works out to $64.35 billion at the top end of the range. About 23 million of the shares will be offered by the company’s seven co-founders, who are each set to make $250 million.

The funding haul could increase significantly if the banks underwriting the IPO exercise their over-allotment option. Anthropic will enable them to buy nearly 124 million shares within 30 days of the IPO. At the top end of the company’s target pricing, that stock would be worth $965 million.

Anthropic logged $17 billion in revenue and a $536 million operating loss last quarter. Its pitch to roadshow participants will likely emphasize its rapid growth. According to the company’s IPO filing, it generated about seven times more revenue during the first nine months of the year than in all of 2025.

Anthropic’s strategy for maintaining its sales growth doesn’t rely solely on new model releases. It’s also building out a portfolio of tools that make its models easier to use. The three newest additions to the lineup made their debut today alongside the launch of the IPO roadshow.

The first offering, Claude Meetings, is an artificial intelligence assistant designed for video conferences. Workers can use it to retrieve information from business applications and generate project plans. They can then use Claude Whiteboard, the second tool that Anthropic debuted today, to brainstorm the AI-generated content and make revisions.

The company’s third new product is also designed for productivity tasks. Claude Sheets is a spreadsheet editor with a natural language interface. It can be used together with Claude Data, an existing Anthropic offering previously known as Claude Dashboards that moved into general availability today. It can automatically turn Claude-generated spreadsheets and other files into dashboards.

Goldman Sachs, one of the IPO’s lead underwriters, reportedly estimates that Anthropic will end the year with about $52 billion in revenue. According to the Financial Times, the bank expects that number to grow more than tenfold by 2030.

Goldman Sachs reportedly believes Anthropic will achieve positive free cash flow in the same time frame. Free cash flow is a profitability metric that measures a company’s revenue minus operating expenses.

In conjunction with Anthropic’s IPO, seven of its top suppliers will buy $26 billion worth of shares through a private placement. The group includes Nvidia Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Broadcom Inc., Google LLC, Micron Technology Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Reuters reported that TSMC also plans to invest $500 million in OpenAI Group PBC’s IPO.

Anthropic is expected to price its shares on Nov. 18. The company will list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

#5501. RealPlus brings HouseCanary Google Listings to NYC clients

RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to offer HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program to NYC residential brokerages. Active listings can appear in Google mobile search with photos, pricing, and click-to-contact links to the listing agent.   AI Summary

RealPlus is partnering with My State MLS to make HouseCanary’s Google Listings Program available to its New York City residential brokerage clients, giving brokers and agents a new channel to surface listings directly in Google mobile search results.

The integration allows active listings to appear in mobile search with property photos, pricing and agent contact information, according to the company announcement. The placements appear above traditional sponsored real estate ads and include a click-to-contact feature that connects prospective buyers directly with the listing agent.

For brokerages, the offering effectively functions as an additional digital listing distribution channel, alongside portals and IDX, but inside Google’s search environment where most buyers begin home searches. In a tight lead-conversion market with rising online advertising costs, direct search visibility and agent-connected lead flows can help firms diversify away from solely portal-driven leads.

“We are always looking for ways to expand the value and capabilities we bring to our clients,” Jennifer Boucher, the chief product officer at RealPlus and a HousingWire Insider, said in a statement. “This partnership is a great addition to our offerings, giving brokers and agents another way to put their listings in front of prospective buyers and generate direct connections.”

The HouseCanary Google Listings Program will be available to RealPlus clients later in November and will be offered at no cost to participating listing brokers and agents, the company said.

RealPlus said the move aligns with its broader strategy of building listing and data infrastructure tailored to New York City residential brokerages at a time when firms are reassessing tech stacks, lead sources and marketing spend. For listing agents, a no-cost path to higher placement in search results could support listing presentations and seller expectations around online exposure.

The Google Listings Program is powered by HouseCanary, which negotiates agreements with multiple listing services to send their brokerage members’ listings to Google. Participating MLSs include  Arizona Regional MLS, Bright MLS, California Regional MLS, IRES MLS, Permian Basin Board of Realtors, REcolorado and San Diego MLS.

HouseCanary said it also works directly with brokerages, like the three announced Wednesday, to ensure their listings flow into the program via a participating MLS. Brokerages that want their listings included need either to belong to an MLS that is in the program or to encourage their local MLS to opt in.

Over the past few weeks, HouseCanary has announced that real estate brokerages REMAX Advantage, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Florida Properties Group, ENRG Realty, Side and The Keyes Company and Illustrated Properties, all RealTrends Verified firms, have signed on to the program, sharing its listings with HouseCanary via My State MLS.

These announcements also comes as HouseCanary continues to work through its Chapter 11 restructuring. Under the firm’s proposed plan, which remains subject to court approval, HouseCanary is targeting emergence from bankruptcy before year-end, with full recovery for all approved creditors. Management has positioned initiatives such as the Google Listings Program and the AI platform as core to its go-forward strategy while it continues to serve existing customers.

Launched in early 2026 and slated to expand to all eligible U.S. markets this fall, the program is one of several industry experiments that put MLS and brokerage listings in front of consumers in new contexts, potentially changing how buyers first encounter a property and which party — portal, brokerage or platform — captures the initial inquiry.

#5500. Western Sydney International Airport Opens After Bechtel-Led Delivery Program Completes Major Construction Works Seven Months Early

Australia's first major greenfield international airport in more than 50 years delivered ahead of schedule: a role model for future infrastructure delivery in Australia

SYDNEY, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport (WSI) opened to passengers on October 25, 2026, following a design, construction, and commissioning program led by Western Sydney Airport Corporation with Bechtel Australia as Delivery Partner that finished months ahead of schedule. The opening marks a new era of aviation, trade, and economic activity for Western Sydney and Australia.

Jetstar operated the airport's first commercial passenger service, flying from WSI to the Gold Coast. Passenger operations follow the start of freight services in July and cap 15 years of planning, seven years of construction, and a year of testing and operational readiness.

"I offer my warm congratulations to our partner, Western Sydney Airport Corporation, our contractors, and all the colleagues and partners who have come together to make this project such a success," said Darren Mort President of Infrastructure and Executive Director at Bechtel. "WSI shows what the integrated model can achieve when a customer, delivery partner, and contractors work as one team around a clear vision. Together, we transformed a 1,780-hectare greenfield site into a modern international airport, months ahead of schedule."

Since 2018, Bechtel has served as Delivery Partner to Western Sydney Airport Corporation, the company responsible for building and operating WSI. Under this model, Bechtel:

The program combined large-scale engineering with new approaches to sustainability and technology. It delivered Australia's largest earthworks program and reused nearly 6 million tonnes of sandstone from Sydney tunnelling projects that would otherwise have gone to landfill. More than 60 software platforms were integrated into one operating environment covering passenger processing, security, retail, and office systems. A 4.5-megawatt solar system, all-electric heating, and rainwater harvesting are built into the airport. And the new terminal includes extensive innovative elements, from the integrated domestic/international check-in area, a state-of-the art baggage system, and departure/arrival gates able to be used for both domestic and international flights.

The airport is designed to initially serve up to 10 million passengers a year, with capacity to expand as demand grows. It has already helped catalyze AU$19 billion in surrounding infrastructure investment and is projected to contribute AU$23.9 billion to Australia's gross domestic product by 2060.

Building on Bechtel's Commitment to Australia

"Today marks years of hard work, collaboration, and commitment from thousands of people, including more than 330 Bechtel colleagues across design, engineering, procurement, and project delivery," said Richard Freer, Managing Director of Bechtel's Public Infrastructure Business in Australia. "Excellent project set up, led by the Federal Infrastructure Department, strong front-end planning, disciplined project controls, and new ways of integrating complex systems kept multiple contractors and interconnected packages moving towards the same completion date. That's how we finished ahead of the schedule set back in 2018. Just as important, more than half of the workforce came from Western Sydney, so this airport was built by the community it now serves."

Bechtel has been serving Australian communities and customers for more than 70 years with projects spanning airports, rail, mines, mineral processing facilities, LNG installations, refineries, chemical plants, power stations, and telecommunications infrastructure. At peak construction on WSI, the project team brought together around 4,000 people; across the full construction period, more than 11,000 people worked on the project, with more than half drawn from Western Sydney. The program also engaged more than 360 local businesses and exceeded its workforce participation targets for local, diverse, First Nations and learner workers.

WSI is Australia's new 24-hour global gateway, providing domestic, international, and freight services, supporting Western Sydney's long-term growth and Australia's future aviation capacity.

Bechtel is a trusted engineering, construction, procurement, and project management partner to industry and government. Differentiated by the quality of our people and our relentless drive to deliver the most successful outcomes, we align our capabilities to our customers' objectives to create a lasting positive impact. Since 1898, we have helped customers complete more than 25,000 projects in 160 countries on all seven continents that have created jobs, grown economies, improved the resiliency of the world's infrastructure, increased access to energy, resources and vital services, and made the world a safer, cleaner place.

Bechtel serves the Energy; Infrastructure; Manufacturing & Technology; Mining & Metals; and Nuclear, Security & Environmental markets. Our services span from initial planning and investment through start-up and operations.

#5499. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5498. Third spaces perform a star turn in this new Florida master plan

Wyld Oaks, a 215-acre mixed-use project in Apopka near Orlando, is underway with 325 apartments starting. The plan totals 6,000 multifamily units, 300,000 SF retail, and major nonresidential uses after a nearly 2-year delay tied to financing constraints.  AI Summary

In a crowded, competitive and bumpy market, residential developers and builders do their best to stand out in a sea of sameness. Some bet that they’ll seize a competitive edge by leaning into walkable communities with “third spaces,” ones where residents can easily connect with one another and feel a sense of belonging.

Wyld Oaks, an upcoming mixed-use community near Orlando, Florida, where construction is now underway, will put that thesis to the test. In October, Hathaway Development became the first developer to begin horizontal construction at Wyld Oaks, where it is building 325 apartment units.

That’s for starters. Once fully built out, the community is expected to have 6,000 multifamily units and a small adjoining single-family portion with fewer than 100 homes.

Residential, mind you, is only part of the plan. Wyld Oaks is designed around a walkable main street anchored by a large park and 300,000 square feet of retail space. Elsewhere in the community, the master plan calls for two hotels, a medical campus, 1.5 million square feet of industrial and distribution space, multiple other parks, an outdoor concert venue and a gas station.

For Wyld Oaks master developer Joseph Beninati, the goal is to create a walkable, mixed-use community that functions like a complete neighborhood, with daily needs all within walking or biking distance.

“Could you take your car? Of course you can,” Beninati said in an interview with HousingWire TBD. “But the option to walk is going to be there.”

With walkability at its core, Wyld Oaks stands apart from the overwhelming majority of new suburban development in the region, which is largely car-centric.

Getting the project off the ground has been difficult, however. The original multifamily development, which only just broke ground, was slated to begin in late 2024 or early 2025. The delay resulted from a challenging local multifamily capital environment that has plagued many other Sun Belt markets.

The 215-acre Wyld Oaks community is located in Apopka, a high-growth suburb of Orlando that saw its population grow by roughly 20% between 2020 and 2025. Despite this growth, and the rapid growth of adjacent communities, there remain relatively few walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods for residents and visitors alike.

This need in the market was among the top considerations for Wyld Oaks, which was designed with walkability, livability and community in mind.

“It all starts with density, and trail systems and parks, and having everything closer to one another as opposed to further apart. We have multifamily, and we’re working on retail, food and beverage, coffee stores and grocery stores, all within walking distance,” Beninati said. “Run the list. [Residents] need fitness. They need healthcare. They need a convenience store and daily conveniences, dry cleaning, hair salons and barber shops.”

All of the commercial uses designed within easy walking distances in the community will work together to keep residents in the neighborhood, bring in employees to work at the industrial park and various businesses and draw in visitors to enjoy the local shops, restaurants and parks. Once fully built out, Beninati expects, or at least hopes, that Wyld Oaks will become a top-tier regional destination.

“Economic activity begets economic activity. If you’re bringing your kids to the dentist, that allows you to also maybe do a little grocery shopping. Or if you’re going to work out and you’re with some friends, maybe you’re going to go out and have a drink or supper together. When everything is in one place, it allows that to happen,” Beninati explained.

Beninati envisions a neighborhood where residents can get outdoors and meet one another, whether at local parks, restaurants, the community’s future farmers market or other events. For visitors, he wants a community that is memorable and draws people back in.

“For me, some of the softer things would be, are prom pictures getting taken and wedding pictures getting taken there? Or is it a meaningful place that the community rallies around? Is there a Christmas tree, and is there going to be a Halloween event for the kids? Things like that are what make a community something that is memorable,” he said.

Although Wyld Oaks is primarily multifamily and non-residential, homebuilders could potentially learn lessons from it. The community’s emphasis on third spaces – places that bridge work, home and school – where residents can connect and feel a sense of belonging, could apply just as well to many single-family neighborhoods.

Central Florida, like many other high-growth Sun Belt markets, experienced a post-COVID multifamily building boom. A surge in new construction following the pandemic led to a coinciding surge in new deliveries.

In 2021 and 2022, developers delivered about 8,500 to 8,800 new multifamily units in the Orlando MSA, according to data from Cushman & Wakefield. In 2023 and 2024, the number of deliveries rose to about 12,500 and 13,000, while 2025 saw about 11,000 new units completed.

Like many other Sun Belt markets, this surge in completions oversupplied the market and pressured rents to soften. As a result, financing new multifamily projects in Central Florida became quite challenging by 2024, the reason the first multifamily community at Wyld Oaks was delayed by nearly two years.

According to Beninati, the biggest challenge in the multifamily financing environment in the Orlando market over the past couple of years hasn’t been securing construction loans so much as finding equity investors to fund projects. Investors have grown more discriminating, directing available capital toward established developers with strong track records and projects in desirable locations.

In Wyld Oaks’ case, the developer’s reputation and the project’s location and desirable master plan helped it secure an equity partner, despite the challenging environment.

However, Beninati believes local financing conditions may be starting to improve. A slowdown in new multifamily development over the past couple of years means that the market has become more balanced, and rent power has begun to stabilize. That dynamic could help other multifamily projects become more financially viable.

For Beninati, breaking ground on the community’s first phase was a major milestone, especially after a delay of nearly two years. But it is only a small piece of a much larger vision, and bringing the full community to life will take years, with market conditions shifting along the way. Weathering those changes, Beninati said, comes down to one thing.

“I think it’s just patience. This is a business where you need to be incredibly, incredibly patient,” he said. “It doesn’t just happen overnight. That’s the nature of the real estate business.”

#5497. GSMA MWC26 Doha welcomed over 10,000 attendees, as world-first ITU co-location puts MENA at the centre of global connectivity policy and innovation

MWC26 Doha brought together senior industry leaders, policymakers and regulators for three days of exhibition, discussion, networking and dealmaking in Doha

DOHA, Qatar, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MWC26 Doha closed today as over 10,000 attendees from 100 countries and territories convened in Qatar, proving the scale and ambition of the Middle East and North Africa's digital growth and transformation. Across three days of keynote sessions, conferences, and summits, and hosted in partnership with the State of Qatar's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT), delegates explored how embedded intelligence, next-generation infrastructure and national digital strategies are reshaping the Middle East and North Africa's role in the global connectivity ecosystem.

In a first-of-its-kind co-location, MWC26 Doha ran alongside the opening days of the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference (PP-26).

Sianne Ryder, CEO, Events and Industry Services, GSMA Ltd, said: "This week at MWC26 Doha, policymakers and regulators sat side by side with industry leaders and innovators to debate, connect and shape MENA's digital future. Co-locating with the opening days of ITU PP-26 created something unique: a place where those setting the global digital agenda could engage directly with the operators, technology companies and investors bringing it to life. The result was sharper conversations, stronger connections and a clearer path from policy to progress. We look forward to seeing the partnerships forged in Doha deliver impact across the region and beyond. Thank you to everyone who joined us - and especially to our hosts at MCIT."

GSMA now turns its attention to MWC27 Barcelona on 1-4 March 2027, with registration now open. We look forward to welcoming the region's connectivity ecosystem back to Doha, from 15-17 November 2027.

#5496. Mamdani gives nonprofits first dibs on buying apartment buildings

Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed COPA, requiring owners to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling covered buildings. The law takes effect in 1 year, as a 38 building portfolio with 850 mostly rent stabilized units heads to foreclosure auctions.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed legislation Tuesday giving vetted nonprofits a first shot at buying troubled city apartment buildings.

The new measure arrived too late to spare hundreds of rent-stabilized units from foreclosure, a second loss in Mamdani’s bid to protect such units.

Mamdani ran for office and won on creating and protecting affordable housing. National attention has since focused on his efforts to build more housing and cut red tape. His political inspiration and influence have spread to other parts of the country.

Nithya Raman is a prime example. Under a similar affordability theme, the Los Angeles City Council member, also a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, ousted an incumbent to become L.A. mayor.

The Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, known as COPA, requires owners of covered buildings to notify the city and qualified nonprofits before selling. Those groups then get time to make an offer and a right to match a later one. The law takes effect one year after enactment, after the Department of Housing Preservation and Development writes rules.

“This law will give New Yorkers a tool to keep their homes out of the hands of predatory investors seeking to make a quick and easy buck,” Mamdani said at a signing event Tuesday.

He also won in court last week. A Brooklyn appellate panel ruled Nov. 4 that the administration can resume collecting its pied-à-terre tax on high-end second homes, reversing a Staten Island judge who found the rollout flawed. Mamdani says the tax could raise $500 million a year. Other legal challenges remain.

But his administration could not stop the sale of a 38-building portfolio with 850 mostly rent-stabilized apartments. Spatial Equity, an affordable housing developer with City Hall’s backing, failed to close a deal to buy the portfolio before an East Harlem auction began Tuesday afternoon.

The 38 buildings belonged to bankrupt Emerald Equities Group. Banks and other institutions that control about $250 million in mortgage loans will foreclose on each building over three auction days.

Lenders rejected Spatial Equity’s initial $68 million bid, according to a City Limits report. They also turned down a $110 million offer last month, tenant leader Cara Polte told Gothamist.

Polte said tenants will keep pushing for a buyer committed to fixing the buildings. Tenants had hoped to turn her building and four others on the block into a community land trust.

A trust managed by several banks and by Sabal Investment Holdings controls the loans. Freddie Mac partially insured them. Sabal has yet to respond to media requests.

Cea Weaver, director of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, said the sale does not end the city’s effort to force owners to improve conditions.

This setback follows Mamdani’s first loss on this front. On Jan. 1, he stood in a Pinnacle-owned building and vowed to take on bad landlords. He then sought a 30-day delay of the bankruptcy auction of Pinnacle’s rent-regulated portfolio, hoping to find a buyer other than Summit Properties USA.

A judge allowed the sale to proceed. Summit won about 5,100 mostly rent-stabilized units from Pinnacle, which had filed for Chapter 11 after Flagstar Bank foreclosed.

Emerald bought the 38 buildings for $350 million in 2016 and began raising rents on stabilized apartments. It took out another $180 million loan in December 2018, six months before state lawmakers passed tenant protections that outlawed many of those tactics.

Lenders foreclosed in 2024. Emerald filed for bankruptcy a year later.

A state investigation found Emerald had illegally removed 21 apartments from rent stabilization. The buildings had more than 2,300 housing code violations in April. A retaining wall behind buildings on East 103rd Street collapsed earlier this year, days before Mamdani and Weaver visited in March.

About 1,600 rent-stabilized buildings face financial distress, according to Rent Guidelines Board data. Landlord groups blame rent restrictions, including the board’s two-year rent freeze. Tenant advocates say owners like Emerald borrowed heavily expecting rent increases that later law barred.

In June, Mamdani won a rent freeze through the Rent Guidelines Board for the city’s roughly 1 million stabilized apartments.

Landlords sued to reverse the freeze. The case began in Staten Island, but Justice Ralph Porzio moved it to Manhattan in August, handing Mamdani a partial win. In September, the judge ordered City Hall to turn over communications with the board and signaled he would likely not rule by Oct. 1.

Oct. 1 came and went without a ruling, and the freeze took effect for new and renewing leases.

Meanwhile, a federal lawsuit remains pending over a 2019 state law that limits rents on stabilized units. Small property owners sued in November 2025, arguing the law unconstitutionally keeps stabilized apartments vacant.

COPA’s path was uneven until Mamdani took office. The City Council passed an earlier version in December 2025, but then-Mayor Eric Adams vetoed it, and the Council did not override him. A revised, narrower version passed Oct. 22.

“Progress … is something that we celebrate, and also, we know that it is not inevitable,” Mamdani said. “It has to be won.”

#5494. Financial institutions confront the complexities of scaling AI

AI in financial services is moving beyond the pilot phase as banks, capital markets firms, mortgage lenders and other organizations begin deploying the technology more broadly. The challenge is shifting toward managing AI responsibly at scale while meeting strict requirements for security, compliance and customer trust.

The AWS Financial Services Symposium highlighted that transition in May. As financial institutions expand their use of AI, they have opportunities to test new applications without committing to large-scale deployments, according to Scott Mullins, former general manager of AWS Worldwide Financial Services at Amazon Web Services Inc.

“You can spin this stuff up really quickly; you can experiment with it,” he said during the symposium. “You can show that it actually achieves the things that you want to achieve within specific policy guidelines and frameworks, and you can actually evaluate whether that governance is holding.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s ongoing coverage of the AWS Financial Services Symposium. (* Disclosure below.)

Moving AI from experimentation into production requires financial institutions to address a different set of challenges. Beyond demonstrating that the technology works, organizations must establish the governance and operational safeguards needed to support AI across regulated business processes, according to Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst for application development at theCUBE Research.

“Our AppDev research shows that 92% of organizations now integrate AI into at least one stage of the software delivery lifecycle, yet only about one-third have established the governance, security, and operational maturity required for production-scale AI,” he said. “In banking, capital markets and insurance, the gap is even more pronounced because compliance, explainability, and customer trust are non-negotiable. The next phase of AI adoption will be defined less by model performance and more by platforms that embed policy controls, auditability and security into AI-enabled workflows while improving customer experiences and operational efficiency.”

Infosys Ltd. is addressing those requirements through its AI platform, which incorporates safeguards and controls intended to help financial institutions deploy AI while managing risk, according to Rajaram R.K., vice president and head of sales for financial services at Infosys.

“It has the securities [and] it has the guardrails. It has the token economics … all the capabilities that an organization would need,” he told theCUBE.

Financial institutions face stringent regulatory requirements, making security, auditability and recovery essential to their operations. As banks, insurers and capital markets firms expand their use of AI, those requirements take on additional importance, particularly when automated systems begin influencing business decisions. Despite these challenges, financial institutions are among the sectors leading the way in AI adoption.

“The organizations that treat AI as a regulated business capability, not simply a technology initiative, will be best positioned to accelerate innovation while maintaining resilience and meeting evolving regulatory expectations,” Nashawaty said.

Applying those established risk-management practices to AI requires organizations to consider how automated systems access data, make decisions and operate within existing policies. The challenge is extending governance and operational controls to AI-enabled workflows without undermining the efficiency and innovation those systems are intended to deliver.

Financial institutions are finding practical applications for AI in customer service and employee productivity. At New York Life Insurance Co., reducing routine manual work is giving employees more time to provide personalized service and respond proactively to customers’ needs, according to Kristina Welke, vice president at New York Life.

“We really felt there was a lot of opportunity to support them, remove the manual work they do every day, enable them to provide that consultative support, be proactive versus reactive,” she told theCUBE.

Fifth Third Bank is using conversational AI to improve customer interactions and reduce average call-handling time. The bank is using Amazon Connect to support its customer-service operations, according to Kevin Anderson, product manager on the AI transformation team at Fifth Third Bank.

“Amazon Connect really lays the foundation as it solves for not only messaging but voice as well, allows for AI and automation,” he explained.

For financial institutions, scaling AI depends in part on modernizing the infrastructure that supports data-intensive workloads. Cloud platforms can provide the flexibility to deploy new capabilities while maintaining access to existing systems, making modernization an important consideration as organizations expand their AI initiatives.

Mortgage lender PennyMac Financial Services recently expanded its agreement with Amazon Web Services to accelerate modernization of its proprietary mortgage servicing platform, Plaisse. The partnership also includes plans to deploy enterprise-grade AI capabilities and further develop the platform.

As financial institutions modernize their infrastructure, they also need ways to move and manage data without disrupting existing operations. NetApp Inc. is addressing those requirements through storage and data-management capabilities designed to support migration, resilience and performance in AWS environments, according to Jacob Lim, cloud solutions architect at NetApp.

“We create value for customers by making it simple to migrate and run their data in AWS by combining proven NetApp ONTAP capabilities, such as space-efficient snapshots, near-instant data cloning capabilities with minimal storage overhead and storage performance,” he told theCUBE. “Then, there is also the highly efficient data replication and ransomware detection engine natively built into the operating system directly. Combined with AWS scale and elasticity, customers gained resilience, performance and operational simplicity in the cloud.”

Scaling AI in financial services brings new challenges

As financial institutions incorporate AI into daily operations, managing the complexity of those deployments is becoming an increasingly important challenge. According to PagerDuty’s 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, 59% of surveyed banks were actively incorporating AI into their operations, while another 34% were discussing implementation. As adoption expands, institutions must determine how to govern these systems, maintain data quality and integrate AI into existing workflows.

“I think you’re going to see AI really become: How do we govern, how do we use [and] how do we make sure the data’s clean? How does it become [about] helping us be more efficient in what we’re doing in day-in and day-out operations?” Todd McNabb, chief revenue officer of PagerDuty Inc., told theCUBE.

Technology providers are responding to the demand for faster enterprise AI deployment. AWS’ recently announced $1 billion investment in forward-deployed engineering, for example, is intended to help customers develop and deploy agentic AI applications more quickly. For financial institutions, however, the measure of success will extend beyond deployment speed to how effectively AI can operate within existing systems, regulatory requirements and business processes.

Bitcoin treasury stocks are set to react sharply to Tuesday’s US CPI release, as these companies’ share prices track Bitcoin closely and Bitcoin has grown more sensitive to inflation data as a macro asset.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI), published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, measures the monthly change in prices paid by urban consumers for a fixed basket of goods and services. Headline CPI includes food and energy; core CPI excludes those volatile categories.

Markets and the Federal Reserve watch it closely because sustained readings above the Fed’s roughly 2% target influence rate decisions, liquidity, and risk appetite. The October 2026 data drops on Tuesday, November 10, at 8:30 a.m. ET.

Key Events This Week:1. October CPI Inflation data – Tuesday 2. OPEC Monthly Report – Wednesday3. Initial Jobless Claims data – Thursday4. October Existing Home Sales data – Thursday5. October PPI Inflation data – Friday 6. Total of 17 Fed Speaker Events This WeekWe…

Consensus forecasts point to a cooling print: headline CPI is expected around +0.2% to +0.3% month-over-month (versus +0.6% in September), with core also near +0.2%.

Year-over-year figures may be limited by prior data gaps, but models such as the Cleveland Fed’s nowcast project roughly 3.7% headline and low 2.5% core. Energy moderation and softer goods prices are cited as drivers.

A print in line with or below these expectations would likely be viewed as dovish, supporting expectations of easier policy or delayed further tightening. That environment typically lifts Bitcoin (and risk assets more broadly) by reducing the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets and improving liquidity conditions.

Bitcoin has shown heightened CPI sensitivity since the 2022 hiking cycle; cooler-than-expected data has often produced positive short-term moves, while hotter prints have triggered quick sell-offs.

Treasury stocks, whose market values are heavily tied to Bitcoin holdings, amplify those swings. A hotter-than-expected number could reverse the dynamic, pressuring Bitcoin and the equities that hold it.

#5491. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5489. Filing: Amazon’s previously announced layoffs include 95 jobs in Washington state

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 6:11 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 7:26 am

A notice made public Tuesday evening, disclosing about 95 Amazon job cuts in Washington state, is part of the company’s previously reported layoffs in its retail business, not a new round of reductions, a spokesperson confirmed.

The filing lists software engineers, product managers and program managers among the affected employees. Most are based in Amazon’s Seattle offices, but others work in Bellevue and Redmond, at warehouses in Sumner and Pasco, or remotely.

Reuters reported in early October that Amazon was laying off fewer than 1,000 corporate employees, mainly in its Stores unit, which runs the company’s e-commerce business. Amazon confirmed to GeekWire at the time that “hundreds” of Stores employees were affected. The notice covers only employees based in Washington state.

“We’ve adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities,” Amazon said in a statement at the time.

Most affected employees were notified in October, including 43 on or about Oct. 7, when the Stores cuts were first reported. Others received notice in September or as early as July 3, according to the filing.

The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act requires large employers to give workers and the government advance notice of mass layoffs. Washington’s version of the WARN Act generally requires 60 days’ notice when a covered employer eliminates 50 or more jobs within 30 days across its Washington operations, excluding part-time employees.

Amazon has made a series of smaller filings under the state law in the past year, including notices covering 121 jobs in August, 57 tech jobs earlier in the summer and 84 jobs last December.

The latest notice covers employees at 17 Amazon offices and warehouses in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Sumner and Pasco, plus 15 remote workers in the state.

The list also includes risk managers, several directors and other senior employees. Employees who land other jobs inside Amazon before their separation dates won’t be laid off, the notice says.

The Stores cuts were much smaller than Amazon’s major corporate cutbacks since last fall. The company eliminated about 14,000 corporate roles globally in October 2025, including 2,303 in Washington, followed by another round in January that included 2,198 Washington employees.

#5488. Starfish Space loses contact with its Otter spacecraft, ending satellite inspection mission

by Alan Boyle on Nov 3, 2026 at 10:50 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 11:10 pm

Starfish Space says it can no longer receive data from its first full-scale Otter space vehicle, bringing a $15 million NASA mission to inspect inoperable satellites to a premature end.

In a LinkedIn post, the Tukwila, Wash.-based startup said its Otter 24C spacecraft was not able to complete all the objectives for the mission, known as Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY). “Starfish and NASA are exploring opportunities to fulfill mission objectives through other Starfish missions,” the company said.

The Otter spacecraft was sent into low Earth orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Oct. 1. “Following a successful launch and deployment, Starfish established two-way contact with the spacecraft and successfully commanded Otter 24C, downlinking significant telemetry during early operations,” Starfish said.

However, the mission team lost contact with the oven-sized spacecraft during the commissioning process. “An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications,” the company said.

Starfish, NASA and Astro Digital determined that the spacecraft was unrecoverable.

In today’s update, Starfish said it is working closely with Astro Digital to fix the fault protection system and update testing procedures for future Otters.

“Developing new capabilities in space requires taking on difficult challenges, learning quickly and applying those lessons to what comes next,” Starfish said. “The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit.”

Greg Stover, director of the Advanced Research and Technology Division at NASA Headquarters, said in a news release that “commercial capabilities like Starfish’s are critical for a competitive U.S. space economy and strong American leadership in low Earth orbit.”

“Technology demonstrations allow us to quickly test new systems, learn from their performance, and iterate so that we are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible with every mission,” Stover said. “NASA will continue taking on bold challenges in close collaboration with our industry partners.”

Several other Otter missions remain on tap — including a satellite disposal job for the Pentagon’s Space Development Agency, two commercial satellite servicing missions in geostationary Earth orbit, and two servicing missions for the U.S. Space Force.

Starfish Space is also continuing to test an Otter Pup prototype that was launched into orbit last year. Last week, it posted a video to LinkedIn showing a close approach to a target satellite known as ElaraSat. The company says it is preparing for a docking attempt “and a chance to make history.”
