#5487. 10 lawmakers who set records for tenure and age in Congress

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A selection of the longest-serving members of Congress and its oldest record holders, from John Dingell's more than 59 years in the House to Strom Thurmond's Senate exit at 100

John Dingell spent more than 59 years in the House of Representatives. Strom Thurmond was still a senator at age 100. Those two careers sit at the far edges of two different records. Together they mark the outer limits of tenure and age on Capitol Hill.

Length of service and age in office are separate measures. Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, holds the record for the longest service in Congress. He entered the House in December 1955 and left in January 2015. Robert Byrd of West Virginia holds the Senate record, with more than 51 years in that chamber. Thurmond, who represented South Carolina, holds a record of a different kind. He was the oldest person ever to serve in the Senate. Ralph Hall of Texas holds the same distinction in the House. He was 91 when he lost his 2014 primary.

Long tenure matters in Congress because seniority shapes power. Committee chairmanships have traditionally gone to members with the most years on a panel. Jamie Whitten of Mississippi, who served in the House for about 53 years, chaired the House Appropriations Committee. That committee writes the bills that fund the federal government. In the Senate, the post of president pro tempore customarily goes to the longest-serving senator in the majority party. Byrd held that office. So did Daniel Inouye of Hawaii, a Medal of Honor recipient who was president pro tempore when he died in 2012.

Dianne Feinstein of California holds a narrower age distinction. She was the oldest sitting senator when she died in office in September 2023 at 90. She had served in the Senate for about 30 years.

The 10 lawmakers below are a selection of the longest-serving members of Congress and its oldest record holders, not a ranking or a complete list. Some hold records outright. Others are included for the length or shape of their careers. Carl Hayden represented Arizona for more than 56 years in the House and Senate, starting in 1912, the year Arizona became a state. Ted Kennedy held a Massachusetts Senate seat for nearly 47 years. Chuck Grassley of Iowa served in the House from 1975 to 1981 before entering the Senate in January 1981. Each slide covers one career: how it began, how it ended and the record or role that defined it.

John Dingell holds the record for the longest service in the history of Congress. The Michigan Democrat served in the House from December 1955 to January 2015, a span of more than 59 years.

His path to Washington began with a family loss. His father, John Dingell Sr., also served in the House and died in office. The younger Dingell won the seat after his father's death. The seat that carried him to the record had first belonged to his father.

House members face voters every two years. Senators serve six-year terms. Dingell's record rested on winning reelection again and again rather than holding a few long terms. Each of those House races could have ended his career.

The record for congressional service counts total time in Congress, including years in both chambers. Dingell spent his entire congressional career in the House. That sets him apart from Robert Byrd, the West Virginia Democrat whose total he overtook. Byrd's total combined his years in the House with his longer run in the Senate. Dingell surpassed that combined figure while serving in one chamber alone.

Dingell passed Byrd's total in 2013. He stayed in the House after setting the new mark. Each term he served after that point extended a record no other member of Congress had reached.

His tenure also carried him past the record for service in the House alone. Jamie Whitten of Mississippi had held that distinction until Dingell surpassed him. That left Dingell holding two marks at once: the longest service in the House and the longest service in Congress overall.

Dingell left the House in January 2015. He died in February 2019.

Robert Byrd of West Virginia holds the record for the longest service in the history of the U.S. Senate. The Democrat took his Senate seat in January 1959 and held it for more than 51 years, until his death on June 28, 2010, at age 92.

Byrd's congressional career started in the other chamber. He won a seat in the House of Representatives and served there from 1953 to 1959. He represented West Virginia in both chambers. He moved directly to the Senate in 1959, the year his House tenure ended.

Those six House years count toward a second kind of record: total time in Congress across both chambers. The longest-serving senator and the longest-serving member of Congress are separate titles. One lawmaker does not always hold both.

For decades, the benchmark for combined congressional service belonged to Carl Hayden of Arizona, who sat in the House and then the Senate. Byrd's House and Senate years together eventually passed Hayden's total, giving the West Virginian the combined record as well.

That combined mark did not last. John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who served only in the House, passed Byrd's total in 2013. Dingell's record rests on House service alone. It did not affect Byrd's Senate record. The two records measure different things.

Byrd also served as president pro tempore of the Senate. Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution creates the office. The president pro tempore presides over the chamber when the vice president is absent. The officeholder is third in the line of presidential succession, after the vice president and the speaker of the House. The Presidential Succession Act of 1947 sets that order.

Byrd's Senate career did not end with a retirement or an election defeat. He was still a sitting senator when he died. His Senate record therefore covers one continuous tenure that began in 1959 and ended in 2010.

Strom Thurmond of South Carolina is the oldest person ever to serve in the U.S. Senate. He retired from the chamber in January 2003 at age 100.

Thurmond was born on December 5, 1902. He was born in the first years of the 20th century, and his Senate service continued into the 21st.

He took an unusual route into the Senate. He first won the seat in 1954 through a write-in campaign. A write-in candidate's name does not appear on the printed ballot. Voters who want to back that candidate must write the name in themselves. Thurmond won the seat that way.

His first stint in the chamber was brief. Thurmond resigned his seat in 1956. He then ran for the same seat in a special election. A special election fills a vacancy outside the regular election calendar. Thurmond won that race and returned to the Senate.

After that return, Thurmond held the South Carolina seat for the rest of his career. His tenure ran through the second half of the 20th century and ended with his retirement in January 2003.

Thurmond's record measures age in office, not length of service. It rests on how old he was while he held the seat, not on how many years he spent in the chamber. That makes it a separate distinction from the tenure records held by other members of Congress.

Thurmond died in June 2003, the same year he left the Senate.

Jamie Whitten, a Mississippi Democrat, held the record for the longest service in the history of the House of Representatives until John Dingell surpassed him. Whitten entered the House in 1941 and left in January 1995. His tenure lasted about 53 years.

His House career began in the same year the U.S. entered World War II. It ended in January 1995, when the 104th Congress convened. That Congress gave Republicans a House majority for the first time since the 1950s. Whitten spent the entire span in a single chamber.

Franklin D. Roosevelt was in the White House when Whitten arrived. Bill Clinton held the office when he left.

Every House seat goes before voters every two years. Holding the seat that long meant winning his Mississippi district again and again over more than half a century.

Whitten chaired the House Appropriations Committee. The panel writes the annual spending bills that keep federal agencies and programs running. Its power traces to Article I, Section 9 of the Constitution. That clause bars any money from being drawn from the Treasury except through appropriations made by law.

The House traditionally handed committee gavels to the members with the longest continuous service on each panel. Whitten's decades on Appropriations put him at the front of that line.

Whitten's mark counted years in the lower chamber alone. Some lawmakers built longer careers by serving in both the House and the Senate. Carl Hayden of Arizona sat in the House from 1912 to 1927 and in the Senate from 1927 to 1969. His combined service exceeded Whitten's House tenure. Robert Byrd also served in both chambers, moving from the House to the Senate in 1959.

Whitten's House record eventually passed to John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who entered the chamber in December 1955. Dingell moved past Whitten's total while still in office and became the longest-serving House member in history.

Carl Hayden represented Arizona in Congress for more than 56 years, serving first in the House and then in the Senate. The Arizona Democrat held the record for the longest congressional service in U.S. history until Robert Byrd passed him.

Hayden's congressional career began in 1912, the year Arizona became a state. Arizona entered the Union on February 14, 1912, as the 48th state. Hayden became the new state's first member of the House of Representatives.

He served in the House from 1912 until 1927. House members face voters every two years. Holding the seat for that long meant winning one election after another.

In 1927, Hayden moved across the Capitol to the Senate. He won the seat in the 1926 election. He held it until 1969. Senators serve six-year terms. After the switch, he faced Arizona voters far less often than he had as a House member.

His Senate career came after a major change in how senators were chosen. The 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, gave voters the power to elect senators directly. Before that, the Constitution left the choice to state legislatures. Every Senate term Hayden served fell under the newer system of popular election.

Hayden's exit from Congress came by choice. He did not seek reelection in 1968. He left the Senate when his final term ended in January 1969.

His combined total in both chambers came to more than 56 years. That figure stood as the benchmark for congressional longevity until Byrd's service in the House and Senate went past it.

Hayden's record depended on time in both chambers rather than either one alone. Byrd, who later took the record, followed the same route. He served in the House from 1953 to 1959 before moving to the Senate. Daniel Inouye of Hawaii also started in the House, in 1959, and moved to the Senate in 1963.

Daniel Inouye represented Hawaii in Congress from 1959 until his death on December 17, 2012, first in the House and then in the Senate. A World War II Medal of Honor recipient, he was serving as president pro tempore of the Senate when he died.

Inouye entered the House in 1959, the year Hawaii became the 50th U.S. state. He was the first Japanese American to serve in Congress. He stayed in the House until 1963, when he moved to the Senate.

He held the Senate seat for the rest of his life. Senators serve six-year terms, compared with two-year terms for House members. Inouye was still in office when he died in December 2012.

His military record came before his political career. During World War II, Inouye fought with the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. That U.S. Army unit was made up largely of Japanese American soldiers. He lost his right arm in combat in Italy in April 1945.

The Army first awarded him the Distinguished Service Cross for those actions. In 2000, President Bill Clinton upgraded the award to the Medal of Honor. Inouye was one of 22 Asian American veterans honored at that White House ceremony. The Medal of Honor is the highest U.S. military decoration for valor in combat.

In the Senate, Inouye sat on the select committee that investigated the Watergate scandal in 1973. He chaired the Senate select committee on the Iran-Contra affair in 1987. From 2009 until his death, he chaired the Senate Appropriations Committee, which handles that chamber's spending bills.

The president pro tempore is a Senate office created by the U.S. Constitution. Its holder can preside over the chamber when the vice president is absent. The office ranks third in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president and the speaker of the House. Inouye took the post in 2010, after Robert Byrd died, and held it until his death.

In 2013, President Barack Obama awarded Inouye the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously.

Ted Kennedy held a U.S. Senate seat from Massachusetts for nearly 47 years. The Democrat entered the Senate in 1962 and kept the seat until he died on August 25, 2009.

Senators serve six-year terms. Holding one seat for nearly 47 years meant Kennedy had to win reelection from Massachusetts voters repeatedly over the course of his career.

Kennedy's Senate service ended with his death in office. He did not retire from the seat.

He was the brother of John F. Kennedy and Robert F. Kennedy.

Dianne Feinstein was the oldest sitting senator when she died in office on September 29, 2023, at age 90. The California Democrat had served in the Senate for about 30 years.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933. She joined the Senate in November 1992.

Her age distinction was relative, not all-time. It compared her with the senators serving alongside her when she died. It did not compare her with every senator in the chamber's history.

She held the seat until her death. Her Senate career did not end through retirement or an election defeat.

Her place among these lawmakers rests on age in office rather than on length of service. Her Senate tenure was shorter than the multi-decade records held by several other members of Congress.

Ralph Hall of Texas is the oldest person ever to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives. Born on May 3, 1923, he lost his 2014 primary at age 91.

Hall's House career began in 1981. He took his seat as a Democrat representing a Texas district.

He did not stay in that party. Later in his House tenure, Hall switched his affiliation and became a Republican. As a result, he served his Texas constituents under two different party labels.

His age record rests on how the Constitution treats House service. Article I sets a minimum age of 25 for representatives but no maximum age. A representative must also have been a U.S. citizen for at least seven years and must live in the state he or she represents. Article I also sets two-year terms. Every member must face voters again at each election to keep the seat.

Congress has no term limits either. In 1995, the Supreme Court ruled in U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton that states cannot impose term limits on their members of Congress. A representative who stays in office into old age has done so by winning one election after another.

Hall's run ended in 2014. A primary is the contest in which a party's voters choose its nominee for the general election. Losing his meant Hall would not appear on the November ballot as his party's candidate for the seat.

He served out the rest of his term. His tenure ended in January 2015, when the new Congress convened and his successor was sworn in. The 20th Amendment sets noon on January 3 as the start of each new Congress, unless lawmakers pass a law choosing a different day.

Hall's mark is a record for age, not for length of service. John Dingell of Michigan holds the record for the longest House tenure. Hall's record also applies to the House alone. The Senate keeps its own separate mark for the oldest person to serve in that chamber.

Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican, served in the U.S. House from 1975 to 1981 and entered the Senate in January 1981. His time in Congress spans both chambers.

Grassley was born on September 17, 1933. That is the same year Dianne Feinstein of California was born.

He began representing Iowa in the House of Representatives in 1975. His House tenure ran through 1981.

The switch to the Senate came at the start of that year. Grassley took his Senate seat in January 1981.

His path from the House to the Senate matches the careers of Robert Byrd, Carl Hayden and Daniel Inouye. Each of them also served in both chambers.

#5486. Mercor raises $750M at $20B valuation to take AI agent evaluation to enterprises

Artificial intelligence training data company Mercor.io Corp. today revealed that it has raised $750 million in new funding at a $20 billion valuation.

Mercor provides the human expertise used to train and evaluate AI models, drawing on a network of more than 5 million domain experts. Most of that work so far has been for frontier AI labs. The new funding is aimed at taking it to enterprises in every industry, which Mercor argues need their own way to measure whether an AI agent can be trusted with a job.

Co-Chief Executive Brendan Foody said “every job in the economy” will need its own AI agents and that companies will need a way to train and evaluate them on their own work. Mercor spent the past two years building that infrastructure with the frontier labs. The lab business has grown fast. Foody said in a post on X in July that annualized revenue had passed $2 billion in June.

Adarsh Hiremath, Mercor’s other co-chief executive, said a model can score well on a public benchmark and still fail on “the systems, policies and edge cases that define how a specific business runs.” For each enterprise customer, Mercor builds a custom benchmark that measures models against that company’s own standards. Post-training starts from there.

Part of that post-training runs on software from Deeptune Inc. Mercor bought the New York startup in July, and its team had spent the two years before that recreating hundreds of enterprise applications for AI agents to practice on. The company said the new money will pay for research and evaluation infrastructure, including more of those environments.

Mercor did not name a lead investor for the Series D round, which drew corporate money from Nvidia Corp., Salesforce Inc. and Zoom Communications Inc. Returning investors Benchmark Capital Management Co., Felicis Ventures Management Co. and General Catalyst Group Management also participated. Other investors in the round were Fundomo, G Squared Equity Management LP, Glade Brook Capital Partners, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group Inc., XTX Ventures and funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management Inc.

The last round came in October 2025, when Felicis led a $350 million Series C round that valued Mercor at $10 billion. Foody’s blog post on the new round says it included a tender offer for employee shares, and the company has not said how the $750 million splits between that and fresh capital.

Frontier labs have been the main buyers of expert-driven training data so far, according to Jai Das, president, partner and co-founder of Sapphire Ventures. He expects that to change as open models get good enough for enterprises to build on, saying Mercor has built “something hard to replicate” from several years of work with the labs.

#5485. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5484. How the Senate filibuster works, from 60-vote cloture to the nuclear option

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A guide to what the Senate filibuster is, how 60-vote cloture works for most bills and how it changed, from an 1806 rules cleanup to the nuclear option

A bill can pass the U.S. Senate with a simple majority. On most legislation, though, it cannot reach that final vote unless 60 of the 100 senators first agree to end debate. The space between a bare majority and 60 votes is where the filibuster operates. It shapes which bills get a vote and which stall on the floor.

So what is the Senate filibuster? It is a tactic in which senators extend debate to delay or block a vote. The Senate ends that debate through a cloture vote. Passing the bill afterward takes only a simple majority. The vice president casts the deciding vote in a tie.

The filibuster appears nowhere in the U.S. Constitution. Article I, Section 5 lets each chamber of Congress set its own rules. The filibuster grew out of the Senate's rules and practice over time. Because it rests on rules and precedent rather than constitutional text, senators have been able to reshape it repeatedly.

In 1806, the Senate cleaned up its rulebook and dropped the "previous question" motion, which had let a simple majority cut off debate. In 1917, it adopted its first cloture rule. Changing the written rules still takes two-thirds of senators present and voting. In 2013, 2017 and 2019, majority-vote precedents changed how the chamber handles nominations without amending the written rule.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of key moments and mechanics, not a record of every rule change. They trace where the word filibuster came from and how Rule 22 introduced cloture after a 1917 fight over arming U.S. merchant ships. Other slides show how Southern senators used the tactic against civil rights bills.

Later slides follow the cloture threshold as it shifted in 1949, 1959 and 1975. They explain the two-track system that ended the need for nonstop floor speeches and the nuclear option for nominations. They also cover budget reconciliation, which lets some budget and tax bills pass with a simple majority. The final slide covers the current argument over keeping the 60-vote rule.

That argument has two sides. Supporters say the filibuster forces compromise and protects the minority party. Critics say it lets a minority block measures that a majority supports. Presidents of both parties have at times called for changing or ending it.

The Senate filibuster is a tactic in which senators extend debate on a measure to delay or block a final vote on it. The chamber ends that debate through a cloture vote, and cloture on most legislation requires the support of 60 of the 100 senators.

That 60-vote figure is the number that defines the filibuster in practice. It is not the number needed to pass a bill. Final passage of a bill takes only a simple majority.

The two votes are separate steps. A cloture vote decides whether debate should end. A passage vote decides whether the bill itself is approved. A bill can have enough support to pass and still never reach a passage vote if senators cannot close debate on it.

The two thresholds translate into specific seat counts. With all 100 senators voting, a simple majority is 51. Cloture on most legislation needs nine more votes than that. Put the other way, 41 senators can keep debate open on most bills, even when the other 59 want to move to a vote.

Tie votes bring in one more participant. The vice president casts tie-breaking votes in the Senate. On a passage vote split 50–50, that vote settles the outcome. A tie offers no route to cloture, though. An evenly divided chamber produces 50 votes on each side. That is still 10 short of the 60 needed to end debate on most legislation.

The arithmetic has a direct consequence for the majority party. Any party with fewer than 60 seats needs votes from outside its own ranks to end debate on most bills. A party holding 51 seats can pass a bill on its own. It cannot close debate on most bills without support from senators outside its caucus.

The word "most" matters in each of these figures. Presidential nominations and budget reconciliation bills, for example, follow different debate rules. The 60-vote cloture requirement does not govern every Senate vote.

The filibuster appears nowhere in the U.S. Constitution. The founding document leaves procedure to each chamber: Article I, Section 5 gives the House and Senate the power to write their own rules. The filibuster is a product of the rules and practices the Senate built under that grant.

The constitutional text sets no vote count for ending debate. Any threshold senators must clear to close debate is one the chamber chose for itself. The chamber can also revise that threshold later.

That legal footing matters for anyone trying to change the tactic. Because the filibuster comes from chamber rules, altering or ending it does not require a constitutional amendment. The Senate can act on its own.

The chamber has two tools for doing so. One is a formal amendment to its written rules. The other is a precedent set by majority vote, which changes how the rules are applied without rewriting their text.

The House operates under the same clause. It writes its own rulebook, separate from the Senate's. Each chamber's procedures for ending debate reflect its own choices rather than a constitutional requirement.

The argument over the filibuster's future is therefore an argument about Senate procedure. Whether to keep it, change it or end it is a question for senators voting on their chamber's rules. The constitutional text does not settle the question either way.

The word filibuster has a separate history from the practice. It traces back to the Dutch vrijbuiter, meaning freebooter. It reached English through the Spanish filibustero. A freebooter was a pirate or plunderer who seized goods by force.

The term was first applied to legislative delay in the 19th century, after the Constitution's rulemaking clause was drafted. It came to name a stalling tactic that grew from the Senate's own rules, not from anything the framers wrote into the founding document.

The filibuster became possible in 1806, when the Senate dropped the "previous question" motion from its rules. That motion had given a simple majority a way to cut off debate.

The previous question motion worked as a closing tool. If a majority of senators backed it, debate ended. The motion did not require a supermajority. A simple majority was enough to stop discussion and move the chamber forward.

Once the motion was gone, the Senate's rules had no mechanism to end debate. A senator who wanted to keep talking could not be cut off by a majority vote. No rule provided for one. That gap is what allowed senators to extend debate as a way to delay or block a vote.

Without a closing motion, debate on a measure ended only when senators stopped speaking. The majority lost its means of forcing a vote on its own schedule.

Senate historians describe the 1806 change as a cleanup of the rulebook. In their account, it was not a deliberate plan to create the filibuster. The senators who removed the motion were tidying their procedures. The tactic that later grew out of the gap was a byproduct of that housekeeping, not its purpose.

The gap lasted more than a century. The Senate did not adopt a rule for ending debate until Rule 22 in 1917. That was 111 years after the previous question motion was dropped. For that whole stretch, the chamber had no formal way to close debate by vote.

The cloture vote that senators use today is not a revival of the old motion. It is a separate procedure the chamber built later. The Senate has never brought the previous question motion back into its rules. Every later limit on debate came from rules, precedents and statutes the Senate and Congress adopted after 1806.

Rule 22, adopted by the Senate in 1917, created the chamber's first formal way to end a filibuster. It allowed debate to be closed by a two-thirds vote of senators present and voting. That procedure is known as cloture.

The rule grew out of a specific fight. In March 1917, 11 senators filibustered a bill to arm U.S. merchant ships. Their extended debate kept the measure from passing.

President Woodrow Wilson responded by calling the 11 senators "a little group of willful men." His complaint centered on the Senate's rules. A small minority had stopped the bill, and the chamber had no procedure for ending their debate.

Under the rules of the time, a majority that wanted a vote could not force one. Senators opposed to a bill could keep the floor and hold off a decision for as long as they kept debating.

Rule 22 gave the majority a tool, but it set a high bar. A cloture vote needed two-thirds support, not a bare majority. The threshold was also tied to attendance. It counted only senators present and voting, not the full membership. As a result, the number of votes required could rise or fall depending on how many senators took part.

Adopting the rule did not produce an immediate result. The first successful cloture vote did not come until 1919. It ended debate on the Treaty of Versailles, the peace settlement that followed World War I. That made a treaty, not an ordinary bill, the first measure on which the Senate used its new power to close debate.

Rule 22 remains the Senate's cloture rule today. The number of votes it requires has been revised several times since 1917. Each of those later changes started from the original two-thirds standard. The rule also fixed a lasting principle in the Senate: ending debate can require more votes than passing the legislation under debate.

Southern senators used the filibuster against civil rights legislation from the 1920s into the 1960s. The first time cloture ended one of those filibusters was in June 1964, when the Senate voted 71–29 to close debate on the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Among the earliest targets were anti-lynching bills, which faced filibusters in the 1920s and 1930s. At the time, the only way to end debate was Rule 22, adopted in 1917. It required a two-thirds vote of senators present and voting.

That threshold shaped the strategy. Opponents did not need a majority to stop a bill. They needed enough votes to keep cloture short of two-thirds. They also needed enough speakers to keep the floor occupied for as long as the bill was pending.

Strom Thurmond made the most sustained individual effort. He spoke for 24 hours and 18 minutes against the bill that became the Civil Rights Act of 1957. No single senator has a longer speech on record.

That record measures one senator's time on the floor, not the total length of a filibuster carried by a group. Thurmond also spoke under a stricter cloture standard than the one in place in 1964. At the time, the bar was two-thirds of the entire Senate. Absent senators did not lower the number of votes needed.

The 1964 fight took place after a 1959 change returned the threshold to two-thirds of senators present and voting. Richard Russell led the Southern opposition to the bill. When the cloture vote came in June, 71 senators voted yes and 29 voted no. With 100 senators voting, cloture needed 67 votes. Supporters cleared that mark by four.

The vote did not change Rule 22 itself. It showed that the existing two-thirds threshold could be met on a civil rights bill. Opponents had kept earlier civil rights bills from reaching that mark for decades.

The Senate changed its cloture threshold three times between 1949 and 1975. The 1975 change set the modern standard for most business: three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn.

The 1949 change pulled in two directions at once. It made cloture available on any matter before the Senate, widening the range of business that debate limits could reach. It also required two-thirds of the entire Senate rather than two-thirds of those voting. With 96 senators serving at the time, that meant 64 votes, no matter how many members showed up.

The difference mattered in practice. Under a present-and-voting standard, absences shrink the number of votes needed. Under a full-Senate standard, they do not. A senator who skipped the vote had the same effect on the count as one who voted no.

The 1959 change reversed that piece of the 1949 rule. The Senate went back to measuring two-thirds against senators present and voting, the basis the original 1917 version of Rule 22 had used. If every seat in a 100-member chamber is filled and every senator votes, two-thirds works out to 67 votes.

The 1975 change lowered the bar for most business to three-fifths. In a 100-seat chamber with no vacancies, that is 60 votes. A two-thirds standard with full attendance would require 67. The 1975 rule cut that requirement by seven votes.

The 1975 standard also changed what the count is based on. It ties the threshold to senators who hold their seats, not to senators who happen to be on the floor. Absences no longer reduce the number of votes cloture needs. In that respect, the 1975 rule echoes the full-Senate logic of 1949, applied to a smaller fraction.

The 1975 change did not cover every question. Ending debate on a proposal to change the Senate's rules still takes two-thirds of senators present and voting. The 60-vote figure therefore describes most legislation, not every matter on which the Senate may try to close debate.

The two-track system, developed in the 1970s by Senate leaders Mike Mansfield and Robert Byrd, lets the Senate set aside a bill that is being filibustered and turn to other business. That change lowered the cost of mounting a filibuster.

Before two-track, a filibustered bill occupied the floor. As long as senators kept debate going on that measure, the rest of the chamber's work waited behind it. Under the newer arrangement, the contested bill can sit on one track while the Senate moves other legislation and business on another.

A senator no longer has to hold the floor continuously to keep a filibuster alive. Opponents no longer pay a physical price for blocking a bill. The image of a lawmaker speaking for hours to stall a vote belongs to an older form of the tactic, often called the talking filibuster.

In the modern Senate, a notice of opposition does much of that work. When senators signal that they object to a measure moving forward, it in effect needs 60 votes to advance. That holds for most legislation. The filibuster shifted from a test of stamina on the floor to a standing vote threshold.

The burden moved with it. Under the talking filibuster, opponents had to keep speaking to block a bill. Under two-track, a bill's supporters must instead find 60 votes to move it forward.

Meeting that threshold follows a fixed sequence. It starts when 16 senators file a cloture petition. The vote on that petition does not take place at once. It comes after an intervening day.

A successful cloture vote does not close debate on the spot. Up to 30 hours of further debate can follow before the Senate takes up the underlying question. Between the petition, the intervening day and the post-cloture debate, even a cloture effort with enough votes can span more than one day of floor time.

The Senate removed the filibuster for presidential nominations in two steps, both made by simple-majority precedent. Democrats ended it for executive branch nominees and most judicial nominees in November 2013. Republicans extended the change to Supreme Court nominees in April 2017.

Both moves are widely known as the nuclear option. The nickname points to the method rather than to any single result. Each majority established its new standard by a simple vote. The standard then stood as precedent for later sessions of the Senate.

The method matters because the formal route is far harder. Amending the Senate's rules requires ending debate on the rules change itself. That step takes two-thirds of senators present and voting. A precedent set by majority vote sidesteps that higher bar.

The first step came under Majority Leader Harry Reid. In November 2013, Senate Democrats established that cloture on executive nominations needed only a simple majority. The same standard applied to judicial nominations below the Supreme Court. A minority could no longer hold up those nominees by denying 60 votes.

Supreme Court nominations stayed outside the 2013 change. A nominee to the high court could still be filibustered under Reid's precedent.

That exception closed in April 2017. Republicans, then led by Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, set a precedent applying the simple-majority standard to Supreme Court nominees. The change cleared the way for Neil Gorsuch to join the court.

A third precedent followed in 2019. It cut the time allowed for debate after cloture to two hours for most nominees. Under the general cloture rule, up to 30 hours of debate can follow a successful cloture vote. The 2019 precedent kept the longer window for legislation and shortened it for most nominations.

Taken together, the three precedents created a split system. Nominations now advance by majority vote. Most legislation still needs 60 votes to end debate. The legislative filibuster remains in place, even though the nominations filibuster is gone.

Budget reconciliation lets certain budget and tax bills pass the Senate by a simple majority, with no opening for a filibuster. Congress has also written a few narrower exceptions into federal statute.

Reconciliation comes from the Congressional Budget Act of 1974. That law caps Senate debate on a reconciliation bill at 20 hours. Once that time is used up, the bill can come to a vote. It needs only a simple majority to pass.

The time limit is what takes the filibuster out of play. A filibuster depends on stretching debate so that a vote never arrives. On most legislation, the only way to stop it is a cloture vote backed by 60 senators. A reconciliation bill has a fixed endpoint. The minority cannot hold it off by talking.

That changes the vote math. With all 100 senators voting, a simple majority is 51, nine fewer than the 60 needed for cloture on most bills.

Parties have turned to reconciliation for major budget and tax legislation. The 2017 tax law went through this process. So did the 2021 American Rescue Plan and the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. Each of those bills cleared the Senate without a 60-vote cloture threshold standing in the way.

The debt limit has received its own treatment. In December 2021, Congress set up a one-time expedited procedure for raising it. As a single-use arrangement, it did not create a standing exception for future debt-limit increases.

Some categories of legislation are shielded from the filibuster by statute. Certain trade measures fall into this group. Certain war powers measures do as well. In those cases, the protection comes from a law passed by Congress rather than from the Senate's own rulebook.

Each of these routes applies only to a defined type of measure. Bills outside those categories remain subject to the 60-vote cloture requirement that governs most legislation. A bill that does not qualify must clear the regular cloture process before it can reach a final vote.

The modern debate over the filibuster turns on whether most legislation should still need 60 votes to end debate in the Senate. A voting rights bill tested that question in January 2022, when it fell short of the 60 votes needed to advance.

Democrats then pushed to change the Senate's rules so the bill could move forward. That push also failed. Two members of their own party, Sens. Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema, opposed the change. Their opposition was enough to stop it.

The rules-change push was a fight over procedure as well as policy. Amending Rule 22 through the formal route would require two-thirds of senators present and voting to end debate on the change itself. The Senate has taken a shorter path before, setting new precedents by simple majority instead of rewriting the rule. A change made that way needs only a simple majority, so defections from inside the majority party can sink it.

Supporters of the filibuster argue that it pushes the two parties toward compromise and shields the Senate's minority party. Under the 60-vote standard for most legislation, a bill's backers generally need at least some votes from senators outside their own party. The exception is a party that holds 60 seats on its own.

Opponents counter that the filibuster hands a minority of senators the power to stop measures with majority backing. The numbers behind that complaint are straightforward. If 41 senators refuse to vote for cloture, debate on most bills cannot be cut off. That is true even though final passage of the same bill would need only a simple majority.

The question has not belonged to one party. Presidents from both sides of the aisle have, at different points, urged changes to the filibuster or called for scrapping it.

The 1939 film Mr. Smith Goes to Washington remains the usual pop-culture reference for the filibuster. It depicts the talking version, in which a senator holds the floor by speaking for as long as possible. The current argument centers on the 60-vote threshold rather than marathon floor speeches.

#5483. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5482. S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months after every midterm since 1950, LPL says

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How the stock market after midterm elections behaved across nine S&P 500 midterm years from 1974 to 2022, and what stocks did in the 12 months that followed

Midterm election years have a reputation on Wall Street as the softest stretch of the four-year presidential cycle. The year after the vote has a different record. The S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after every midterm election since 1950, according to LPL Research.

That contrast between a shaky run-up and a firmer aftermath is the pattern this slideshow examines. Tracking the stock market after midterm elections means looking at more than politics, though. The vote rarely arrives alone. It lands alongside interest rate decisions, recessions, wars, oil shocks and financial crises.

This slideshow walks through nine midterm years, from 1974 to 2022. It also includes one slide on the broader presidential cycle pattern. The nine years are a selection, not a complete record. The 2006 and 2014 midterms are not covered, and the S&P 500 finished higher in both of those years.

Each year follows the same thread. It starts with the date of the election and the backdrop for markets that year. It then looks at whether the year's market low came before or after the vote. The last part covers what stocks did in the year that followed.

The answers vary. In 1974, the index fell about 30% during Watergate and a deep bear market. In 1982, a new bull market began on Aug. 12, months before the Nov. 2 vote. In 1998, the index rose about 27% despite a sharp late-summer selloff. In four of these years, the low came in October, weeks before voters went to the polls. In 2018, the low arrived on Christmas Eve, well after the vote.

All figures here are S&P 500 price returns. They exclude dividends. Total returns for investors who reinvested those payments would have been higher. Percentages and index levels are rounded.

The record offers context for anyone asking whether stocks rise after midterms. It is still a record of the past, built on a small number of elections. It is not a forecast, and it cannot say how markets will respond to the next midterm.

The midterm year has historically been the weakest of the four-year presidential cycle for U.S. stocks. The 12 months after the vote have a steadier record. LPL Research has found that the S&P 500 has been higher 12 months after every midterm election since 1950.

Yale Hirsch, who founded the Stock Trader's Almanac, is usually credited with popularizing the presidential cycle theory. It splits each four-year term into the post-election year, the midterm year, the pre-election year and the election year. Market historians track how stocks have tended to behave in each phase. In that framework, the midterm year is the soft spot. The pre-election year that follows has traditionally been the strongest.

The nine midterm years in this slideshow show how uneven that soft spot can be. Six of them ended with the S&P 500 below where it started. The losses ranged from about 1.5% in 1994 to about 30% in 1974. The three gains came in 1982, 1998 and 2010. The 1998 advance came despite a Russian debt default and the collapse of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management.

Timing is the other recurring thread. In 1974, 1990, 2002 and 2022, the S&P 500 hit its low for the year in October, before voters went to the polls. In 1982, a new bull market began on Aug. 12, less than three months ahead of the Nov. 2 vote. The 2018 midterm breaks that pattern. Its closing low came on Dec. 24, weeks after the election.

The forces behind each year differed. Federal Reserve rate hikes weighed on stocks in 1994, 2018 and 2022. Other years turned on Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, the Watergate scandal, euro-zone debt fears or the end of the dot-com boom. The vote was one event among many in each of them.

The LPL Research finding is a record of the past, not a forecast. Midterms come only once every four years. That means the record since 1950 rests on 19 elections. A pattern drawn from so few cases can fail the next time. Anyone asking whether stocks rise after midterms is looking at history, not a guarantee.

The S&P 500 fell about 30% in 1974, a midterm year dominated by the Watergate scandal and the 1973–74 bear market. The index reached its low on Oct. 3, 1974, weeks before voters went to the polls on Nov. 5.

On a price basis, the index began the year at about 97.55 and ended it at about 68.56. That decline came on top of losses in 1973, when the bear market first took hold.

The political backdrop set 1974 apart. Richard Nixon resigned the presidency in August 1974 as the Watergate investigation closed in. He remains the only U.S. president to have resigned. Vice President Gerald Ford $F took office. In September, Ford granted Nixon a pardon for any federal crimes he may have committed while in office.

The economy was under strain at the same time. The Arab oil embargo, which began in October 1973 and lasted into March 1974, had pushed up energy prices. Inflation reached double digits during the year. The U.S. economy was also in a recession that had begun in late 1973.

Political upheaval, rising prices and a shrinking economy all weighed on stocks at once. The market slid through the summer and into the autumn. The index rebounded from its October low before Election Day.

The vote delivered a clear shift in Washington. Democrats expanded their majorities in both the House and the Senate. The large class of new Democratic House members elected that year became known as the "Watergate babies."

The following year brought a different picture for investors. Stocks rose strongly in 1975. The recession ended in March of that year. The Federal Reserve had lowered interest rates as the downturn deepened.

The 1974 midterm year is an example of a market low that came before the vote rather than after it. It also shows how deep a midterm-year decline could run when a political crisis and an economic one arrived together.

The S&P 500 rose about 15% in 1982, and its turning point came well before the Nov. 2 midterm vote. A major bull market began on Aug. 12, 1982, less than three months before Americans went to the polls.

The index started the year near 123 and finished near 141. That works out to a gain of roughly 18 points. The figure is a price change only and leaves out dividends.

The year's low came in the summer, not in the fall. By Election Day, the rally was already more than two months old.

The backdrop was a deep recession. The Federal Reserve, led by Paul Volcker since 1979, had held interest rates very high to break the inflation of the late 1970s and early 1980s. Tight credit slowed borrowing and spending across the economy.

The National Bureau of Economic Research dates that recession from July 1981 to November 1982. Its official end fell in the same month as the midterm vote. It came soon after a shorter recession in the first half of 1980.

By the second half of 1982, the pressure was lifting. The Fed cut rates, and the recession was easing. Stocks began to climb as the outlook for borrowing costs improved.

The vote was the first midterm of Ronald Reagan's presidency. Reagan had taken office in January 1981, about six months before the recession began. Democrats gained seats in the House, while Republicans kept control of the Senate.

The order of events defines 1982. The market did not wait for the election, or for its results, before turning higher. It moved first, on shifts in monetary policy and the economy that were already underway in August.

The rally that began that summer marked the start of a bull market that ran through much of the 1980s. The index stood higher a year after the 1982 election. Gains in 1983 extended the climb that started in August 1982.

In 1982, the recovery was underway before any ballots were cast. The election arrived in the middle of a rally, not at its start.

The S&P 500 fell about 7% in 1990 as Iraq's invasion of Kuwait drove up oil prices and the U.S. economy slid into recession. Stocks hit their low for the year in October, before voters went to the polls on Nov. 6, 1990.

The index began 1990 at about 353 and ended the year near 330. Stocks climbed into the summer and reached a high in mid-July. The turn came on Aug. 2, 1990, when Iraqi forces under Saddam Hussein invaded neighboring Kuwait.

The invasion took Kuwait's oil off world markets. It also put Iraq's army on the border of Saudi Arabia, near the kingdom's oil fields. The United Nations imposed a trade embargo on Iraq within days. That embargo cut off Iraqi oil exports as well. Crude prices rose sharply through the late summer and into the autumn.

Higher fuel costs hit an economy that was already weakening. The National Bureau of Economic Research later dated the recession from July 1990 to March 1991. The savings and loan crisis was also still weighing on the U.S. financial system.

Washington responded to the invasion with Operation Desert Shield. U.S. troops began deploying to Saudi Arabia in August. A coalition of countries built up forces in the Gulf over the following months. With the outcome of the standoff uncertain, stocks slid into October and bottomed that month.

The 1990 vote was the first midterm for President George H.W. Bush. Democrats kept control of both the House and the Senate. By the time ballots were cast, the year's market low was already in place.

The larger gains arrived in early 1991. The coalition began the air campaign of Operation Desert Storm in mid-January. Oil prices dropped as the fighting started, and stocks rallied on the news. The ground war ended in late February 1991.

A year after the 1990 vote, the S&P 500 stood higher than it had on Election Day. The year followed a sequence seen in several other midterm years. Stocks fell during the year, set their low before the election and then recovered in the months that followed.

The S&P 500 ended 1994 about 1.5% lower in price terms, slipping from about 466 to about 459. Federal Reserve tightening dominated the year. Voters went to the polls on Nov. 8, 1994, and gave Republicans control of both chambers of Congress.

Interest rates set the tone. The Fed, led by Alan Greenspan, began raising its federal funds target in February 1994, starting from 3%. It raised the target six times over the course of the year, reaching 5.5% by December. That added up to 2.5 percentage points of tightening within a single year.

The February move also changed how the Fed communicated. For the first time, it announced a policy decision with a public statement after the meeting. Before that, traders had to infer changes from the Fed's activity in the money markets.

Bonds took the heaviest losses. Prices fell sharply as yields climbed. The selloff hurt investors who had borrowed to bet that rates would stay low. Orange County, California, was among the hardest hit. Its treasurer, Robert Citron, had used borrowed money to magnify the county investment pool's bets on low rates. The county filed for bankruptcy in December 1994 after the pool lost heavily.

The election landed in the middle of this tightening. Republicans won a House majority for the first time in 40 years. Newt Gingrich became speaker in January 1995. President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, faced a Republican Congress for the rest of his first term.

The Fed did not pause for the vote. On Nov. 15, one week after Election Day, it raised the target by three-quarters of a percentage point to 5.5%. That was the largest single increase of the cycle. The Fed made one more increase in February 1995, lifting the target to 6%, and then cut rates that July.

The index then rose well in 1995 as the economy slowed without tipping into recession.

The S&P 500 gained about 27% in 1998, a midterm year interrupted by a steep selloff in late summer. Stocks bottomed in early October, about a month before the Nov. 3 election, after the Federal Reserve began cutting interest rates.

The year started calmly. The index opened 1998 near 970 and pushed higher through the spring and early summer. Investors were still absorbing the Asian financial crisis of 1997. That crisis had hit currencies and stock markets in Thailand, South Korea and Indonesia.

The trouble arrived in August. On Aug. 17, 1998, Russia devalued the ruble and defaulted on its domestic government debt. The move rattled bond markets worldwide. Investors fled riskier assets and crowded into U.S. Treasurys.

That flight to safety upended Long-Term Capital Management. The Greenwich, Connecticut, hedge fund was run by John Meriwether, a former Salomon Brothers executive. Its partners included Nobel-winning economists Myron Scholes and Robert Merton. LTCM had made heavily leveraged bets that price gaps between related bonds would narrow. After the Russian default, those gaps widened instead. The fund's capital collapsed within weeks.

In September 1998, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brought together a group of Wall Street firms to recapitalize the fund. The rescue used private money rather than public funds. Its aim was to prevent a disorderly unwinding of LTCM's positions across global markets.

The Fed then moved on rates. It cut its federal funds target three times that autumn, on Sept. 29, Oct. 15 and Nov. 17. Each cut was a quarter of a percentage point. The October cut was an unscheduled move. It came between the central bank's regular policy meetings.

The index climbed from its early October low through the weeks before and after the midterm vote. The gains held through political turmoil at the end of the year. The House impeached President Bill Clinton on Dec. 19, 1998. The S&P 500 still finished the year at about 1,229.

The recovery carried into the next year. Stocks rose again in 1999, with technology shares leading the market toward the dot-com peak in early 2000.

The S&P 500 fell about 23% in 2002, its third straight annual decline after the dot-com peak. The bear market's closing low of 776.76 came on Oct. 9, 2002. That was less than a month before the Nov. 5 midterm vote.

The index began the year near 1,148 and finished near 880. That price-return loss followed losing years in 2000 and 2001. Investors entered the midterm year still absorbing the collapse in technology and internet stock valuations that had peaked in early 2000.

Corporate scandals added to the pressure. Enron filed for bankruptcy in December 2001. Its accounting fraud put reported earnings across corporate America under scrutiny. WorldCom filed for bankruptcy in July 2002. It had disclosed billions of dollars in improperly booked expenses weeks earlier.

Lawmakers acted during the selloff. President George W. Bush signed the Sarbanes-Oxley Act on July 30, 2002. The law tightened rules on corporate financial reporting and auditor independence. It also made senior executives personally responsible for certifying their companies' accounts.

At the October low, the index stood about 32% below where it had started the year. Stocks then recovered part of that ground before the year ended. The year-end close sat about 13% above the Oct. 9 level, though still well below the January starting point.

Republicans won control of the Senate in the Nov. 5 vote. The market low had already passed by then. The election arrived during an early rebound rather than at the bottom of the decline.

The recovery was uneven. Stocks slid again into March 2003, in the weeks before the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq began. That retest held above the October 2002 closing low. The earlier mark stood as the bottom of the bear market.

A year after the 2002 vote, the S&P 500 was trading higher than it had been on Election Day. The timing of the 2002 bottom matched 1974 and 1990. In both of those midterm years, the market low also came before voters went to the polls.

The S&P 500 gained about 13% in 2010. Its losses that year came in the spring and summer on euro-zone debt fears. Stocks had recovered much of that ground before the Nov. 2 midterm vote.

The index started the year near 1,115 and finished it near 1,258. That price gain came in the second year of the recovery from the 2008 financial crisis. Unemployment was still high, and the economic rebound was uneven.

The main threat came from Europe. Greece's debt problems raised doubts in the spring about other heavily indebted euro-zone governments. In May 2010, Greece received a rescue package from euro-zone countries and the International Monetary Fund. Investors questioned whether that aid would contain the problem. U.S. stocks slid through the late spring and into the summer.

Trading itself added to the strain. On May 6, 2010, the episode later called the flash crash sent major U.S. stock indexes plunging and then rebounding within minutes. The event prompted regulators to review how electronic trading behaved under stress.

The turn came from the Federal Reserve. In late August, Fed chair Ben Bernanke used the central bank's annual Jackson Hole conference to signal that the Fed was ready to do more to support the economy. Stocks climbed through September and October as investors priced in more bond buying. The year's low had come in the summer, months before voters went to the polls.

The election itself shifted power in Washington. Republicans won control of the House of Representatives, while Democrats kept their Senate majority.

On Nov. 3, the day after the vote, the Fed announced its second round of bond purchases, known as QE2. The plan called for buying $600 billion of longer-term Treasury securities by the end of the second quarter of 2011. With a major policy decision arriving a day after the political result, the market's post-election moves cannot be credited to the vote alone.

The following year was choppier. The S&P 500 ended 2011 almost exactly where it began. A renewed euro-zone crisis and Standard & Poor's downgrade of the U.S. credit rating in August 2011 drove a sharp summer selloff. Stocks then recovered part of the loss.

The S&P 500 fell about 6% in the 2018 midterm year, and its lowest close came after the vote. Americans went to the polls on Nov. 6, 2018. The index did not bottom until Dec. 24, when it closed at 2,351.10.

The election split control of Congress. Democrats won a majority in the House of Representatives, and Republicans kept the Senate. That left a divided Congress for the second half of President Donald Trump's term.

Two forces shaped the year for investors. The first was monetary policy. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates four times in 2018 under Jerome Powell, who became Fed chair in February of that year. The hikes lifted the federal funds target range from 1.25%–1.50% to 2.25%–2.50%. Each increase raised borrowing costs for companies and households. The final hike came on Dec. 19, in the middle of the late-year slide.

The second force was trade. The U.S. and China imposed several rounds of tariffs on each other's goods during 2018. The dispute between the world's two largest economies weighed on sentiment. Companies with supply chains or customers in China drew particular scrutiny. Investors had to judge how far the conflict might spread and how long it might last.

The index began the year at about 2,674 and finished at about 2,507. That full-year figure hides how uneven the path was. The heaviest losses came in the final quarter, in October and again in December. A partial federal government shutdown that began on Dec. 22 added to the pressure heading into the holiday.

The rebound started almost as soon as the Christmas Eve close was in. Stocks rallied in the final days of December and ended the year above that low. The S&P 500 then gained about 29% in 2019.

Monetary policy changed course during that recovery. The Fed stopped raising rates in early 2019 and began cutting them in July. In 2018, the vote itself did not mark the turning point. The bottom came about seven weeks after Election Day, and the gains followed in the next calendar year.

The S&P 500 fell about 19% in 2022 as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates seven times. The index hit its closing low for the year on Oct. 12. That was nearly four weeks before the Nov. 8 midterm election.

The index began the year at about 4,766, close to its record high, and ended it near 3,840. Inflation was the central problem. Price increases that took hold during the pandemic recovery kept building into 2022. Russia's invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24 pushed energy and food prices higher still.

The Fed responded with its most aggressive tightening in decades. Its first hike came in March and lifted the fed funds target off near zero. By December, after seven increases, the target range stood at 4.25%–4.50%. Four of those moves were 75 basis points each. The Fed had not raised rates by that much at a single meeting since 1994.

Higher rates hit stocks and bonds at the same time. Bond prices fall when yields rise. That left a mixed portfolio of stocks and bonds with little of its usual cushion. Technology and other growth shares were among the hardest hit. Much of their value rests on profits expected far in the future. Higher rates shrink what those future profits are worth today.

The S&P 500 closed in bear market territory in June, more than 20% below its peak. It rallied in the summer, then slid again into the early autumn. The Oct. 12 close of 3,577.03 left the index about 25% below where it started the year.

By Election Day, the index had already climbed off that low. The Fed's fourth straight 75-basis-point hike landed on Nov. 2, six days before the election. Republicans won control of the House, and Democrats kept the Senate.

Stocks ended the year about 7% above the October low, though still well below their starting level for 2022. The Fed raised rates once more in December, by half a percentage point. The S&P 500 was higher a year after the election.

#5481. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.
