#5480. Jim Jordan and the 2027 House speaker vote: 10 things to know

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Jim Jordan and the 2027 House speaker vote, explained through his record, his 2023 bid and the rules that decide who holds the gavel after the midterms

The next speaker of the House will be chosen by a chamber that has not been elected yet. Voters set its membership in the November 2026 midterm elections. The members they send to Washington will then pick a speaker on the opening day of the new Congress in January 2027. Until those two events happen, no one can say who will hold the gavel.

That uncertainty frames any question about Jim Jordan and the House speaker vote. Jordan is a Republican who has represented Ohio's 4th Congressional District since January 2007. He has chaired the House Judiciary Committee since January 2023. In 2015 he helped found the House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. He wrestled at the University of Wisconsin. Before he reached Congress, he served in the Ohio legislature and worked as an assistant wrestling coach at Ohio State University.

Jordan has also been a speaker candidate before. In October 2023, after Kevin McCarthy was removed from the post, the Republican conference chose Jordan as its nominee. He lost three successive floor votes that month, and the conference then dropped his bid. Mike Johnson of Louisiana was elected speaker on October 25, 2023.

The job carries weight beyond the House floor. Under federal succession law, the speaker is second in line for the presidency, after the vice president.

The Constitution says only that the House chooses its speaker. It does not require the speaker to be a House member, though every speaker so far has been one. The winning threshold is a majority of the votes cast for a named person. Absences and "present" votes lower that threshold.

The 10 slides that follow do not predict an outcome. They set out Jordan's record, the events of 2023, the mechanics of electing a speaker and the calendar that leads to January 2027. Each one explains a single piece of how the next leader of the House will be chosen, using facts already on the record.

Jim Jordan, an Ohio Republican, has held the U.S. House seat for Ohio's 4th Congressional District since January 2007. His route to Washington ran through college wrestling, a coaching job at Ohio State University and a stretch in the Ohio legislature.

Jordan competed on the wrestling team at the University of Wisconsin. The university's flagship campus sits in Madison, the state capital. Wisconsin and Ohio State both compete in the Big Ten Conference. His years as an athlete and his later coaching work took place inside the same college league.

After his own competitive career, he worked as an assistant wrestling coach at Ohio State. The university's main campus is in Columbus, which is also Ohio's capital. The Ohio Statehouse, where the state legislature meets, stands in the same city.

Jordan went on to serve in that legislature, formally called the Ohio General Assembly. It has two chambers. The Ohio House of Representatives has 99 members elected to two-year terms. The Ohio Senate has 33 members elected to four-year terms. Jordan served in both chambers. Together they write state law and pass the state budget.

His move to Congress came in the 2006 election. He won the 4th District seat after Mike Oxley, the Republican who had held it, retired. Jordan took office with the 110th Congress, which convened in January 2007.

U.S. House members serve two-year terms. Every one of the 435 seats is on the ballot in each even-numbered year. Holding the 4th District without a break since 2007 means Jordan has won it in every general election from 2006 onward. The 119th Congress, which runs through early January 2027, is his 10th in a row.

His own seat is part of the next turnover. The 4th District is on the ballot again in November 2026. Its voters will choose who represents it in the 120th Congress, the body that elects a speaker on its opening day.

Jim Jordan has chaired the House Judiciary Committee since January 2023. The Ohio Republican leads one of the oldest standing committees in the House, created in 1813.

He took the gavel at the start of the 118th Congress, after Republicans won the House majority in the 2022 midterm elections. Committee chairs in the House come from the majority party. When control of the chamber changes hands, the leadership of each committee usually changes with it.

The Judiciary Committee's jurisdiction covers a wide stretch of federal law. It handles bills on the federal courts, criminal law, immigration, antitrust, intellectual property and civil liberties. Proposed amendments to the U.S. Constitution also pass through it before reaching the House floor.

The committee has a central role in impeachment. Articles of impeachment against presidents have usually been drafted and approved there. The committee approved articles against Richard Nixon in 1974, Bill Clinton in 1998 and Donald Trump in 2019.

The House panel does not vote on judicial nominees. The Senate confirms federal judges. That work belongs to the Senate Judiciary Committee. The House committee shapes the courts through legislation and oversight instead.

Much of a chairman's power lies in setting the agenda. The chair decides which bills get hearings and markups, schedules witnesses and directs the majority's committee staff. Legislation that the chair declines to take up rarely advances.

Oversight is the other major lever. House committees can investigate executive branch agencies within their jurisdiction. For Judiciary, that includes the Justice Department and the FBI. Hearings, document requests and subpoenas are the standard tools.

The gavel does not carry over automatically. Each new Congress reorganizes its committees, and the full House approves committee assignments by resolution. Who chairs Judiciary in the Congress that begins in January 2027 depends first on which party holds the majority after the November 2026 midterms.

Jim Jordan was one of the founding members of the House Freedom Caucus in 2015, and he served as the group's first chairman. The caucus is an organized bloc of conservative Republicans inside the House.

A caucus in the House is an informal group of lawmakers who organize around a shared interest, region or ideology. It is not a formal House body. It cannot hold hearings, report bills or assign committee seats. Its influence depends on members voting together. That leverage grows on floor votes where a party's margin is narrow.

A caucus also differs from a party conference. The Republican conference includes every Republican in the House, and it chooses the party's leaders. The Freedom Caucus is a smaller group within that conference. Its members can press their own leadership from inside the party without leaving it.

The Freedom Caucus was announced in January 2015, at the start of the 114th Congress. It had nine founders. Alongside Jordan, they included Scott Garrett of New Jersey, Raúl Labrador of Idaho, Mick Mulvaney of South Carolina and Ron DeSantis of Florida. The other four were Justin Amash of Michigan, Matt Salmon of Arizona, John Fleming of Louisiana and Mark Meadows of North Carolina.

Several founders later held posts outside the House. DeSantis became governor of Florida, and Labrador became Idaho's attorney general. Mulvaney served as acting White House chief of staff. Meadows later held that job outright. Amash left the Republican Party in 2019.

Membership in the caucus is by invitation. The group does not publish a full roster of its members.

Jordan came to the chairmanship with experience leading House conservatives. He chaired the Republican Study Committee, a larger conservative group, during the 112th Congress. He led the Freedom Caucus through its first two years. Meadows succeeded him as chairman in 2017.

The new caucus moved against its own party's leadership within months. In July 2015, Meadows filed a resolution to remove John Boehner as speaker. Boehner announced his resignation that September. He left Congress at the end of October 2015.

Jim Jordan won the House Republican conference's nomination for speaker in October 2023, after Kevin McCarthy was removed from the post. He then lost three successive floor votes that month, and the conference dropped his bid.

The vacancy that opened the door was itself without precedent. On October 3, 2023, the House voted to remove McCarthy through a motion to vacate the chair. No speaker had been ousted that way before.

Patrick McHenry of North Carolina became speaker pro tempore while the chamber searched for a replacement. The temporary role kept the post filled in name. The House still had to elect a permanent speaker.

Jordan was not the conference's first choice. Republicans initially nominated Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the House majority leader. Scalise withdrew from the race a day later. The conference then held another internal vote and selected Jordan.

The nomination settled only the party's internal choice. It did not make Jordan speaker. That decision belongs to the full House, in a public roll call on the floor.

The first floor vote took place on October 17, 2023. Jordan did not win. The House voted again the next day, October 18, and he fell short a second time. A third ballot on October 20 produced the same result.

After the third loss, House Republicans met privately and voted by secret ballot to drop Jordan as their nominee. His candidacy ended without his taking the gavel.

The contest then reopened inside the conference. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the majority whip, won the next nomination on October 24 but withdrew the same day. The speakership stayed vacant until the full House elected Mike Johnson of Louisiana later that month.

For anyone following the 2027 contest, the 2023 bid is a record, not a forecast. It shows that Jordan won his conference's nomination and did not win on the floor. It does not settle whom the next Congress will choose when it elects a speaker in January 2027.

The House elects its speaker by roll call on the first day of a new Congress. The winner needs a majority of the votes cast for a named person. That vote comes before nearly all other business. The chamber cannot fully organize itself until someone holds the gavel.

The authority comes from Article I, Section 2 of the Constitution, which says the House chooses its speaker and other officers. The text sets no further qualifications. It does not require the speaker to be a member of the House. In practice, every speaker in the chamber's history has been a sitting member.

On opening day, the clerk of the House from the previous Congress presides over the chamber. At that point, members-elect have not yet taken the oath of office. The clerk calls the roll, and each member-elect answers aloud with the name of a candidate. Each party usually puts forward a nominee before the vote. Members are still free to name anyone they choose.

The math turns on who actually votes for a person. That is not the same as a majority of the full chamber. If all 435 seats are filled and every member names a candidate, the threshold is 218. Members who are absent drop out of the count. So do members who answer "present." Each of those lowers the number a candidate needs to win.

When no one reaches a majority, the clerk calls the roll again. The House repeats the process until a candidate clears the threshold. In January 2023, Kevin McCarthy needed 15 ballots before he won the gavel at the start of the 118th Congress.

Once a speaker is elected, the new speaker takes the oath of office. The longest-serving member, known as the dean of the House, typically administers it. The speaker then swears in the rest of the members as a group. Only after that can the House adopt its rules and turn to legislative business.

Mike Johnson, a Republican from Louisiana, was elected speaker of the House on October 25, 2023. He won the post after Jim Jordan's bid ended. He was re-elected speaker on January 3, 2025, when the 119th Congress convened.

Johnson represents Louisiana's 4th Congressional District, which covers the northwest part of the state and includes Shreveport. He won the seat in 2016 and took office in January 2017. Before Congress, he served in the Louisiana House of Representatives. He earned his law degree at Louisiana State University's Paul M. Hebert Law Center and practiced as an attorney focused on constitutional cases.

His rise inside the House Republican conference came through internal party posts rather than a committee gavel. From 2019 to 2021 he chaired the Republican Study Committee, a large caucus of conservative House members. He then became vice chair of the Republican conference, a lower-ranking leadership job he still held when the 118th Congress began in 2023.

The October 2023 contest changed his position. The House removed Kevin McCarthy as speaker on October 3, 2023. Patrick McHenry of North Carolina then served as speaker pro tempore. The House did not take up regular legislation while the post sat empty. After Republicans dropped Jordan's candidacy, the conference turned to other contenders. Johnson won its nomination and was then elected on the House floor.

His route to the chair bypassed the top rungs of party leadership. Before the vote, he held none of the three highest House Republican leadership posts: speaker, majority leader or majority whip. He had never chaired a standing committee. Jordan's candidacy also came before his that month.

The January 2025 vote reflected a basic rule of the chamber. A speaker's election lasts only as long as the Congress that chose him. The 119th Congress runs through early January 2027.

Johnson's current term as speaker ends with the 119th Congress. The members who take their seats in January 2027 will hold a new vote. No House procedure carries the gavel from one Congress to the next. A sitting speaker who wants to keep the job must win it again on the floor.

The November 2026 midterm elections decide who gets a vote for speaker in January 2027. Every voting seat in the House is on the ballot. The members who win those races choose the speaker on the opening day of the next Congress.

House members serve two-year terms. All 435 voting seats come up for election at the same time. That includes the seat of the sitting speaker and the seat of every committee chair. Jim Jordan's seat in Ohio's 4th Congressional District is on the same ballot.

Federal law sets congressional elections for the Tuesday after the first Monday in November. In 2026, that date is November 3. The vote is called a midterm because it falls midway through a presidential term.

The results settle two questions that matter for the speaker vote. The first is which party holds a majority of seats. The second is how large that majority is. Neither will be known until the votes are counted.

Margin matters on the floor. With all 435 seats filled and every member voting for a named candidate, the winning number is 218. A party with a narrow edge has little room to spare. If a handful of its own members back someone else, its nominee can fall short even though the party holds more seats than the other side.

The House may not have all 435 members on opening day. A death, a resignation or an unresolved race can leave a seat empty when the new Congress convenes. The Constitution directs the governor of the affected state to call an election to fill a House vacancy. That process can take months.

The House also has six nonvoting members. They represent the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and four other U.S. territories. They do not take part in the speaker election.

The vote happens before the new members take their oath. On opening day, the clerk of the House presides while members-elect call out their votes. Once a candidate wins, the new speaker is sworn in and then administers the oath to the rest of the chamber.

The midterms fix who sits in that room. Each party's choice of a nominee comes after that, followed by the floor vote.

The speaker of the House is second in the line of presidential succession, behind only the vice president. Whoever wins the speaker vote in January 2027 will hold that place for as long as they keep the gavel.

The order comes from the Presidential Succession Act of 1947. After the vice president, the law lists the speaker, then the president pro tempore of the Senate, then members of the Cabinet. Cabinet officers follow in the order their departments were created, starting with the secretary of state.

The line has not always looked this way. An 1886 law left congressional officers out and ran succession through the Cabinet. Harry Truman became president in April 1945, following the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt. He then served nearly four years with no vice president. Truman pushed for a change. He favored putting an elected official next in line rather than a Cabinet secretary appointed by the president.

A speaker does not step into the presidency automatically. The 1947 act requires a speaker who acts as president to resign both the speakership and the House seat. That person must also meet the Constitution's eligibility rules for the presidency. Those rules require a natural-born citizen who is at least 35 years old and has lived in the U.S. for 14 years.

The 25th Amendment, ratified in 1967, made long vacancies in the vice presidency less likely. It lets the president nominate a new vice president, who takes office after majority votes in both the House and the Senate. Before the amendment, the office could stay empty until the next presidential term began.

Short gaps still occur while a nominee awaits confirmation. Spiro Agnew resigned as vice president in October 1973. Speaker Carl Albert stood first in line for the presidency until Gerald Ford $F was confirmed as vice president that December.

No speaker has ever become president through the line of succession. James K. Polk, a former speaker, is the only person to have held both offices. He reached the White House by winning the 1844 election.

The speaker's place in the line ties a House leadership contest to the executive branch. The speaker is chosen by members of one chamber, not by a national electorate. The winner still becomes the first person in line after the vice president. That link applies to whoever the House elects when the next Congress convenes in January 2027.

A party's speaker nominee is chosen inside that party before the full House votes, but the nomination itself decides nothing. The binding choice comes only on the House floor, where the whole chamber takes part.

The Constitution gives the power to choose a speaker to the House as a whole. It does not mention political parties, and it sets out no nominating process. The internal party step operates outside the constitutional text.

In the House, Republicans organize as the House Republican Conference. Democrats organize as the House Democratic Caucus. Each group settles on its own candidate for speaker. Its members then carry that choice to the floor.

The gap between those two stages is where a nomination can come apart. A candidate can win the party's internal backing and still fall short once the full chamber votes. Only the floor result decides who holds the gavel.

Jim Jordan's experience in October 2023 put that distinction on the record. After Kevin McCarthy was removed as speaker, the Republican conference made Jordan its nominee. Jordan then lost three successive floor votes that month. The conference then dropped his bid. Mike Johnson of Louisiana won the speakership later that month.

The episode showed that a conference nomination opens the way to a floor vote but does not secure the result.

A nomination does not bind individual members once the roll call begins. Each member answers by naming a candidate aloud, and any member can name someone other than the party's choice. A vote for any other person does not count toward the nominee's total.

The minority party also nominates a candidate of its own. Its members' votes count toward the total even when its nominee cannot win. When the majority is narrow, that leaves the majority party's nominee little room to lose votes from within the conference.

The same two-step sequence applies when the next Congress convenes in January 2027. Each party's internal choice comes first. The vote that decides the speaker follows on the floor on opening day.

The next House speaker will be chosen on the opening day of a new Congress in January 2027. Two milestones come before that vote: the November 2026 midterm elections and the close of the 119th Congress in early January 2027.

Election Day falls on November 3, 2026. Federal law sets congressional elections on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November of even-numbered years. All 435 House seats are on the ballot. House members serve two-year terms, so the entire chamber faces voters every cycle.

The votes cast that night are not the final word. Each state counts and certifies its own results on its own schedule. Close races can take weeks to resolve, and recounts can stretch the process further. The membership that will vote for speaker is not settled until those counts are complete.

The weeks between Election Day and the new year belong to the outgoing 119th Congress. Mike Johnson of Louisiana was re-elected speaker when that Congress convened in January 2025. He holds the post until its term formally ends in early January 2027. Members who lost or retired keep their votes until then. A session held in this stretch is known as a lame-duck session.

The Twentieth Amendment to the Constitution sets the timing of the handover. It ends House members' terms at noon on January 3. It also directs Congress to meet on that date unless it passes a law naming a different day.

Electing a speaker is the first order of business on opening day. The members-elect have not yet taken the oath of office when they vote. The clerk of the House presides over the chamber until a speaker is chosen. Members call out their choice by name as the clerk reads the roll.

The chamber can do little else until that vote is settled. Members cannot be sworn in, and the House cannot adopt its rules for the new Congress. If no candidate wins on the first ballot, the House keeps voting. In January 2023, it took 15 ballots over four days to elect Kevin McCarthy.

After a candidate wins, the longest-serving member, known as the dean of the House, administers the oath of office to the new speaker. The speaker swears in the rest of the chamber as a group. The House can then take up its rules package, which governs how it operates for the next two years.

#5479. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5478. The debt ceiling explained: 10 things to know about the U.S. borrowing limit

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The debt ceiling explained in 10 parts, from its 1917 origins and extraordinary measures to the X-date, credit downgrades and proposed workarounds

The U.S. government puts a legal cap on its own borrowing, even though Congress has already passed the spending and tax laws that make the borrowing necessary. That cap is the debt ceiling. The gap between what lawmakers have committed the country to pay and what the Treasury Department may borrow is the source of recurring fiscal standoffs in Congress.

The debt ceiling is also called the debt limit. It is a dollar figure set in federal law. Once total federal debt reaches it, the Treasury cannot borrow more until Congress raises or suspends the cap. Tax revenue keeps arriving, and obligations under existing programs keep coming due. What disappears is the ability to cover the difference by borrowing.

The stakes reach well beyond Congress. The central question in every standoff is what happens if the U.S. defaults, meaning it cannot pay all of its obligations on time. Treasury securities are held by investors, banks and governments around the world. Each deadline draws attention far outside the U.S.

The U.S. credit rating has also changed in recent years. All three major rating agencies have lowered the country from their top grade: Standard & Poor's in 2011, Fitch Ratings in 2023 and Moody's $MCO in 2025. The first two downgrades followed debt limit fights. Fitch listed repeated standoffs among its governance concerns.

This is the debt ceiling explained from the ground up. The first slides cover what the cap is, what it does not do and how it grew out of a World War I-era borrowing law. A fourth slide looks at which kinds of federal debt count against the limit. Two more explain the extraordinary measures Treasury uses to buy time and the X $TWTR-date, when that time would run out.

The rest of the piece traces three recent turning points: the 2011 Budget Control Act, the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act and the 2025 increase under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It closes with proposed alternatives, from a legal argument built on the 14th Amendment to a platinum coin to abolishing the limit outright. None of those ideas has been tested.

The debt ceiling is a cap, written into federal law by Congress, on the total amount of money the Treasury Department may borrow. Only a new law, passed by both chambers of Congress and signed by the president, can change that figure.

The statute sits in Title 31 of the U.S. Code, at section 3101. It sets a single dollar figure for the government's borrowing as a whole. It does not set separate caps for individual programs or agencies.

Borrowing fills the gap between what the federal government collects and what it pays out. Treasury raises that money by selling securities to investors. In any year the government runs a deficit, it has to borrow to cover the difference.

The debt limit runs on a separate track from the budget. Congress decides how much agencies can spend through appropriations bills, which fund the government one fiscal year at a time. Programs such as Social Security and Medicare pay benefits under permanent law and do not need yearly approval. Tax law determines how much revenue comes in. The debt ceiling is a separate vote on whether Treasury may borrow to cover the result of those decisions.

The House has at times tried to link the two tracks. Under a procedural rule known as the Gephardt rule, adopting a budget resolution automatically produced a matching debt limit measure in the House. The chamber has dropped and restored that rule several times.

Changing the limit takes ordinary legislation. A debt limit bill can move on its own or inside a larger package. In the Senate, a standalone bill can face a filibuster, which takes 60 votes to end. A budget reconciliation bill can pass the Senate with a simple majority.

Congress has two main ways to change the cap. It can raise it, replacing the old dollar figure with a higher one. Or it can suspend it, setting the limit aside until a fixed date. Either way, the new room to borrow lasts only until debt catches up with the higher figure or the suspension period ends.

Raising the debt ceiling does not approve a single dollar of new federal spending. The obligations it covers come from spending and tax laws Congress has already passed. The limit decides only whether Treasury may borrow to pay for them.

The distinction comes from the order in which Congress makes its decisions. Spending choices are made elsewhere in the legislative process. Congress passes annual appropriations bills that fund agencies such as the Defense Department. It also keeps permanent laws on the books that set benefits for programs including Social Security and Medicare. Those programs pay out without a yearly vote.

Revenue is set the same way. Tax laws determine how much money flows into Treasury from income, payroll and corporate taxes. When those laws together call for more spending than taxes bring in, the government runs a deficit. Treasury covers that gap by selling securities to investors.

The debt limit enters only at that final step. It does not change how much an agency may spend or how large a benefit payment is. It governs whether Treasury can raise the cash to honor commitments already written into law.

A common comparison is a household credit card. Raising the debt limit resembles paying off charges already made on the card, not approving new purchases. The analogy has limits. A household that hits its card limit can stop buying things. The federal government's obligations keep arriving under laws that remain in force until Congress changes them.

Those obligations span the full range of federal activity. They include salaries for military personnel and civilian employees, payments to Social Security recipients, tax refunds and interest owed to holders of Treasury securities.

The power behind both sides of this arrangement sits with Congress. Article I, Section 8 of the Constitution gives Congress the authority to borrow money on the credit of the U.S., along with authority over taxes and spending. The debt limit is a separate statutory vote layered on top of those earlier decisions.

Future borrowing is shaped through the budget itself. Changing tax rates or reducing appropriations alters future deficits. Declining to raise the limit does not erase obligations that already exist.

The U.S. debt limit traces back to the Second Liberty Bond Act of 1917. That wartime law let the Treasury borrow to pay for World War I without returning to Congress to approve every bond issue. The single overall cap that exists today came later, through the Public Debt Act of 1939.

Before 1917, Congress typically authorized federal borrowing one issue at a time. A law would spell out the purpose of a loan and often its terms, such as the amount, the interest rate and the maturity. That approach suited a federal government that borrowed only occasionally and in modest amounts.

World War I changed the scale. The U.S. entered the war in April 1917. The cost of raising an army and supplying allies far outran tax revenue. Congress needed a faster way to raise money than passing a new bill for each sale of bonds.

The Second Liberty Bond Act, passed that September, gave Treasury Secretary William Gibbs McAdoo broad authority to issue bonds and other debt within limits Congress set. The government sold these Liberty Bonds directly to the public through large national campaigns. Ordinary households bought them alongside banks and businesses.

The 1917 law did not create one overall ceiling. It set caps on particular kinds of borrowing, and Congress adjusted those separate limits by category in the years that followed. The arrangement moved routine borrowing decisions from lawmakers to the Treasury. Congress still decided how much could be borrowed within each category.

The Public Debt Act of 1939 replaced that patchwork. It folded the separate limits into a single aggregate limit on federal debt. That change gave the Treasury freedom to choose the mix of bills, notes and bonds it issued, as long as the total stayed under the cap. The modern debt ceiling grew directly out of that 1939 framework.

That history explains why the ceiling works as a cap on total borrowing rather than a vote on individual loans. Lawmakers have raised, extended or suspended the limit many times since 1939, but the basic structure set that year remains in place.

Nearly all federal debt counts toward the debt limit. That covers money the government owes to outside investors and money it owes to its own trust funds, such as Social Security. The ceiling applies to the combined total, not to either piece on its own.

The first piece is debt held by the public. Most of it consists of marketable Treasury securities sold at auction. Treasury bills mature in a year or less. Treasury notes mature in two to 10 years, and Treasury bonds mature in 20 or 30 years. Savings bonds sold to households also fall into this category.

The buyers of that debt range widely. They include individuals, banks, pension funds, mutual funds, state and local governments, foreign governments and the Federal Reserve. Securities held by the Federal Reserve still count as debt held by the public, even though the Fed is part of the broader federal system.

The second piece is intragovernmental debt. Some federal programs collect dedicated revenue, such as payroll taxes, and credit it to trust funds. When a trust fund takes in more than it pays out, federal law directs it to invest the surplus in special-issue Treasury securities. These securities are not sold on the open market. Holders include the Social Security trust funds, Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, the Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund and the Military Retirement Fund.

Because both pieces count, the limit can bind even when debt held by the public sits well below it. Debt held by the public is the measure the Congressional Budget Office typically uses in its budget projections. The figure that matters for the ceiling, known as debt subject to limit, is larger.

The balance between the two pieces shifts over time. When Social Security collects more in payroll taxes than it pays in benefits, its trust funds buy new special-issue securities. That pushes debt subject to limit higher even if Treasury borrows nothing new from investors.

The reverse happens when a trust fund draws down its balance. The fund redeems its securities to pay benefits, and Treasury generally borrows from the public to raise that cash. Intragovernmental debt falls and debt held by the public rises. The total counted against the limit changes little.

The word nearly matters. Treasury reports debt subject to limit in its Monthly Statement of the Public Debt, and that figure differs slightly from total public debt outstanding. The gap comes from small technical adjustments, such as accounting for the discount at which Treasury bills are sold.

Extraordinary measures are accounting steps the Treasury Department uses to keep paying the government's bills for a period after federal debt reaches the statutory limit. They create temporary room under the cap. They do not raise the limit or give Treasury any new borrowing authority.

The tools work by reducing the amount of debt that counts against the limit. A large share of federal debt is owed to government trust funds and retirement accounts, which hold special Treasury securities. When Treasury stops issuing new securities to some of those funds, the debt subject to the limit falls or holds steady. That opens space to sell securities to the public and keep paying obligations.

The Thrift Savings Plan's G Fund is one of the main tools. The Thrift Savings Plan is the retirement savings plan for federal employees and members of the uniformed services. Its G Fund invests in special-issue Treasury securities. During a standoff, Treasury can suspend new investments in the G Fund.

The Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund is another source of headroom. That fund pays pensions to retired federal civilian workers. Treasury can suspend new investments in it as well. Federal law also allows Treasury to redeem some of the fund's existing holdings ahead of schedule during these periods.

The process has a formal starting point. The Treasury secretary declares a debt issuance suspension period. That declaration is the legal trigger for using the retirement fund measures. Treasury notifies Congress when it begins.

Two smaller tools sit alongside the retirement funds. Treasury can suspend reinvestment of the dollar balance in the Exchange Stabilization Fund, which it uses for operations in currency markets. It can also halt sales of State and Local Government Series securities, which state and local governments buy to manage the proceeds of their own bond sales.

Federal law requires the affected funds to be made whole afterward. Once the limit is raised or suspended, Treasury issues the securities that were held back. It also credits the interest those securities would have earned. The restoration is designed so the funds do not lose money because of the maneuver.

The measures are finite. How much headroom they provide depends on the balances in the funds involved and on the pace of the government's tax receipts and spending. Once they are used up, only Treasury's remaining cash stands between the government and missed payments.

The X $TWTR-date is the day the Treasury Department would run out of both cash and extraordinary measures. After that point, it could no longer pay all of the federal government's obligations on time. The X-date is a projection, not a fixed deadline, and it moves as money flows in and out of the Treasury.

The X-date is a later and more consequential point than the day the debt limit is reached. Once debt hits the ceiling, Treasury can keep paying bills for a period by drawing down its cash balance and using accounting steps. The X-date marks the point at which those resources are gone.

No one can pin down the day in advance. It depends on how much the government collects in taxes and how much it pays out, and both totals swing from week to week. Federal cash flows are uneven. Large outflows such as Social Security benefits, Medicare payments, military pay and veterans' benefits cluster at particular points in the month. Tax receipts also arrive in bursts rather than at a steady pace.

The calendar plays a large role. Individual income tax payments due in mid-April can lift Treasury's cash position sharply. Quarterly estimated tax payments due in June add another inflow. A stronger or weaker tax season than forecast can move the X-date earlier or later.

Treasury keeps its operating cash in the Treasury General Account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It reports daily receipts, outlays and the account balance in the Daily Treasury Statement. Forecasters use those reports to track how fast the cushion is shrinking.

Three sources have produced estimates during past standoffs. The Treasury secretary has sent letters to Congress warning when the department expects to exhaust its measures. The Congressional Budget Office and the Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, have published their own projections. Those estimates have shifted when tax receipts and spending ran higher or lower than expected. They have sometimes been presented as a window of possible dates rather than a single day.

The federal government has never reached the X-date. What would follow has therefore never been tested. Treasury would still have cash arriving each day, but not enough to cover every payment due. That gap would force decisions about delaying payments to bondholders, beneficiaries, contractors or federal employees. No law sets out an order for making those choices.

The 2011 debt ceiling standoff ended when President Barack Obama signed the Budget Control Act on Aug. 2, 2011. Three days later, on Aug. 5, Standard & Poor's lowered the U.S. credit rating from AAA to AA+. It was the first time S&P had ever downgraded the country.

The dispute ran for months. Republicans won control of the House in the 2010 midterm elections, while Democrats kept the Senate and the White House. The two sides negotiated over whether an increase in the borrowing limit should be paired with deficit reduction, and on what terms. Talks stretched into the summer while Treasury relied on extraordinary measures to keep paying the government's bills.

Treasury had identified Aug. 2 as the day its borrowing authority would run out. The deal was signed on that same day, leaving almost no margin before the government risked missing payments.

The Budget Control Act raised the debt limit in stages. It also set caps on discretionary spending that ran through fiscal 2021. A third piece created the Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction, a panel of 12 lawmakers split evenly between the two parties. Its job was to propose further deficit reduction for Congress to vote on.

The law built in a penalty for failure. If Congress did not enact a committee plan, automatic across-the-board spending cuts known as sequestration would take effect. The committee announced in November 2011 that it could not reach an agreement. Sequestration began in March 2013.

S&P based its decision on two main concerns. It judged that the deficit plan fell short of what would be needed to stabilize the country's medium-term debt path. It also pointed to the brinkmanship of the standoff as a sign that U.S. policymaking had become less stable and less predictable. S&P paired the AA+ rating with a negative outlook, signaling that a further cut was possible.

AAA is the top grade on S&P's scale, and AA+ sits one notch below it. The other two major agencies did not follow in 2011. Moody's $MCO kept its Aaa rating but assigned a negative outlook, and Fitch affirmed its AAA rating. That left the U.S. with a split rating among the big three agencies for years afterward.

Markets reacted unevenly. U.S. stocks fell sharply in the first trading days after the downgrade. Demand for Treasury securities held up, though, and Treasury yields declined.

The Fiscal Responsibility Act, signed June 3, 2023, ended that year's debt ceiling standoff by suspending the borrowing limit until Jan. 1, 2025. The law also set caps on federal spending. Fitch Ratings then lowered the U.S. credit rating from AAA to AA+ on Aug. 1, 2023.

The act came out of negotiations between President Joe Biden and House Speaker Kevin McCarthy. The House passed the bill on May 31, 2023. The Senate approved it on June 1, and Biden signed it into law on June 3.

The act did not lift the cap to a new dollar amount. Instead, it switched the cap off for a set period. That approach is called a suspension, and it works differently from a straightforward increase. An increase writes a higher number into law. A suspension removes the number entirely until a chosen date.

While a suspension is in effect, the Treasury Department can borrow what it needs to cover the government's obligations without running into a fixed ceiling. When the suspension ends, the limit does not return to its old level. It resets to the amount of debt outstanding on that date.

That reset folds any borrowing done during the suspension into the new ceiling. On paper, a suspension looks like a pause. In practice, it works as an increase. Lawmakers avoid voting on a specific dollar figure, yet the limit still rises by whatever the government borrowed in the interim.

The spending caps applied to discretionary spending — the portion of the budget Congress sets through annual appropriations bills. The act set those caps for fiscal years 2024 and 2025.

Fitch had placed the U.S. on rating watch negative in May 2023, while the negotiations were still underway. Its downgrade arrived after the standoff was over. In explaining the decision, Fitch pointed to an erosion of governance, including the repeated standoffs over the debt limit. The agency also cited expected fiscal deterioration and a high and growing government debt burden.

At the time of the Fitch decision, Moody's $MCO still rated the U.S. Aaa, its highest grade.

A rating of AA+ sits one notch below AAA and remains investment grade. The downgrade did not signal a default. It reflected Fitch's judgment that the U.S. no longer met its standard for the highest rating it assigns.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, raised the federal debt limit by $5 trillion, to roughly $41.1 trillion. The increase restored Treasury's borrowing room after the cap had returned in January 2025 at roughly $36.1 trillion.

That January figure was not a number lawmakers chose. The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 had suspended the limit until Jan. 1, 2025. When the suspension ended, the ceiling came back at the level of debt then outstanding. The limit and the debt were the same amount. Treasury had no fresh capacity to issue new debt from the moment the cap returned.

Treasury began using extraordinary measures in January 2025 to keep meeting the government's obligations. Those accounting steps postponed a breach but did not add any room under the cap. A lasting fix required Congress to pass a new law.

That law was a broad tax and spending package. It extended individual tax cuts first enacted in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, alongside many other fiscal changes. Congress passed it through budget reconciliation. That procedure lets the Senate approve certain budget legislation with a simple majority. Reconciliation bills cannot be filibustered. As a result, the debt limit increase did not need the 60 votes most Senate bills require to move forward.

The 2025 change was an increase, not a suspension. A suspension sets a date when the limit comes back. An increase sets a dollar amount instead. The next deadline therefore depends on how fast federal borrowing climbs toward roughly $41.1 trillion, not on a date written into the statute.

The increase came after another change to the U.S. credit rating. Moody's $MCO lowered its U.S. rating from Aaa to Aa1 in May 2025. Moody's had rated U.S. government debt at Aaa since 1917. It had also been the last of the three major agencies to keep the U.S. at its top grade.

Three main alternatives to the debt ceiling have been proposed: invoking the 14th Amendment, minting a high-value platinum coin and repealing the cap entirely. None has been put into practice. Each remains a proposal rather than settled law.

The constitutional argument rests on Section 4 of the 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 after the Civil War. Its text says the validity of the public debt of the U.S., authorized by law, shall not be questioned. The same section bars the U.S. and the states from paying any debt incurred in aid of insurrection against the country. Supporters of the 14th Amendment approach argue that a statutory cap cannot force the government to miss payments on debt Congress has already authorized. In their view, the limit would become unenforceable once Treasury could no longer meet those obligations.

No court has ruled on that argument. The amendment's text does not mention a borrowing cap. The statute that sets the debt limit remains in force.

The platinum coin idea comes from a provision of federal law, 31 U.S.C. 5112(k). That section gives the Treasury secretary authority to mint platinum coins and leaves their specifications to the secretary's discretion. Proponents argue this would let Treasury strike a single coin with a very high face value. Under the proposal, Treasury would deposit the coin at the Federal Reserve. Treasury keeps its main operating cash account, the Treasury General Account, at the Fed. It would then spend the resulting balance instead of issuing new debt. Treasury has never minted such a coin.

Abolishing the limit is the third option. The debt ceiling exists in statute, so Congress could repeal it through ordinary legislation. Borrowing would then follow from the spending and tax laws Congress passes, without a separate vote on the total amount the government owes.

Denmark offers a point of comparison. The country has a statutory debt limit, but it is set high enough that it does not bind.

The U.S. has followed a different path. Congress has kept its limit and adjusted it over time through increases and suspensions.

#5477. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”
