#5476. How House and Senate vacancies are filled, and what changes in each chamber

Free daily briefing on global business news.

When a member of Congress dies or resigns, the Constitution, state law and chamber rules decide who fills the seat, who runs the office and how votes change

The Constitution treats an empty seat in the House of Representatives very differently from an empty seat in the Senate. A House district stays without a voting representative until its voters choose a replacement in a special election. In many states, a Senate seat can be filled by a governor's appointment before any ballot is cast.

That split comes from two parts of the Constitution. Article I, Section 2 sets the rules for House vacancies. The 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, moved Senate elections to a popular vote and set the rules for Senate vacancies.

Understanding what happens when a member of Congress dies or resigns means following several tracks at once. The seat itself is only one of them. A departing lawmaker also leaves behind a staff, a constituent office, committee assignments and a floor vote that no one can cast.

Each of those pieces runs on its own set of rules. State law sets the timing of special elections, and the governor issues the writ that calls one. In the House, the Clerk takes over administration of a vacant office and its staff. The Secretary of the Senate does the same job for an empty Senate office. Constituents can still get help with casework while they wait for a new member.

Committee seats open up, and party and chamber processes decide who fills them. Seniority, which shapes committee standing in both chambers, does not pass to whoever wins the seat next. A successor does not inherit the predecessor's place in line.

Vote math shifts as well. In the House, a vacancy lowers the whole number of the chamber, the figure used to calculate a quorum. Most House votes are decided by a majority of members present and voting. The Senate keeps working with an empty seat, and the vice president votes only when senators are equally divided. In a closely divided chamber, a single vacancy can narrow a party's working margin.

Resignation follows a set procedure too. A member usually sends a letter to the state's governor and to the chamber's presiding officer, and can choose the date it takes effect. Final pay, retirement and survivor benefits follow separate federal rules.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of these mechanics, from filling the seat to settling a member's pay. Each slide explains one piece of the process on its own.

A vacant seat in the U.S. House of Representatives can be filled in only one way: a special election. The Constitution gives no one the power to appoint a temporary replacement. That includes a governor, a political party and the House itself.

The rule comes from Article I, Section 2, Clause 4. It says that when a vacancy happens in a state's House delegation, the state's executive authority shall issue writs of election to fill it. In practice, that executive authority is the governor. A writ of election is the formal order that sets an election in motion.

The wording matters. The clause tells the governor to call an election, not to choose a person. The decision about who represents the district stays with its voters, just as it did for the member who left.

This design matches the House's original role. Article I, Section 2 says representatives are chosen by the people of the several states. From the start, the House was the one part of the federal government whose members were elected directly. An appointed House member would break that link between voters and their representative.

The process begins once the seat is formally empty. A member who dies, resigns or is expelled leaves the seat vacant. The Clerk of the House then notifies the executive of the member's state, which opens the path to a writ and a new election.

Until voters choose a successor, the district has no voting member in the House. No stand-in can cast floor votes or introduce bills on the district's behalf. Legislative representation for those residents waits for the special election.

The winner does not start a fresh two-year term. A special election fills only the rest of the departed member's term. The seat then appears on the ballot again at the next regular election.

Changing this arrangement would take more than a new law. The special election requirement is written into the Constitution itself. Allowing anyone to appoint a temporary House member would therefore require a constitutional amendment.

That makes the House different from the Senate, where a separate provision governs vacancies. Every House member who fills a vacancy arrives through the ballot box.

The 17th Amendment, ratified in 1913, sets the basic rule for an empty Senate seat: the state's governor must issue writs of election to fill it. It also lets each state legislature authorize the governor to appoint a temporary senator until voters choose a replacement.

That two-part structure explains why Senate vacancies are handled differently from one state to the next. The Constitution supplies the framework. Each state legislature decides how much of it to use.

The amendment grew out of a larger change. Under the original text of Article I, Section 3, state legislatures chose U.S. senators. The 17th Amendment moved that choice to the voters, who now elect senators directly. The vacancy clause follows the same logic. Voters pick senators in regular elections, and they also get the final say when a seat opens early.

Before the amendment, the Constitution handled vacancies another way. If a seat opened while a state legislature was in recess, the governor could make a temporary appointment. That appointee served until the legislature met again and filled the seat. The 17th Amendment replaced that arrangement with the writ-of-election requirement.

The amendment's text makes any appointment temporary. An appointed senator holds the seat only until "the people fill the vacancies by election as the legislature may direct." The appointment bridges the gap until an election and does not replace one. The legislature also directs how that election takes place.

States are not required to allow appointments at all. The power belongs to the legislature to grant or withhold. Some states fill Senate vacancies only by special election, leaving the seat empty until voters act. Others authorize the governor to appoint someone and then hold an election later.

Because the amendment leaves these choices to each state, the details vary. The timing of the special election, any conditions on the governor's pick and the length of an appointee's service all depend on state law. The constant is that an election eventually decides who holds the seat.

The winner of that special election generally serves the remainder of the departing senator's six-year term. Senate terms are staggered under Article I, and a vacancy does not reset the cycle for that seat. A senator who wins a special election and wants to stay must run again when the original term ends.

The amendment also included a transition provision. Its final paragraph said it would not affect the election or term of any senator chosen before it became part of the Constitution. Senators already picked by state legislatures finished their terms under the old system.

In most states, a governor can name a temporary senator to fill a vacant seat. That appointee serves only until voters choose a successor in a special election. Each state legislature decides whether its governor has that power and what limits come with it.

The authority comes from a single clause of the 17th Amendment. It lets a state legislature empower the governor to make temporary appointments "until the people fill the vacancies by election as the legislature may direct." That wording leaves the details to each state.

Some states let the governor pick anyone who meets the constitutional requirements. Others attach conditions. A number of states require the appointee to belong to the same political party as the senator who left. Some go further and require the governor to choose from a short list of names submitted by that party.

Any appointee must meet the same qualifications as an elected senator. Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution requires a senator to be at least 30 years old. The appointee must also have been a U.S. citizen for at least nine years and an inhabitant of the state when chosen.

The appointment becomes official through paperwork. The governor issues a certificate of appointment, which is presented to the Senate as the new member's credentials. The Senate holds the final say on seating. Article I, Section 5 makes each chamber the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members.

An appointee takes the same oath of office as an elected senator. Once sworn in, an appointed senator holds the same vote as any other member. The appointee can introduce bills and vote on legislation and nominations.

The appointment is temporary by design. State law sets when the special election takes place, and the winner serves out the remainder of the unexpired term. Some appointees run in that election to keep the seat. Others serve as placeholders and leave once the elected successor takes office.

Each state decides when and how its own House special elections run. The governor issues the writ that starts the process, but state election law shapes the calendar, the nomination method and the ballot. As a result, the wait for a new representative varies from state to state.

Federal law leaves the scheduling to the states. Under 2 U.S. Code Section 8, state law sets the time for holding an election to fill a House vacancy. Some states give the governor a fixed window in which to call the election. Others leave the governor wider discretion over the date.

Nomination rules differ just as much. In many states, voters choose party nominees in a special primary before the special general election. In others, party committees or conventions pick the nominees, and a single election follows. Some states use an all-candidate primary, in which every contender appears on one ballot regardless of party.

Those choices shape the calendar. A primary followed by a general election takes longer than a single election with party-selected nominees. Candidate filing deadlines, ballot printing and certification periods add further time. Ballots must also reach military and overseas voters early enough to be returned.

Some all-candidate systems add a runoff. If no candidate wins a majority in the first round, the top finishers meet in a second election. That step pushes the swearing-in date back further.

A governor may also place the special election on the same day as an already scheduled primary or general election. Combining the two spares local election offices the expense of running a separate vote. The trade-off is a longer stretch without a voting representative for the district.

The winner does not start a fresh two-year term. A special election fills only the remainder of the departing member's term, in the same district that member represented. Once the result reaches the House, the winner takes the oath of office and can begin voting. The seat then comes up again at the next regular election.

When a House seat becomes vacant, the Clerk of the House takes charge of the departed member's office and supervises its staff until a successor is sworn in. In the Senate, the Secretary of the Senate handles the administration of a vacant senator's office.

This arrangement keeps a district or state from losing access to help with the federal government while the seat sits empty. Phones stay answered, and constituent requests can still move forward in Washington and in local offices back home.

In the House, the authority comes from the chamber's own rules. They direct the Clerk to oversee the staff of a member who has died, resigned or been expelled. The Clerk does not represent the district or speak for its voters. The role is administrative, covering payroll, the office budget and the daily work of the remaining employees.

Casework is the main function that continues. A constituent who needs help with a Social Security claim, a veterans' benefit, a delayed passport or an immigration case can still contact the office. Staff can make inquiries with federal agencies for that person, much as they did before the vacancy.

The staff cannot act as a lawmaker. With no member in the seat, no one in the office casts votes, introduces bills or signs on as a cosponsor. Nobody in the office speaks for the district on pending legislation.

The staff jobs are temporary. Employees remain on the chamber's payroll during the vacancy, but a newly elected member picks their own team. The successor may keep some previous employees, hire new ones or combine the two.

The Senate follows a parallel path through the Secretary of the Senate, the chamber's chief administrative officer. In states where a governor can appoint a temporary senator, the appointee takes over the office and its staffing decisions once sworn in.

The member's own papers follow a separate rule. Congress treats a member's office papers as the member's personal property. Committee records, by contrast, belong to the chamber. After a death in office, the family or estate often decides where those personal files end up.

Timing also shapes the handoff. A member who plans a resignation can prepare staff and wrap up open cases in advance. A sudden death in office gives the staff no such warning.

A departing member's committee seats become vacant, and that member's seniority ends with the vacancy. Each party, working through its own internal rules and a vote of the full chamber, chooses who takes the open slots. A successor starts with no inherited rank and builds seniority from his or her own first day of service.

Committee membership belongs to the individual lawmaker, not to the district or the state. When a House member or senator resigns or dies, every assignment that person held opens up. That includes seats on full committees and on subcommittees. Congressional practice does not reserve those seats for whoever wins the special election or receives a governor's appointment.

In the House, each party fills its own committee slots. Republicans route assignments through their Steering Committee. Democrats use their Steering and Policy Committee. The full party conference or caucus then approves the selections, and the House adopts a resolution formally electing members to committees.

The Senate follows a similar path. Each party conference makes its selections, and the chamber ratifies them by resolution.

A party has options once a seat opens. It may give the slot to the incoming member, move a sitting colleague into it or leave it unfilled for a time. The parties negotiate the split of majority and minority seats on each committee, usually at the start of a new Congress. That ratio determines which party controls the vacant slot.

The departure of a committee chair carries more weight than the loss of a rank-and-file member. The majority party chooses a new chair through its own internal rules, followed by a House or Senate resolution. House rules also require each standing committee chair to designate a vice chair from the majority party. The vice chair presides over meetings and hearings when the chair is absent.

Seniority cannot be handed to anyone else. A successor's standing on a committee and in the chamber begins with his or her own swearing-in. That standing affects where a member sits on the committee dais and where the member falls in line for a future chairmanship or ranking-member post. In the Senate, seniority also sets the order in which senators choose office suites.

An appointed senator is treated the same way. Service counts from the day the appointee takes the oath, not from the day the former senator first took office.

A vacancy shrinks the whole number of the House, the base for calculating a quorum, but it leaves the rule for passing most bills unchanged. Those votes turn on a majority of members present and voting, not a majority of the full membership.

Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution makes a majority of each chamber a quorum to do business. Under House precedent, that majority is measured against members who are chosen, sworn and living. A seat left empty by death, resignation or expulsion drops out of the count.

The Speaker announces each vacancy and the adjusted whole number from the floor. With all 435 seats filled, a quorum is 218 members. With one vacancy, the whole number falls to 434, and a quorum stays at 218. With two vacancies, the whole number is 433, and a quorum drops to 217.

Delegates and the resident commissioner of Puerto Rico sit outside this calculation. They do not count toward a quorum of the full House. They also cannot vote on final passage of legislation.

Passing a bill follows a separate rule. A measure succeeds when the yeas outnumber the nays among members who vote. A tie defeats it. Members who are absent or who answer "present" do not affect the margin. An empty seat has the same effect on the tally as a member who skips the vote.

The practical effect shows up in party margins. When a vacancy falls in the majority party's ranks, that party has one fewer vote to spare on a measure that splits along party lines. A vacancy in the minority party gives the majority more room on the same kind of vote.

Some decisions require more than a simple majority. Passing a bill under suspension of the rules needs two-thirds of those present and voting. Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds of members voting in each chamber, with a quorum present. In both cases, vacant seats are left out of the math.

The election of a Speaker has its own arithmetic. The winning candidate needs a majority of the votes cast for a person by name. Vacancies, absences and "present" votes all lower the number of votes needed to win the gavel.

The House presumes a quorum is present unless a member raises a point of order that one is not. A quorum call or recorded vote then measures attendance against the adjusted whole number.

A Senate vacancy does not stop the chamber from working. The Senate keeps debating and voting with fewer than 100 members, and the vice president still casts a vote only when senators are equally divided.

The tiebreaking rule comes from Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution. It names the vice president as president of the Senate but gives that officer no vote unless the chamber is evenly split. A vacancy leaves that limit unchanged.

A vacancy does change the arithmetic around a tie. With 99 senators in office, a vote in which every senator takes part cannot split evenly. One side will always hold at least one more vote than the other. Ties remain possible when senators are absent or decline to vote, so the vice president's role does not disappear.

The Senate's quorum also adjusts. Senate Rule VI defines a quorum as a majority of the senators duly chosen and sworn. An empty seat lowers that base. With 99 senators serving, 50 make a quorum, compared with 51 when all 100 seats are filled.

Final passage of most bills requires a simple majority of senators voting. Under that standard, a vacancy matters most through its effect on party balance. Take a Senate split 50-50, where the vice president breaks party-line ties. If one side loses a member, the other side holds 50 of the 99 filled seats. With full attendance, that side can win a party-line vote without the vice president.

Ending a filibuster follows a different rule. Senate Rule XXII sets the cloture threshold for most measures at three-fifths of the senators duly chosen and sworn. With 99 senators serving, three-fifths still rounds up to 60 votes. A single vacancy leaves that usual bar in place.

The affected state keeps one voice in the chamber. Every state holds two Senate seats regardless of population. A single vacancy cuts a state's Senate delegation in half until the seat is filled. Its remaining senator continues to vote on the floor. The empty seat casts no vote until a successor, whether appointed or elected, takes the oath of office.

A member of Congress resigns by putting the decision in writing. The letter usually goes to two recipients: the governor of the member's home state and the presiding officer of the chamber where the member serves.

Each recipient has a separate role. The governor is the state's executive authority. That is the official who issues the writ of election that starts the process of filling the seat. The presiding officer informs the chamber that one of its members is leaving.

In the House, the presiding officer is the Speaker. In the Senate, it is the vice president, who holds the title of president of the Senate under the Constitution.

The departing member picks the effective date. A resignation can take effect immediately, on the day the letter is delivered. It can also take effect on a specific future date named in the letter.

That choice controls when the seat legally becomes empty. The vacancy begins on the effective date. It does not begin on the day the member announces plans to leave or on the day the letter is written.

Until the effective date arrives, the lawmaker remains a sitting member. A member who sets a future date keeps the powers of the office in the meantime, including the right to vote on the floor and in committee.

The chamber does not hold a vote to approve a resignation. Colleagues and party leaders have no power to accept or reject it. The written notice is the act that matters.

The letter itself is usually short. It typically states the decision to resign and the date it takes effect. A member is not required to give a reason.

In the House, a resignation letter is typically laid before the chamber and printed in the Congressional Record. That creates a public, official record of the departure and its timing.

Resignation differs from expulsion. Under Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution, either chamber can expel a member only with a two-thirds vote.

A member's congressional salary stops when service ends, whether that happens through resignation or death. Retirement benefits a member has already qualified for are not erased by leaving early. A deceased member's family may qualify for survivor payments under federal retirement and Social Security rules.

Pay follows the same basic logic as other federal salaries. It is earned for time in office. A member who resigns is paid through the effective date of the resignation and no further. A successor is paid for that person's own service, not for the stretch when the seat sat empty.

Retirement coverage depends on when a member first entered federal service. Members who first arrived in 1984 or later are generally covered by the Federal Employees Retirement System, known as FERS. That system combines three parts: Social Security, a basic annuity and the Thrift Savings Plan. The Thrift Savings Plan is a 401(k)-style investment account. Members who entered earlier may be covered by the older Civil Service Retirement System.

Leaving office does not cancel a pension a member has already earned. A member needs at least five years of service to be eligible for a congressional annuity. A House member who serves a single two-year term therefore does not earn one. Eligible former members draw benefits once they meet their system's age and service requirements. Money a member contributed to a Thrift Savings Plan account stays with that person after departure.

A death in office brings a different set of provisions. Surviving spouses and eligible children can receive survivor benefits under the retirement system the member belonged to. The amount and eligibility depend on factors such as the member's length of service. Members also pay into Social Security. Their families may qualify for Social Security survivor benefits under the same rules that apply to other workers.

Congress has a long-standing custom of approving a separate death gratuity for a deceased member's survivors. The payment is not automatic. Lawmakers have traditionally provided it through legislation, often as a provision in an appropriations measure.

Members can also enroll in the Federal Employees' Group Life Insurance program, which pays out to the beneficiaries they name. None of these benefits pass to the member's successor. The new member starts building service credit and retirement eligibility from the first day in office.

#5475. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5474. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5473. What the U.S. government spends money on, from Social Security to interest

Free daily briefing on global business news.

See where federal tax dollars go, from Social Security and Medicare to defense and interest on the debt, in 10 major areas of the U.S. budget

Many federal payments are never voted on line by line in a given year. Social Security checks, Medicare claims and interest on Treasury debt go out under permanent law or binding obligations. They keep flowing whether or not lawmakers act. The difference between that spending and the money Congress approves annually is the starting point for understanding where federal tax dollars go.

Federal spending falls into two broad groups. Mandatory spending is set by standing law. The rules that decide who qualifies for Social Security or Medicare, and what they receive, stay in force until Congress changes them. Spending on these programs depends on how many people qualify and what the law entitles them to, not on a yearly vote.

Discretionary spending works differently. Congress sets it each year by passing appropriations bills, which fund agencies and programs for a single fiscal year. Defense is the largest part of this category. The rest covers a wide range of federal activity, from scientific research to much of veterans' health care. The federal fiscal year runs from Oct. 1 to Sept. 30. That means the budget calendar does not line up with the calendar year.

Borrowing adds a third layer. When spending exceeds revenue in a given year, the government borrows to cover the difference. That one-year gap is the deficit. The accumulated total of past borrowing is the national debt. The Treasury owes interest on the securities it sells to finance that debt. Those payments are a legal obligation rather than a program Congress votes on.

Knowing which group a program falls into helps explain the federal budget breakdown. It shows which costs lawmakers can adjust in one appropriations cycle and which require rewriting the underlying law. Financing is a separate question. Some programs draw on dedicated payroll or fuel taxes, while others rely on general revenue.

What follows is a selection of 10 major areas of federal spending and finance. It is not a ranking by size or a complete accounting of what the U.S. government spends money on. Each spending slide explains what a program or obligation does, who runs it, how it is paid for and whether it is mandatory or discretionary. The final slide turns to the revenue side, covering where the money comes from and how borrowing fills the rest.

Social Security sends monthly payments to retired workers, disabled workers and the families of workers who have died. Most of the money comes from payroll taxes collected under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act, better known as FICA.

The combined tax rate is 12.4% of wages up to an annual earnings cap. Workers pay 6.2% through paycheck withholding. Employers pay a matching 6.2%. The cap is adjusted each year to track average wage growth. Earnings above it are not subject to the Social Security portion of the payroll tax.

Self-employed people pay both halves themselves. Their contribution falls under the Self-Employment Contributions Act rather than FICA. The combined rate is the same 12.4%.

Payroll tax receipts are credited to two trust funds held at the Treasury. The Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund pays retirement and survivor benefits. The Disability Insurance Trust Fund pays benefits to workers who can no longer work because of a qualifying medical condition. Any surplus in the funds is invested in special-issue Treasury securities.

The system largely operates on a pay-as-you-go basis. Taxes paid by today's workers fund the checks going to today's beneficiaries. The money is not saved in individual accounts.

Benefits go straight to individuals. The Social Security Administration calculates each payment from a person's lifetime earnings record. Higher lifetime earnings produce larger checks, up to a maximum. Retirement benefits can start as early as age 62 at a reduced amount. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. Waiting past full retirement age earns delayed retirement credits until age 70.

Survivor benefits can go to widows, widowers, dependent children and, in some cases, dependent parents. Disability benefits require enough recent work history to qualify. They also require a medical finding that the person cannot sustain substantial work.

Payments rise in most years through an automatic cost-of-living adjustment. The adjustment is tied to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Congress does not vote on each year's increase.

Social Security is mandatory spending. Its benefit formulas and eligibility rules are set in the Social Security Act, which President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed in 1935.

Some higher-income beneficiaries also pay federal income tax on part of their benefits. Much of that revenue is credited back to the Social Security trust funds. A portion goes to Medicare's hospital insurance trust fund instead.

Medicare is the federal health insurance program for Americans 65 and older and for some younger people with disabilities. Its coverage is split into parts: Part A pays for hospital care, Part B for doctor visits and outpatient services, and Part D for prescription drugs.

President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare into law in 1965 as an amendment to the Social Security Act. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services, runs the program. Medicare is classified as mandatory spending. Anyone who meets the eligibility rules set in law can enroll.

Age is the main route in, but it is not the only one. People who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months become eligible before 65. So do people with end-stage renal disease, which is permanent kidney failure, and people with ALS.

Part A is financed mainly by a payroll tax. The combined rate is 2.9% of wages, with employees and employers each paying 1.45%. Self-employed workers pay the full 2.9% themselves. Unlike the Social Security payroll tax, the Medicare tax has no cap on the wages it applies to. The Affordable Care Act added a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages above set income thresholds. That tax took effect in 2013.

Part A revenue flows into the Hospital Insurance Trust Fund. Most enrollees pay no monthly premium for Part A. They qualify for premium-free coverage because they or a spouse paid Medicare taxes for at least 40 quarters, or about 10 years of work.

Parts B and D work differently. They draw on general federal revenue and on premiums paid by beneficiaries, through the Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund. Enrollees with higher incomes pay larger premiums for both parts.

Part D is the newest major piece. Congress created it in the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003, and coverage began in 2006. Private insurers that contract with Medicare deliver the drug plans. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 gave Medicare authority to negotiate prices for certain high-cost drugs.

Many beneficiaries get their coverage through Medicare Advantage, also called Part C. These private plans bundle Part A and Part B benefits, and most include drug coverage. Medicare pays the plans to provide those benefits.

Medicaid is a health coverage program paid for jointly by the federal government and the states. The federal share differs from state to state and is set by a formula called the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage, or FMAP.

That shared structure separates Medicaid from Medicare, which the federal government runs on its own. Each state administers its own Medicaid program within federal rules. States decide many details, including some optional benefits, payment rates for doctors and hospitals, and how people enroll. The federal government then reimburses its share of qualifying costs.

The FMAP formula compares each state's per capita income with the national average. States with lower incomes receive a larger federal match. Wealthier states receive a smaller one. Federal law sets a floor of 50%. No state covers more than half of its standard Medicaid costs on its own.

Federal Medicaid funding is mandatory spending, and it is open-ended. The federal government matches whatever qualifying amount a state spends rather than sending a fixed sum. Federal costs therefore rise and fall with enrollment and with medical prices in each state.

Medicaid covers several groups with limited incomes: children, parents, pregnant women, older adults and people with disabilities. It is also a major payer for long-term care in nursing homes. Medicare covers only limited skilled nursing stays. Many older Americans who need extended nursing home care qualify for Medicaid after spending down their savings to meet its eligibility limits.

The Affordable Care Act of 2010 let states extend Medicaid to most adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level. The federal government pays 90% of the cost for that expansion group. That is a higher match than the regular formula provides. Not every state has adopted the expansion.

The Children's Health Insurance Program, known as CHIP, fills a different gap. It covers children in families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid. Congress created the program in 1997. Unlike Medicaid, CHIP is funded through capped federal allotments to each state. Its federal match rate is higher than the regular Medicaid rate. States can run CHIP as part of Medicaid, as a separate program or as a combination of the two.

Medicaid itself dates to 1965. It was signed into law alongside Medicare as part of amendments to the Social Security Act.

Defense is the largest part of discretionary federal spending, and most of that money flows through the Department of Defense. Congress sets the level each year through the National Defense Authorization Act and a separate defense appropriations bill.

The two bills do different jobs. The National Defense Authorization Act sets policy and authorizes programs. It covers matters such as troop levels, military pay raises and which weapons programs may go forward. The appropriations bill provides the money the Pentagon can actually spend. A program can be authorized and still go unfunded if appropriators do not supply the dollars.

The Pentagon's budget is organized into a handful of broad accounts. Military personnel funding covers pay and allowances for active-duty and reserve troops. Operations and maintenance is the account that keeps forces ready. It pays for training, fuel, equipment repairs, base operations and the salaries of many civilian employees. A separate account, the Defense Health Program, runs military hospitals and clinics and the Tricare health plan.

Procurement covers the purchase of ships, aircraft, combat vehicles, missiles and munitions. Research, development, test and evaluation pays for designing and proving new systems before they are bought in quantity. Military construction pays for barracks, runways and other facilities. It moves through a separate appropriations bill that also funds the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Some national security spending sits outside the Pentagon. Nuclear warheads are designed, built and maintained by the Department of Energy through its National Nuclear Security Administration. That work counts toward the federal government's broader national defense budget category. It is not part of the Department of Defense's own budget. The Coast Guard also sits outside the Pentagon. In peacetime, it falls under the Department of Homeland Security.

Timing shapes how the money is spent. The defense appropriations bill is one of 12 regular spending bills Congress is meant to pass before each new fiscal year begins. When lawmakers miss that deadline, the Pentagon typically operates under a continuing resolution. That stopgap generally holds funding at the prior year's levels. It also generally bars new programs from starting until a full-year bill passes.

Net interest is the federal government's cost of carrying the Treasury securities it has sold, minus the interest income it collects. Federal law pays interest on the public debt through a permanent, indefinite appropriation, with no yearly vote required.

The calculation starts with interest on debt held by the public. That debt consists of securities owned by individuals, banks, pension funds, mutual funds, state and local governments, foreign governments and the Federal Reserve. Interest the government receives from other sources is then subtracted to reach the net figure.

Interest the Treasury owes to its own trust funds, such as those for Social Security, sits outside the net figure. Those payments move money from one government account to another. In the overall budget, they cancel out.

Budget presentations from the Congressional Budget Office list net interest as its own category, separate from mandatory and discretionary spending.

Two forces set the cost: how much debt is outstanding and what interest rates the Treasury pays. A larger debt raises the bill even when rates hold steady. Higher rates raise it even when the debt stops growing.

The mix of securities shapes how quickly rate changes reach the budget. Treasury bills mature in one year or less. Treasury notes run from two to 10 years, and Treasury bonds run 20 or 30 years. When a security matures, the Treasury usually sells a new one to repay the holder. The new security carries whatever rate the market sets at auction.

Debt weighted toward short-term bills reprices fast when rates move. A 30-year bond keeps the rate set at its original auction until it matures.

Some securities adjust on their own. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities raise their principal in line with inflation. The interest paid on them rises as that principal grows. Floating rate notes mature in two years. Their interest payments reset with the rate on 13-week Treasury bills.

Missing an interest payment would count as a default on U.S. government debt. That risk surfaces during standoffs over the statutory debt limit, the cap Congress places on total federal borrowing. Hitting the limit does not erase interest already owed. It restricts the Treasury's ability to borrow the cash needed to meet all of its obligations, interest included.

The Department of Veterans Affairs spends federal money in two main ways. It runs a nationwide health system through the Veterans Health Administration, and it pays benefits to veterans, including monthly disability compensation for conditions connected to military service.

The Veterans Health Administration owns and operates its own hospitals and clinics. It also employs its own doctors, nurses and support staff. That sets it apart from Medicare and Medicaid, which mostly pay outside hospitals and physicians for care. The VA also buys care from community providers. The VA MISSION Act of 2018 set the rules for when veterans can see community doctors at VA expense.

Much of the VA health care budget is discretionary. Congress sets that money each year through appropriations bills.

Disability compensation works on different terms. It is a monthly, tax-free payment to veterans whose illnesses or injuries were caused or made worse by their service. The VA assigns each eligible veteran a disability rating from 0% to 100%, in 10% steps. The payment rises with the rating. Veterans rated at 30% or higher can receive more if they have a spouse, children or dependent parents.

Disability compensation is mandatory spending. A veteran who meets the eligibility rules is entitled to the payment.

Education benefits trace back to the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, the original GI Bill. Its current main version, the Post-9/11 GI Bill, was enacted in 2008. It can cover tuition and fees and pay a monthly housing allowance to eligible veterans and service members. Some service members can transfer unused benefits to a spouse or children.

The VA home loan program also dates to the 1944 law. The VA usually does not lend the money itself. Instead, it guarantees part of a mortgage made by a private lender. That guarantee lowers the lender's risk if the borrower defaults. It also allows many eligible borrowers to buy a home with no down payment.

Compensation, education benefits and home loans are run by the Veterans Benefits Administration, a separate arm of the department from the health system. A third arm, the National Cemetery Administration, maintains national cemeteries and provides burial benefits for eligible veterans.

SNAP, Supplemental Security Income and the Earned Income Tax Credit are three major federal income-support programs, and each runs through a different agency. One provides food aid, one pays monthly cash and one delivers money through the tax system.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program is run by the Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service. It helps low-income households buy groceries. For decades it was known as food stamps. Congress renamed it SNAP in the 2008 farm bill. Benefits now arrive on an Electronic Benefit Transfer card, which works like a debit card at the checkout counter.

The federal government pays for the SNAP benefits themselves. States take applications and determine eligibility, and they share the cost of administering the program. Benefit levels are tied to the Thrifty Food Plan, a USDA estimate of what a low-cost, nutritious diet costs. Congress reauthorizes and revises SNAP through the farm bill, the same legislation that covers crop subsidies and other agriculture programs.

Supplemental Security Income is run by the Social Security Administration. It pays monthly cash to people with low incomes and limited assets who are 65 or older, blind or disabled. Congress created SSI in 1972, and it began paying benefits in 1974. It replaced earlier aid programs for older, blind and disabled people that the states had administered.

SSI is separate from Social Security disability benefits, even though the same agency runs both. SSI does not depend on a recipient's work history. It is paid from general tax revenue rather than from payroll-tax trust funds. Many states add their own supplement on top of the federal payment.

The Earned Income Tax Credit works through the tax code instead of a benefit office. Workers claim it on their federal income tax returns, and the IRS administers it. Congress enacted the credit in 1975. Only people with earnings from work can receive it. The credit grows as earnings rise, levels off, then phases out at higher incomes. It is larger for families with qualifying children.

The credit is refundable. When it exceeds a household's income tax liability, the IRS pays out the difference. That refunded amount counts as federal outlays. The part of the credit that only reduces a tax bill shows up as lower revenue instead.

All three programs are classified as mandatory spending.

Most federal money for roads, bridges and public transit moves through the Highway Trust Fund. Fuel taxes are its main source of revenue, including the federal gasoline tax of 18.3 cents per gallon.

The fund works differently from much of the federal budget. Drivers pay the gas tax at the pump as part of the price of each gallon. That money is credited to the trust fund instead of being pooled with general Treasury revenue. Spending from the fund is reserved for surface transportation.

Congress created the fund in 1956, the same year it authorized the Interstate Highway System. Lawmakers set its spending programs through surface transportation laws that typically cover several years at a time.

The fund has two parts. The Highway Account pays for building, repairing and replacing roads and bridges. The Mass Transit Account, added in 1982, supports bus and rail systems in cities and regions.

The federal government builds very little of this itself. The money reaches the ground mainly as grants to state and local governments. Those governments build and maintain most of the country's roads. They choose and plan projects, hire contractors and handle routine upkeep.

Two agencies inside the Department of Transportation handle the grants. The Federal Highway Administration oversees road and bridge funding. The Federal Transit Administration oversees money for transit systems.

The gas tax is a fixed charge per gallon, not a percentage of the pump price. Revenue depends on how many gallons are sold, not on what each gallon costs. A jump in fuel prices does not increase the tax collected on a gallon.

The rate is also not indexed to inflation, so each cent buys less construction over time. Cars that burn less fuel pay less tax per mile driven. Fully electric vehicles pay no federal gasoline tax at all.

Fuel taxes alone have not covered what the fund pays out. In recent years, Congress has transferred money from general revenue to keep the fund able to meet its obligations. As a result, part of the cost of highways and transit falls on taxpayers generally, not only on drivers at the pump.

The National Institutes of Health, part of the Department of Health and Human Services, funds biomedical research at universities, medical schools and laboratories across the U.S. NASA and the National Science Foundation pay for much of the government's other scientific work, from space missions to basic research in physics, biology and engineering.

All three agencies are funded with discretionary money. Their budgets can rise, fall or stay flat from one fiscal year to the next, depending on what Congress appropriates.

The agencies sit in different spending bills. NIH funding moves through the bill covering the departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education. NASA and the National Science Foundation are both funded through the Commerce, Justice, Science bill.

Most NIH money leaves the agency. It goes out as competitive grants to researchers at outside institutions, a category known as extramural research. Applications go through peer review. Panels of outside scientists score proposals before funding decisions are made. NIH also runs its own intramural research program, with government scientists working largely at its main campus in Bethesda, Maryland.

The agency is organized into 27 institutes and centers. Each one focuses on a disease, an organ system or a field of study. The National Cancer Institute and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases are two examples.

The National Science Foundation is an independent agency created by the National Science Foundation Act of 1950. It supports basic research and science education across most nonmedical fields, including mathematics, computer science, geosciences and the social sciences. It awards its funding largely through grants chosen by merit review. It also supports large research facilities, including telescopes and the research stations of the U.S. Antarctic Program.

NASA was created under the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958. Its budget covers human spaceflight as well as science. The Science Mission Directorate oversees work that includes planetary science, Earth science, astrophysics and heliophysics, the study of the sun and its effects across the solar system. Its missions are built and run by NASA centers working with contractors and university partners.

Grants to universities generally cover two kinds of cost. Direct costs pay for salaries, equipment and supplies tied to a specific project. Indirect costs, also called facilities and administrative costs, cover shared expenses such as buildings, utilities and regulatory compliance. Each institution negotiates its indirect cost rate with the government.

Science funding is not limited to these three agencies. The Department of Energy's Office of Science supports a network of national laboratories. The Department of Agriculture funds research on crops, food safety and farming.

The federal government pays for its spending mainly with three taxes: individual income taxes, payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare, and corporate income taxes. Smaller levies add to those receipts, and the Treasury borrows whatever they do not cover.

The individual income tax has been a permanent part of the federal system since the 16th Amendment was ratified in 1913. It applies graduated rates to wages, salaries, business profits and investment income. Most workers pay it through withholding from each paycheck. The Internal Revenue Service collects it along with payroll taxes.

Payroll taxes follow a different logic. They are tied to wages and earmarked for specific programs. The money is credited to dedicated trust funds instead of being pooled with general revenue.

Corporate income taxes fall on the profits of companies organized as C corporations. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 replaced graduated corporate rates with a single flat rate, effective in 2018. Many businesses, including partnerships and S corporations, pass their income through to their owners. Those owners report it on individual returns and pay individual income tax on it instead.

Smaller streams round out federal receipts. Excise taxes apply to specific goods and activities, such as gasoline, tobacco, alcohol and airline tickets. Customs duties are tariffs on imported goods, collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection. When the Federal Reserve earns more than it spends on its own operations, it sends the excess to the Treasury.

Revenue has fallen short of spending in nearly every recent year. To make up each year's gap, the Treasury sells securities to investors, including individuals, pension funds, banks and foreign governments. Treasury bills mature in a year or less, notes in two to 10 years, and bonds in 20 or 30 years.

That borrowing accumulates in the national debt until it is repaid. A year in which revenue exceeded spending would produce a surplus instead, which could be used to pay down debt held by the public.

Congress also sets a statutory debt limit, a cap on the total amount the Treasury may borrow. The limit does not authorize new spending. It determines whether the Treasury can borrow to pay for obligations Congress has already approved. Raising or suspending the limit requires separate legislation.

#5472. The White House isn't retreating on tariffs after an election wipeout

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Aide Jim Goyer said the administration will continue its pace, while Gary Cohn called tariffs a consumption tax on U.S. consumers

Jim Goyer, director of the White House Office of Public Liaison, spoke at the B20 USA Summit in Washington on Tuesday and said the administration will keep up its tariff pace through the end of President Donald Trump's term, according to CNBC.

Goyer argued that tariffs help bring industrial production back home, make supply lines more reliable and safeguard the country's security, according to CNBC. "We are just getting started," Goyer said.

Gary Cohn, IBM $IBM vice chairman and former director of the National Economic Council, offered a different view in an onstage interview with POLITICO Playbook co-author Dasha Burns at the summit. "Tariffs are a consumption tax on the U.S. consumer… The producers and the importers don't pay the tariff," Cohn said.

Cohn cited aluminum tariffs as an example. "You and I, if we're buying a new car, we are eating that cost," he said. On the elections, Cohn said, "The U.S. consumer voted their financial well-being."

Cohn believes Republicans and Democrats could reach a compromise on trade, according to CNBC. Cohn proposed that Trump and the Democrats who will soon control Congress could lock in permanent safeguards aimed at China, while tariffs on Canada are scaled back.

Dow Executive Chairman Jim Fitterling took the other side, according to CNBC. He conceded that tariffs can push prices higher but called them essential for guarding against unfair competition and defending domestic manufacturing.

Democrats emerged from the Nov. 3 midterm elections with their biggest Senate and House majorities since at least 2008, according to Reuters. They assume control once the incoming Congress is seated on Jan. 3.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday showed that 62% of Americans favor rolling back Trump's tariffs, according to Reuters. The poll put Trump's approval rating at 32%.

Democrats intend to take on the tariffs once they are running Congress in January, according to CNBC. Trump's ability to veto legislation, along with his sweeping authority over trade, could make the duties hard to undo.

Price pressures are building as the debate unfolds. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October after a 0.6% increase in September. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3%, matching September and August. Gasoline prices rose 37.4% over 12 months.

#5471. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5470. Why Is Crypto Down? Jensen Huang Chinese Spy Scandal Sends AI Stocks Into Chaos

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

We’re back to the same question again: Why is crypto down? Bitcoin and altcoins are taking another beating as Wall Street’s AI trade starts unraveling. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is now at the center of a growing Chinese espionage scandal. His alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset has put the world’s most valuable chipmaker under fresh scrutiny.

The timing could hardly be worse for investors. Technology stocks have already suffered a brutal selloff, with the Nasdaq entering correction territory. Nvidia shares plunged 9.3% during Thursday’s rout, while semiconductor stocks suffered their worst session in years.

NEW: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admits to cheating on his wife two days after a report dropped that U.S. intelligence believes he had a relationship with a Chinese spy."I was unfaithful to my wife," Huang said in a letter to Nvidia staff."My actions hurt her and our children.… pic.twitter.com/moB9B3nYlI

Now, an investigation into Huang’s personal and professional connections could introduce another shock. If confidence in Nvidia starts cracking, the consequences could extend well beyond the AI industry. Bitcoin and the wider crypto market are already feeling the pressure.

The latest crypto selloff follows a dramatic reversal across US technology markets. Bitcoin erased its post-election rally, falling below $75,000. Ethereum dropped more than 7%, while XRP and Solana also suffered heavy losses.

The Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.5% during the same session. The Nasdaq 100 lost 6.4%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index crashed 12%. Nvidia and AMD were among the biggest casualties.

This selloff has been DEVASTATING.The AI stocks have erased $13.2 TRILLION in market value from stocks’ 2026 highs.Only U.S and China have an annual GDP larger than that loss.Market value erased at six AI giants:– Alphabet: $1.62 trillion lost (−32%)– Nvidia: $1.49… pic.twitter.com/i065m2W4b4

More than $2.5 trillion in Nasdaq market cap disappeared during October. Investors are increasingly questioning if massive AI infrastructure investments will deliver sufficient returns. Major technology companies continue pouring billions into chips, data centers, and computing infrastructure.

Then add political uncertainty, which is adding another headache. Democrats secured control of both congressional chambers during the US midterm elections. Investors now fear greater opposition to data center expansion and potentially tougher regulatory scrutiny.

The resulting selloff has exposed how closely crypto trades with speculative technology investments. Bitcoin increasingly moves alongside high-growth equities when institutional investors adjust their risk exposure.

The damage has also spread into derivatives markets. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions disappeared during Thursday’s selloff. Most liquidations involved traders betting on higher prices.

That forced selling can quickly turn an ordinary correction into something considerably uglier. As Bitcoin falls, liquidations push prices lower and expose leveraged altcoin positions to further losses.

Nvidia’s problems have suddenly become considerably more personal. The company’s board announced an independent investigation yesterday. It wants to examine reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

The controversy involves Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed. US authorities reportedly suspected her of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

Megaspeed has also faced scrutiny over allegations involving access to advanced Nvidia chips restricted from export to China. Republican lawmakers have requested a briefing from Huang regarding the allegations.

Separately, Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife. He apologized to his family and colleagues, accepting responsibility for his actions.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang sends a company-wide email regarding his recently reported relationship with a Chinese spy. pic.twitter.com/NTdoSgaxoy

The combination creates an uncomfortable situation for Nvidia shareholders. Huang is not simply another corporate executive. He remains the public face of the AI revolution and one of its most influential decision-makers.

A prolonged investigation could introduce uncertainty around Nvidia’s leadership, relationships with international customers, and exposure to geopolitical tensions.

Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. However, the investigation could keep the controversy alive while investors are already questioning AI valuations.

The biggest concern for crypto is what happens if the AI selloff spreads. Nvidia has become a central pillar of the global technology investment cycle. Its chips power the infrastructure behind many of the world’s largest AI projects.

If investors begin questioning the sustainability of that investment cycle, semiconductor stocks, data center operators, and technology companies could face another round of selling.

Bitcoin is particularly exposed because institutional investors increasingly treat it as part of their risk portfolios. When confidence disappears from technology markets, crypto often loses buyers alongside speculative equities.

The Binance security incident has added another source of pressure. The exchange’s clients withdrew approximately $6.1 billion following the exchange’s recent security breach.

That creates an uncomfortable combination of falling institutional confidence, weaker market liquidity, and leveraged positions being forced out. Bitcoin now needs a recovery in risk appetite to regain momentum. Otherwise, another wave of technology stock selling could drag crypto prices lower.

So why is crypto down? The AI market has a new problem to deal with, and Bitcoin is discovering that Nvidia’s troubles can become its troubles too.

#5469. Homeowners are tapping home equity lines of credit at the fastest pace in decades

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Total U.S. household debt rose 1.8% to $19.1 trillion in the quarter, and 5.0% of outstanding debt was in some stage of delinquency

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported that home equity line of credit balances rose $23 billion in the third quarter, the biggest quarterly jump since 2005. The figures come from the bank's Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit, released on Tuesday.

Home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balances totaled $481 billion at the end of the quarter, up $59 billion from a year earlier. HELOC limits rose $31 billion in the quarter, continuing an expansion that began in 2022.

The quarterly rise was the 18th in a row, according to CNBC.

Total household debt grew $334 billion, or 1.8%, to $19.1 trillion. Mortgage balances increased $257 billion to $13.4 trillion, and mortgage originations reached $595 billion.

"Household debt levels rose moderately, led by increases in mortgage and home equity line of credit originations," Donghoon Lee, economic research advisor at the New York Fed, said in a statement. "Although delinquency transition rates for housing debts have crept up, the overall credit quality of these loans remains strong."

Overall, 5.0% of outstanding debt was in some stage of delinquency, up 0.3 percentage point from the previous quarter. The share of HELOC balances moving into serious delinquency, meaning 90 days or more past due, was 1.17%, compared with 1.27% a year earlier.

The increase in HELOC balances is occurring while the housing market remains stagnant and numerous owners are unwilling to trade away their low mortgage rates, according to CNBC. HELOCs let borrowers draw on their equity while keeping those rates.

"HELOCs let them borrow against their equity without giving up the low interest rate on their home," certified financial planner Douglas Boneparth, president and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, told CNBC.

HELOCs generally carry variable interest rates, according to CNBC. The average rate on a $30,000 HELOC stood at 7.49% on Nov. 4. Many HELOCs have a draw period during which borrowers typically pay only interest, followed by a repayment period that adds principal.

"Payments potentially could double overnight, and you really want to know that before you sign anything," Boneparth said.

The housing market has weakened since mortgage rates returned to 7% in mid-September, and an index tracking contract signings for previously owned homes hit a record low in September. Thirty-year mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, 110 basis points above a year earlier.
